items.title: Every Price Is a Hypothesis. I Built an Open-Source AI Agent Workflow to Test It
items.summary: What happens when competitor research, customer value, buyer preferences, demand analysis and delivery economics become parts of one pricing investigation? I asked an AI agent to price a fictional invoice tool. It refused to guess a number. It asked me seven questions first, and later its own devil’s advocate reviewer caught two mistakes in its work. That refusal to guess is the whole point of what I built. A pricing decision usually begins with a number. A competitor charges €49. Another charges €79. The finance team wants a particular gross margin. Someone suggests €59. But what supports that number? Competitor prices tell us what other businesses charge, not necessarily what customers value. Cost models tell us what a business needs to earn, not what a buyer will pay. Surveys reveal stated preferences, which may differ from purchasing behaviour. Historical transactions show what happened under previous conditions, but do not automatically explain what would happen at another price. Each method answers a different question. Pricing decisions often combine their outputs without checking whether the evidence is comparable or whether the methods support the conclusion. I built Value Pricing as an open-source research workflow for investigating those questions. It brings together market references, customer value, buyer research, demand analysis and delivery economics. It does not calculate a universally optimal price. It helps document the evidence behind a pricing decision, identify conflicts between methods and turn findings into hypotheses that can be tested with buyers. If you want to follow along, the walkthrough near the end installs the plugin, runs a pricing study for a fictional product in three prompts, and shows which reviewer agents it calls and what they concluded. Pricing is a research problem Consider a fictional B2B software company reconsidering its pricing structure. It wants to know what comparable alternatives charge, which capabilities differentiate its offering, how much economic value the service creates, which buyer segments value those outcomes, how usage affects delivery costs and how observed transaction quantities vary with realised prices. These questions require different evidence. A competitor comparison cannot establish willingness to pay. A value model cannot establish whether the business can deliver profitably. A simulated buyer panel cannot establish real purchasing behavior. Figure 1. Market observations, economic value models, simulated buyer research and real-buyer validation contribute different kinds of evidence to a pricing decision. Image by author. Define the decision before selecting methods The first stage is discovery. Before selecting a research method, the workflow needs to understand what is sold, who buys it and what decision the business needs to make. A usage-based software service requires different research from a professional-services retainer or a one-off digital product. The billing unit, customer segments, alternatives and distinction between buyer and user all affect the research design. A study can be configured using a structured YAML specification: decision: question: "Evaluate the current pricing structure" constraints: - "Maintain delivery profitability" offering: id: example-service name: "Example Service" description: null business_model: null market: geography: null target_market: null alternatives: [] currency: EUR segments: axis: null bands: [] research: methods: [] scenarios: [] sensitivity_assumptions: {} validation_requirements: [] This is intentionally incomplete. It does not supply fictional market prices, customer shares or operating costs. Those inputs must come from the business or be labelled as assumptions in a synthetic exercise. A blank field should remain a gap until somebody provides evidence. Figure 2. Study configuration and method selection: define the decision, offering and buyers, assess the available evidence, then either select methods or record evidence gaps. Image by author. Understand the market before estimating a premium A competitor comparison needs more than a list of prices. One vendor might charge €30 per month for a limited number of transactions. Another might charge €80 for a larger allowance, priority support and additional capabilities. Comparing those numbers without considering scope, billing units and commercial terms can produce misleading conclusions. Value Pricing records market references with their source, observation date, geography, commercial terms and relevant attributes. It distinguishes public prices from quote-based and undisclosed pricing. Hedonic price analysis When enough comparable offers are available, a hedonic model can investigate the association between product attributes and listed prices: ln(Pᵢ) = β₀ + Σⱼ₌₁ᵏ βⱼXᵢⱼ + εᵢ Here, Pᵢ is the observed listed price, Xᵢⱼ represents an attribute of offering i, and βⱼ estimates the association between that attribute and price. The coefficients are not automatically causal premiums. An attribute may appear alongside other capabilities, different customer segments or different commercial terms. A synthetic recovery test The repository includes a synthetic market fixture that generates 260 fictional vendors, multiple plans per vendor, structured product attributes, public and quote-based offers, usage allowances and random price variation. Three planted attribute effects are: Delivery scope: +0.50 Service quality: +0.45 Outcome measurement: +0.60 These are constructed values, not estimates from an actual market. The self-test checks whether the estimated coefficients’ 90% confidence intervals contain the planted values. It also tests a planted relationship between usage allowances and listed prices. Figure 3. Synthetic hedonic model recovery: a fixture with planted log-price coefficients is estimated, and the self-test checks whether the 90% intervals contain the planted values. Image by author. Estimate customer value independently of market prices Market references establish what alternatives charge. They do not establish what an alternative is worth to a particular buyer. Economic Value to the Customer (EVC) compares an offering with the buyer’s next-best alternative, considering the economic outcomes that differ between them. Suppose a fictional software service reduces manual work. A basic value model might be: V = H × C × R Where: H is the number of hours saved. C is the economic cost per hour. R is the proportion of theoretical savings that can actually be realised. The realisation term matters. A system might theoretically save 100 hours, but if the customer can convert only 60% of those hours into productive capacity, treating all 100 hours as realised financial value overstates the benefit. Value Pricing includes a configurable Monte Carlo workflow for scenarios where uncertainty can be represented meaningfully. The model examines how different assumptions affect the resulting value distribution. The result is a modelled value estimate, not an observed willingness-to-pay figure. Figure 4. From customer outcomes to a value distribution. The model connects the next-best alternative, operational savings, financial conversion and uncertainty assumptions to produce a distribution of modelled economic value. Image by author. Investigate buyer preferences without confusing simulation with research Customers may value functionality, implementation support, service quality or different access levels. Their preferences do not necessarily translate into the same willingness to pay for every feature. The workflow supports qualitative interviews, price-sensitivity research, Van Westendorp, Gabor-Granger, choice-based conjoint and exploratory simulated buyer research. These methods answer different questions. Van Westendorp investigates perceived price acceptability. Gabor-Granger examines stated purchase likelihood across presented prices. Choice-based conjoint investigates preferences across combinations of attributes and prices. Testing the conjoint implementation The repository includes a synthetic panel test with planted willingness-to-pay contributions: Access level: $25 Service level: $30 Onboarding: $8 Support: $5 The fixture creates synthetic respondents and choice tasks with controlled preferences. The test runs the panel analysis and conjoint estimation, then checks whether the estimated willingness-to-pay contribution for the service-level attribute falls within a specified tolerance of its planted value. Simulated buyers can help pilot questions, identify confusing terms and generate hypotheses. They are not a substitute for human respondents or observed behaviour, and their outputs should not be reported as empirical findings or demand forecasts. Figure 5. Synthetic conjoint experiment: attribute and price design, generated choice tasks, respondent selections, estimated willingness to pay and comparison with planted values. Image by author. Separate listed-price elasticity from transaction demand elasticity The word elasticity appears in different parts of pricing research, but it does not always describe the same relationship. Market-meter elasticity The market analysis can investigate how listed prices vary with a competitor’s usage allowance or another pricing metric. The synthetic market fixture plants an elasticity of 0.75 for usage-based pricing. The self-test checks whether the implementation recovers that relationship within a tolerance of 0.05. This concerns the relationship between market-listed prices and plan limits. It is not customer demand elasticity. Transaction-based demand elasticity A separate module examines how observed transaction quantities vary with realised unit prices: ε = (% change in quantity) / (% change in realised unit price) Equivalently: ε = (%ΔQ) / (%ΔP) The repository implements a hierarchical Bayesian negative-binomial model. It accounts for repeated customer transactions, partial pooling across segments, seasonality and available controls such as promotions, channel and contract duration. The synthetic demand fixture creates two fictional customer segments, 36 customers per segment and 12 monthly observations per customer. It plants a price elasticity of −0.80 and introduces deliberately invalid rows to test data validation. The self-test checks whether segment-level estimates recover the planted value within a defined tolerance, whether their 90% posterior intervals contain the known value, whether convergence diagnostics pass, and whether insufficient price variation blocks estimation. The model conditions on observed positive transactions, so it does not estimate purchase incidence. Historical prices may also be endogenous. Without a defensible identification design, the result is an observational association, not a causal estimate. Figure 6. Transaction elasticity. The synthetic fixture supplies a planted price-response relationship, while the hierarchical Bayesian model estimates segment-level responses and posterior uncertainty. Predictions are conditional on observed positive transactions. Image by author. Bring delivery economics into the decision A price can appeal to customers and still be commercially unsustainable. The cost model investigates what it takes to deliver the offering. Depending on the business, inputs can include infrastructure, support, onboarding, labour, payment processing, channel commissions, fixed platform costs and capacity constraints. The model calculates cost and contribution scenarios using configured inputs. Cost is an independent constraint in the research. It should not automatically determine what customers should pay. A cost-plus calculation can establish a minimum commercially viable price under stated assumptions, but it cannot establish perceived customer value. Figure 7. Customer value and delivery economics stay separate evidence streams and are combined only when evaluating candidate pricing structures. Image by author. Synthesis: keep the evidence streams separate Imagine an investigation produces several observations: competitor listings suggest an association between certain capabilities and higher prices; the EVC model suggests that one customer outcome creates potential economic value; buyer research indicates a preference for additional support; transaction analysis suggests that observed quantity declines as realised prices increase; and delivery economics shows that additional support has a meaningful cost. None independently determines the price. The synthesis stage brings the findings together while retaining their separate evidence bases. It should expose disagreements rather than hide them in a weighted average. The handover records the decision, selected methods and rationale, evidence and source dates, modelled results and uncertainty, assumptions, unresolved gaps, candidate pricing hypotheses where supported, trade-offs and a validation plan. A model-selected candidate remains conditional on its inputs. It is not a guaranteed optimal price. How the implementation is organised Value Pricing is an open-source Agent Skill with supporting Python analysis tools. Its structure separates workflow instructions, method references, configurable templates and analytical scripts. Intake: Define the offering, buyer, decision and evidence Market research: Competitor references, attribute comparison and hedonic analysis Customer value: EVC, scenario modelling and sensitivity Buyer research: Price sensitivity and conjoint methods Demand analysis: Transaction-based price-response modelling Cost analysis: Cost-to-serve and contribution Synthesis: Compare evidence and evaluate candidate structures Validation: Define real-world tests and decision criteria The project includes specialised perspectives such as a pricing strategist, competitive analyst, behavioural economist, buyer persona, CFO/unit-economics reviewer and devil’s advocate. These perspectives structure different questions; they are not independent experts or empirical evidence. The implementation includes data-handling safeguards. Scripts run only when invoked. Crawling is optional. External model calls require explicit confirmation of data transfer. The workflow is designed to work without sending confidential study material to a model provider. Repository: https://github.com/C-Kapsalis/value-pricing Calibration against published research The repository includes an optional calibration procedure based on Brand, Israeli and Ngwe’s Using LLMs for Market Research (Harvard Business School Working Paper 23–062). The procedure is designed to reproduce selected choice tasks using original study materials and compare simulated willingness-to-pay estimates with a human-research benchmark. The calibration script requires the relevant choice sets and original prompt template as inputs; these materials are not bundled with the repository. It generates repeated prompts, processes responses and estimates willingness to pay using a multinomial logit model. It reports a bootstrap 90% confidence interval and the ratio between the simulated estimate and the supplied human benchmark. The procedure does not automatically adjust the main study’s estimates. Its existence should not be confused with a completed calibration experiment. Figure 8. Calibration workflow: published human choice tasks and prompt materials, repeated simulated responses, estimated willingness to pay and comparison against the human benchmark. Image by author. Walkthrough: install it and run a pricing study in three prompts To show what the workflow does in practice, I installed it into Claude Code and ran a study for a fictional product: Ledgerly, an invoice-reconciliation tool for small accounting firms that charges $49 per firm per month and is considering tiers based on invoice volume. Below are the exact prompts I typed and what happened after each one. An agent will not phrase things identically on your machine, but the steps, files and checks will be the same. Step 1: Install In Claude Code, add the marketplace and install the plugin: /plugin marketplace add C-Kapsalis/value-pricing /plugin install value-pricing@value-pricing In Codex or another Agent Skills client, run npx skills add C-Kapsalis/value-pricing. The install adds one skill (value-pricing), a /value-pricing command and seven reviewer agents: a pricing strategist, competitive analyst, buyer persona, CFO, behavioural economist, go-to-market lead and devil's advocate. The analysis scripts need Python 3.12 or later and the packages in the skill's requirements file; the agent can set that up, or you can do it yourself: python3.12 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install -r skills/value-pricing/scripts/requirements.txt Step 2: Describe the decision in plain language Help me research pricing for our product. Ledgerly is a (fictional) invoice-reconciliation tool for small accounting firms. Today it costs $49 per firm per month, flat. We’re deciding whether to move to tiers based on the number of invoices a firm processes each month. No slash command was needed. Claude Code matched the request to the skill and loaded value-pricing on its own, then read the skill's intake guide (references/1-intake.md). It did not run anything. Instead, it asked whether I wanted to work from real data or from labelled assumptions, followed by seven discovery questions. The first three: How many invoices do firms process each month? Tier cut-offs are only defensible if they follow the real distribution. Why change now? Heavy users costing too much, money left on the table, or $49 being too high for tiny firms each lead to a different design. Does cost grow with invoices? If it is mostly flat, the case for tiers rests on value, not margin. This is the behaviour I designed for: scope the decision before choosing methods, and never fill a gap with a plausible-sounding number. Step 3: Answer, and let it build the study Option B. Assumptions: 300 firms, US, USD, monthly self-serve billing. Invoice volume per firm per month: under 100 for 45% of firms, 100 to 500 for 40%, over 500 for 15%. Variable cost is OCR at $0.02 per invoice plus about 20 minutes of support per firm per month at $30 an hour. Ledgerly saves about 3 minutes of staff time per invoice at $40 an hour […] Constraint: no existing customer’s bill can rise more than 30% in year one. We have no customer research. Set up the study and run the value and cost phases. The agent created a pricing-study/ folder from the skill's templates (study.yaml, offering.yaml, costs.yaml, value_drivers.yaml) and started a DECISIONS.md log that records each ruling and who made it. It ran the bundled cost_model.py. For value, it chose not to use the bundled Monte Carlo script and logged why: with a single value driver, splitting value across features would be meaningless. It wrote a small study-specific model instead. The headline results: 50 (light): modelled value per month $100; $49 as a share of value 49% 300 (mid): modelled value per month $600; $49 as a share of value 8% 1,000 (heavy): modelled value per month $2,000; $49 as a share of value 2.5% Value only passes $49 at about 25 invoices a month, or about 130 in the pessimistic case. Light firms are 45% of customers but about 8% of total value; heavy firms are 15% of customers and about 51% of value. At $49, variable cost only exceeds price above about 1,950 invoices a month. If support time grows with volume, that drops to about 920. The binding constraint is the 30% cap: existing firms can go to at most $63.70 in year one. It also listed the inputs that would change the answer most, starting with the real distribution of invoices per firm. Step 4: Draft tiers and convene the council Draft two or three tier structures that respect the 30% cap, then convene the pricing council to critique them and tell me which one to test first. The agent drafted three structures in proposals.yaml, modelled them against the 300 firms and wrote a council dossier. It then spawned five of the seven reviewer agents in parallel. It left out the competitive analyst because no market phase had been run, and the buyer persona because there was no persona evidence, which would have made its answers pure invention. A: Rebalance: pricing $39 / $59 / $99; year-2 revenue +14%; largest year-2 jump +102% (heavy) B: Keep $49 floor: pricing $49 / $79 / $149; year-2 revenue +55%; largest year-2 jump +204% (heavy) C: Base plus usage: pricing $29 incl. 25 invoices, then $0.10 each; year-2 revenue +14%; largest year-2 jump +158% (heavy) The reviewers disagreed in a useful way. The pricing strategist, behavioural economist and go-to-market lead favoured A, because cutting the light tier to $39 gives 45% of firms good news in the migration message. The CFO and the devil’s advocate favoured B, because the $1,350 a month lost on light firms is certain while the gains elsewhere are assumed. All five agreed that invoices processed is the right unit, that single-month tiering would swing with tax season, and that the real risk is the year-two jump once the cap expires. The devil’s advocate also caught two mistakes in the main agent’s own work: a claim in the dossier that the heavy tier became unprofitable at 2,500 invoices, and an unknown that had not been saved to the cost file. The agent corrected both and re-ran the cost model before answering. The final recommendation was an adjusted structure, A+, tested on new sign-ups only: Starter: up to 100 invoices for $39. Practice: up to 500 invoices for $59, then $0.08 per extra invoice. Tiers based on a three-month average, so tax season does not push firms up and down. Existing firms capped at $63.70 in year one and $82.81 in year two, with a bill preview and 60 days’ notice. A 60–90 day test against the previous $49 cohort, with explicit pass criteria and a kill rule: pause the migration if 9 or more mid-volume firms cancel or downgrade within 90 days. Its first action item was free: pull twelve months of invoice counts per firm from the OCR logs, because that one input decides between A and B. Under the hood: the statistical self-test The Ledgerly run used the value and cost tools. The heavier statistical methods (hedonic regression, Bayesian demand elasticity, choice-based conjoint) are checked by a self-test that builds a synthetic study with known answers and verifies that each method recovers them: python tests/selftest_value_pricing.py --dir ./demo-study On my run, all 18 checks passed: Hedonic premium: delivery scope: planted +0.50; recovered +0.51 (90% interval 0.36 to 0.66) Hedonic premium: outcome measurement: planted +0.60; recovered +0.63 (0.46 to 0.79) Demand elasticity, two segments: planted −0.80; recovered −0.83 and −0.79 Conjoint WTP, premium service level: planted $44.1; recovered $41.7 (81% of held-out choices predicted, 25% by chance) Not everything was perfect. One hedonic premium came out 0.09 high, and the conjoint estimates run slightly low across the board. The self-test also leaves a full study in demo-study/. Its synthesis flags that competitor prices ($103 to $130) sit above what the value model says any segment could capture ($22 to $71), and that the large segment has no defensible price window at all. That is the behaviour the synthesis stage exists for: when evidence streams conflict, it shows the conflict instead of averaging it away. What the tests establish, and what they do not The synthetic self-test checks analytical components against known values. It does not establish that competitor listings represent transaction prices, synthetic buyers behave like real customers, modelled value becomes realised benefit, historical price relationships are causal, or a recommended structure will maximise revenue. The quality of the workflow depends on the research design and inputs. A sophisticated model cannot compensate for an incorrectly defined segment, a misleading counterfactual or a poorly measured cost driver. What I want to improve next I want to validate the methods against appropriately sourced real pricing studies, improve how evidence quality is represented across research streams, and develop a more complete treatment of purchase incidence. I also want to make the handover between analytical components easier to inspect. A reader should be able to trace a pricing hypothesis back to its source evidence, assumptions, model and uncertainty. Try the workflow Value Pricing is available at https://github.com/C-Kapsalis/value-pricing . The repository includes the Agent Skill, specialised perspectives, configurable study templates, Python analysis scripts, synthetic self-tests and method references. Consult the README and tests/selftest_value_pricing.py for setup and execution details. Disclosure: I am the author of Value Pricing. The project and synthetic examples discussed here are independent open-source work. Synthetic figures and test data are illustrative; they are not customer research, market benchmarks or evidence of commercial pricing performance. The objective is to make the reasoning behind a pricing decision explicit, reproducible and open to challenge. If you’ve made a pricing call recently, what evidence did you lean on, and what did you wish you had? Tell me in the replies. I’m looking for real cases to test the workflow against. References [1] J. Brand, A. Israeli and D. Ngwe, Using LLMs for Market Research (2023), Harvard Business School Working Paper 23–062 This story was drafted on TK . Christoforos (Chris) Kapsalis is a technical author and marketer with a passion for building open-source tools that will hopefully help businesses in disadvantaged parts of the world or run by members of disadvantaged communities improve their workflows and maximize the value generated by their marketing efforts. Every Price Is a Hypothesis. I Built an Open-Source AI Agent Workflow to Test It was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

When enough comparable offers are available, a hedonic model can investigate the association between product attributes and listed prices:

ln(Pᵢ) = β₀ + Σⱼ₌₁ᵏ βⱼXᵢⱼ + εᵢ

Here, Pᵢ is the observed listed price, Xᵢⱼ represents an attribute of offering i, and βⱼ estimates the association between that attribute and price.

The coefficients are not automatically causal premiums. An attribute may appear alongside other capabilities, different customer segments or different commercial terms.

A synthetic recovery test

The repository includes a synthetic market fixture that generates 260 fictional vendors, multiple plans per vendor, structured product attributes, public and quote-based offers, usage allowances and random price variation.

Three planted attribute effects are:

  • Delivery scope: +0.50
  • Service quality: +0.45
  • Outcome measurement: +0.60

These are constructed values, not estimates from an actual market. The self-test checks whether the estimated coefficients’ 90% confidence intervals contain the planted values. It also tests a planted relationship between usage allowances and listed prices.

Figure 3. Synthetic hedonic model recovery: a fixture with planted log-price coefficients is estimated, and the self-test checks whether the 90% intervals contain the planted values. Image by author.Estimate customer value independently of market prices

Market references establish what alternatives charge. They do not establish what an alternative is worth to a particular buyer.

Economic Value to the Customer (EVC) compares an offering with the buyer’s next-best alternative, considering the economic outcomes that differ between them.

Suppose a fictional software service reduces manual work. A basic value model might be:

V = H × C × R

Where:

  • H is the number of hours saved.
  • C is the economic cost per hour.
  • R is the proportion of theoretical savings that can actually be realised.

The realisation term matters. A system might theoretically save 100 hours, but if the customer can convert only 60% of those hours into productive capacity, treating all 100 hours as realised financial value overstates the benefit.

Value Pricing includes a configurable Monte Carlo workflow for scenarios where uncertainty can be represented meaningfully. The model examines how different assumptions affect the resulting value distribution.

The result is a modelled value estimate, not an observed willingness-to-pay figure.

Figure 4. From customer outcomes to a value distribution. The model connects the next-best alternative, operational savings, financial conversion and uncertainty assumptions to produce a distribution of modelled economic value. Image by author.Investigate buyer preferences without confusing simulation with research

Customers may value functionality, implementation support, service quality or different access levels. Their preferences do not necessarily translate into the same willingness to pay for every feature.

The workflow supports qualitative interviews, price-sensitivity research, Van Westendorp, Gabor-Granger, choice-based conjoint and exploratory simulated buyer research.

These methods answer different questions. Van Westendorp investigates perceived price acceptability. Gabor-Granger examines stated purchase likelihood across presented prices. Choice-based conjoint investigates preferences across combinations of attributes and prices.

Testing the conjoint implementation

The repository includes a synthetic panel test with planted willingness-to-pay contributions:

  • Access level: $25
  • Service level: $30
  • Onboarding: $8
  • Support: $5

The fixture creates synthetic respondents and choice tasks with controlled preferences. The test runs the panel analysis and conjoint estimation, then checks whether the estimated willingness-to-pay contribution for the service-level attribute falls within a specified tolerance of its planted value.

Simulated buyers can help pilot questions, identify confusing terms and generate hypotheses. They are not a substitute for human respondents or observed behaviour, and their outputs should not be reported as empirical findings or demand forecasts.

Figure 5. Synthetic conjoint experiment: attribute and price design, generated choice tasks, respondent selections, estimated willingness to pay and comparison with planted values. Image by author.Separate listed-price elasticity from transaction demand elasticity

The word elasticity appears in different parts of pricing research, but it does not always describe the same relationship.

Market-meter elasticity

The market analysis can investigate how listed prices vary with a competitor’s usage allowance or another pricing metric. The synthetic market fixture plants an elasticity of 0.75 for usage-based pricing. The self-test checks whether the implementation recovers that relationship within a tolerance of 0.05.

This concerns the relationship between market-listed prices and plan limits. It is not customer demand elasticity.

Transaction-based demand elasticity

A separate module examines how observed transaction quantities vary with realised unit prices:

ε = (% change in quantity) / (% change in realised unit price)

Equivalently:

ε = (%ΔQ) / (%ΔP)

The repository implements a hierarchical Bayesian negative-binomial model. It accounts for repeated customer transactions, partial pooling across segments, seasonality and available controls such as promotions, channel and contract duration.

The synthetic demand fixture creates two fictional customer segments, 36 customers per segment and 12 monthly observations per customer. It plants a price elasticity of −0.80 and introduces deliberately invalid rows to test data validation.

The self-test checks whether segment-level estimates recover the planted value within a defined tolerance, whether their 90% posterior intervals contain the known value, whether convergence diagnostics pass, and whether insufficient price variation blocks estimation.

The model conditions on observed positive transactions, so it does not estimate purchase incidence. Historical prices may also be endogenous. Without a defensible identification design, the result is an observational association, not a causal estimate.

Figure 6. Transaction elasticity. The synthetic fixture supplies a planted price-response relationship, while the hierarchical Bayesian model estimates segment-level responses and posterior uncertainty. Predictions are conditional on observed positive transactions. Image by author.Bring delivery economics into the decision

A price can appeal to customers and still be commercially unsustainable.

The cost model investigates what it takes to deliver the offering. Depending on the business, inputs can include infrastructure, support, onboarding, labour, payment processing, channel commissions, fixed platform costs and capacity constraints.

The model calculates cost and contribution scenarios using configured inputs. Cost is an independent constraint in the research. It should not automatically determine what customers should pay. A cost-plus calculation can establish a minimum commercially viable price under stated assumptions, but it cannot establish perceived customer value.

Figure 7. Customer value and delivery economics stay separate evidence streams and are combined only when evaluating candidate pricing structures. Image by author.Synthesis: keep the evidence streams separate

Imagine an investigation produces several observations: competitor listings suggest an association between certain capabilities and higher prices; the EVC model suggests that one customer outcome creates potential economic value; buyer research indicates a preference for additional support; transaction analysis suggests that observed quantity declines as realised prices increase; and delivery economics shows that additional support has a meaningful cost.

None independently determines the price.

The synthesis stage brings the findings together while retaining their separate evidence bases. It should expose disagreements rather than hide them in a weighted average.

The handover records the decision, selected methods and rationale, evidence and source dates, modelled results and uncertainty, assumptions, unresolved gaps, candidate pricing hypotheses where supported, trade-offs and a validation plan.

A model-selected candidate remains conditional on its inputs. It is not a guaranteed optimal price.

How the implementation is organised

Value Pricing is an open-source Agent Skill with supporting Python analysis tools. Its structure separates workflow instructions, method references, configurable templates and analytical scripts.

  • Intake: Define the offering, buyer, decision and evidence
  • Market research: Competitor references, attribute comparison and hedonic analysis
  • Customer value: EVC, scenario modelling and sensitivity
  • Buyer research: Price sensitivity and conjoint methods
  • Demand analysis: Transaction-based price-response modelling
  • Cost analysis: Cost-to-serve and contribution
  • Synthesis: Compare evidence and evaluate candidate structures
  • Validation: Define real-world tests and decision criteria

The project includes specialised perspectives such as a pricing strategist, competitive analyst, behavioural economist, buyer persona, CFO/unit-economics reviewer and devil’s advocate. These perspectives structure different questions; they are not independent experts or empirical evidence.

The implementation includes data-handling safeguards. Scripts run only when invoked. Crawling is optional. External model calls require explicit confirmation of data transfer. The workflow is designed to work without sending confidential study material to a model provider.

Repository: https://github.com/C-Kapsalis/value-pricing

Calibration against published research

The repository includes an optional calibration procedure based on Brand, Israeli and Ngwe’s Using LLMs for Market Research (Harvard Business School Working Paper 23–062).

The procedure is designed to reproduce selected choice tasks using original study materials and compare simulated willingness-to-pay estimates with a human-research benchmark. The calibration script requires the relevant choice sets and original prompt template as inputs; these materials are not bundled with the repository.

It generates repeated prompts, processes responses and estimates willingness to pay using a multinomial logit model. It reports a bootstrap 90% confidence interval and the ratio between the simulated estimate and the supplied human benchmark.

The procedure does not automatically adjust the main study’s estimates. Its existence should not be confused with a completed calibration experiment.

Figure 8. Calibration workflow: published human choice tasks and prompt materials, repeated simulated responses, estimated willingness to pay and comparison against the human benchmark. Image by author.Walkthrough: install it and run a pricing study in three prompts

To show what the workflow does in practice, I installed it into Claude Code and ran a study for a fictional product: Ledgerly, an invoice-reconciliation tool for small accounting firms that charges $49 per firm per month and is considering tiers based on invoice volume. Below are the exact prompts I typed and what happened after each one. An agent will not phrase things identically on your machine, but the steps, files and checks will be the same.

Step 1: Install

In Claude Code, add the marketplace and install the plugin:

/plugin marketplace add C-Kapsalis/value-pricing
/plugin install value-pricing@value-pricing

In Codex or another Agent Skills client, run npx skills add C-Kapsalis/value-pricing. The install adds one skill (value-pricing), a /value-pricing command and seven reviewer agents: a pricing strategist, competitive analyst, buyer persona, CFO, behavioural economist, go-to-market lead and devil's advocate. The analysis scripts need Python 3.12 or later and the packages in the skill's requirements file; the agent can set that up, or you can do it yourself:

python3.12 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r skills/value-pricing/scripts/requirements.txt
Step 2: Describe the decision in plain language
Help me research pricing for our product. Ledgerly is a (fictional) invoice-reconciliation tool for small accounting firms. Today it costs $49 per firm per month, flat. We’re deciding whether to move to tiers based on the number of invoices a firm processes each month.

No slash command was needed. Claude Code matched the request to the skill and loaded value-pricing on its own, then read the skill's intake guide (references/1-intake.md). It did not run anything. Instead, it asked whether I wanted to work from real data or from labelled assumptions, followed by seven discovery questions. The first three:

  • How many invoices do firms process each month? Tier cut-offs are only defensible if they follow the real distribution.
  • Why change now? Heavy users costing too much, money left on the table, or $49 being too high for tiny firms each lead to a different design.
  • Does cost grow with invoices? If it is mostly flat, the case for tiers rests on value, not margin.

This is the behaviour I designed for: scope the decision before choosing methods, and never fill a gap with a plausible-sounding number.

Step 3: Answer, and let it build the study
Option B. Assumptions: 300 firms, US, USD, monthly self-serve billing. Invoice volume per firm per month: under 100 for 45% of firms, 100 to 500 for 40%, over 500 for 15%. Variable cost is OCR at $0.02 per invoice plus about 20 minutes of support per firm per month at $30 an hour. Ledgerly saves about 3 minutes of staff time per invoice at $40 an hour […] Constraint: no existing customer’s bill can rise more than 30% in year one. We have no customer research. Set up the study and run the value and cost phases.

The agent created a pricing-study/ folder from the skill's templates (study.yaml, offering.yaml, costs.yaml, value_drivers.yaml) and started a DECISIONS.md log that records each ruling and who made it. It ran the bundled cost_model.py. For value, it chose not to use the bundled Monte Carlo script and logged why: with a single value driver, splitting value across features would be meaningless. It wrote a small study-specific model instead. The headline results:

  • 50 (light): modelled value per month $100; $49 as a share of value 49%
  • 300 (mid): modelled value per month $600; $49 as a share of value 8%
  • 1,000 (heavy): modelled value per month $2,000; $49 as a share of value 2.5%
  • Value only passes $49 at about 25 invoices a month, or about 130 in the pessimistic case.
  • Light firms are 45% of customers but about 8% of total value; heavy firms are 15% of customers and about 51% of value.
  • At $49, variable cost only exceeds price above about 1,950 invoices a month. If support time grows with volume, that drops to about 920.
  • The binding constraint is the 30% cap: existing firms can go to at most $63.70 in year one.

It also listed the inputs that would change the answer most, starting with the real distribution of invoices per firm.

Step 4: Draft tiers and convene the council
Draft two or three tier structures that respect the 30% cap, then convene the pricing council to critique them and tell me which one to test first.

The agent drafted three structures in proposals.yaml, modelled them against the 300 firms and wrote a council dossier. It then spawned five of the seven reviewer agents in parallel. It left out the competitive analyst because no market phase had been run, and the buyer persona because there was no persona evidence, which would have made its answers pure invention.

  • A: Rebalance: pricing $39 / $59 / $99; year-2 revenue +14%; largest year-2 jump +102% (heavy)
  • B: Keep $49 floor: pricing $49 / $79 / $149; year-2 revenue +55%; largest year-2 jump +204% (heavy)
  • C: Base plus usage: pricing $29 incl. 25 invoices, then $0.10 each; year-2 revenue +14%; largest year-2 jump +158% (heavy)

The reviewers disagreed in a useful way. The pricing strategist, behavioural economist and go-to-market lead favoured A, because cutting the light tier to $39 gives 45% of firms good news in the migration message. The CFO and the devil’s advocate favoured B, because the $1,350 a month lost on light firms is certain while the gains elsewhere are assumed. All five agreed that invoices processed is the right unit, that single-month tiering would swing with tax season, and that the real risk is the year-two jump once the cap expires.

The devil’s advocate also caught two mistakes in the main agent’s own work: a claim in the dossier that the heavy tier became unprofitable at 2,500 invoices, and an unknown that had not been saved to the cost file. The agent corrected both and re-ran the cost model before answering.

The final recommendation was an adjusted structure, A+, tested on new sign-ups only:

  • Starter: up to 100 invoices for $39. Practice: up to 500 invoices for $59, then $0.08 per extra invoice.
  • Tiers based on a three-month average, so tax season does not push firms up and down.
  • Existing firms capped at $63.70 in year one and $82.81 in year two, with a bill preview and 60 days’ notice.
  • A 60–90 day test against the previous $49 cohort, with explicit pass criteria and a kill rule: pause the migration if 9 or more mid-volume firms cancel or downgrade within 90 days.

Its first action item was free: pull twelve months of invoice counts per firm from the OCR logs, because that one input decides between A and B.

Under the hood: the statistical self-test

The Ledgerly run used the value and cost tools. The heavier statistical methods (hedonic regression, Bayesian demand elasticity, choice-based conjoint) are checked by a self-test that builds a synthetic study with known answers and verifies that each method recovers them:

python tests/selftest_value_pricing.py --dir ./demo-study

On my run, all 18 checks passed:

  • Hedonic premium: delivery scope: planted +0.50; recovered +0.51 (90% interval 0.36 to 0.66)
  • Hedonic premium: outcome measurement: planted +0.60; recovered +0.63 (0.46 to 0.79)
  • Demand elasticity, two segments: planted −0.80; recovered −0.83 and −0.79
  • Conjoint WTP, premium service level: planted $44.1; recovered $41.7 (81% of held-out choices predicted, 25% by chance)

Not everything was perfect. One hedonic premium came out 0.09 high, and the conjoint estimates run slightly low across the board. The self-test also leaves a full study in demo-study/. Its synthesis flags that competitor prices ($103 to $130) sit above what the value model says any segment could capture ($22 to $71), and that the large segment has no defensible price window at all. That is the behaviour the synthesis stage exists for: when evidence streams conflict, it shows the conflict instead of averaging it away.

What the tests establish, and what they do not

The synthetic self-test checks analytical components against known values. It does not establish that competitor listings represent transaction prices, synthetic buyers behave like real customers, modelled value becomes realised benefit, historical price relationships are causal, or a recommended structure will maximise revenue.

The quality of the workflow depends on the research design and inputs. A sophisticated model cannot compensate for an incorrectly defined segment, a misleading counterfactual or a poorly measured cost driver.

What I want to improve next

I want to validate the methods against appropriately sourced real pricing studies, improve how evidence quality is represented across research streams, and develop a more complete treatment of purchase incidence.

I also want to make the handover between analytical components easier to inspect. A reader should be able to trace a pricing hypothesis back to its source evidence, assumptions, model and uncertainty.

Try the workflow

Value Pricing is available at https://github.com/C-Kapsalis/value-pricing.

The repository includes the Agent Skill, specialised perspectives, configurable study templates, Python analysis scripts, synthetic self-tests and method references. Consult the README and tests/selftest_value_pricing.py for setup and execution details.

Disclosure: I am the author of Value Pricing. The project and synthetic examples discussed here are independent open-source work. Synthetic figures and test data are illustrative; they are not customer research, market benchmarks or evidence of commercial pricing performance.

The objective is to make the reasoning behind a pricing decision explicit, reproducible and open to challenge.

If you’ve made a pricing call recently, what evidence did you lean on, and what did you wish you had? Tell me in the replies. I’m looking for real cases to test the workflow against.

References

[1] J. Brand, A. Israeli and D. Ngwe, Using LLMs for Market Research (2023), Harvard Business School Working Paper 23–062

This story was drafted on TK.

Christoforos (Chris) Kapsalis is a technical author and marketer with a passion for building open-source tools that will hopefully help businesses in disadvantaged parts of the world or run by members of disadvantaged communities improve their workflows and maximize the value generated by their marketing efforts.

items.title: YouTuber MKBHD on the Cybertruck's discontinuation: 'Doesn't bode well for the Roadster'
items.summary: MKBHD also said his hair is probably safe after placing a bet related to the Cybercab. Chance Yeh/Getty Images for HubSpot MKBHD says the Cybertruck's wind-down could be bad news for the elusive Roadster. Tesla is clearing factory space for the steering-wheel-less, gold-painted Cybercab. Due to a bet, a 2026 Cybercab consumer launch could cost MKBHD his hair — but he's not sweating it. Tesla's decision to wind down Cybertruck production has Marques Brownlee worried about a different delayed vehicle. "This doesn't bode well for the Roadster," Brownlee, the YouTube reviewer popularly known as MKBHD, said on a Friday episode of the "WVFRM Podcast." On November 6, Tesla CEO Elon Musk announced on X that the EV maker would stop building the Cybertruck by mid-2027 to focus on production of the steering wheel-less Cybercab. Earlier this year, Tesla also retired its Model S and Model X, as it shifts more of its attention toward autonomous vehicles and humanoid robots. That makes the Roadster, Tesla's twice-revealed and long-delayed supercar, a questionable fit in the automaker's lineup, MKBHD said. It's the only vehicle in Tesla's lineup that the automaker isn't trying to make fully autonomous. People look at a prototype of the 2028 Tesla Roadster Thrust, an all-electric vehicle featuring SpaceX-developed thrusters. Caroline Brehman / AFP via Getty Images MKBHD has followed the Roadster saga particularly closely. He previously held two reservations for the high-flying vehicle, but he said in September 2025 that he had canceled one after waiting nearly a decade for delivery. And, for the Cybertruck, he said he thinks Tesla missed a golden opportunity. "If they just made like a good, simple SUV type-thing, like the EV9 ," he said. "That would have sold a lot. People would have wanted that everywhere." About MKBHD's hair… The YouTuber has a big bet with Tesla stans: If Tesla, as it once predicted, sells Cybercabs to US consumers by the end of 2026 under $30,000, he'll shave his head. Tesla debuted its gold-painted Cybercabs in Austin in September , but the vehicles were used exclusively in Tesla's own ride-hailing service — not sold to individual drivers. On Friday, he said that Tesla's plan to continue making Cybertrucks until mid-2027 made him more confident in his bet. "Alright, I'm probably good," MKBHD said on the podcast. "I did just get a haircut." That bet got a little more complicated late Friday and into Saturday. Tesla opened early Cybercab orders to select customers and is predicting a December delivery for its first units. The consumer Cybercab has a $29,990 starting price (before a $300-a-month subscription) — and MKBHD was among the initial invitees . "My hair is safe for several reasons," he wrote, pointing to the car's invite-only sales run and the fact that owners can't use it at first as a ride-hail. "It's a paperweight if I take this thing home." Musk responded on Saturday: "He's a chicken." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Scott Bessent says Nvidia should look outside the company for a new CEO: ‘They needed a dramatic shake-up'
items.summary: US Treasury Secretary has shared his thoughts on the search for Nvidia's new CEO. Star Tribune/Getty Images US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has thoughts about Nvidia's search for a new CEO. Bessent told Fox's "Sunday Morning Futures" that Nvidia should look outside the company. Former CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week after he admitted to an affair. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has thoughts about Nvidia's search for a new CEO. Bessent said Nvidia's board of directors should focus on candidates "outside the company" during an interview on Fox's "Sunday Morning Futures." "They need a dramatic shake-up," Bessent said. Last week, now former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after the company's board of directors opened an investigation into whether he was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort." The same day, Huang admitted to an extramarital affair in a memo to staff. The New York Times and Reuters reported in the days following that Huang also had relationships with two different Nvidia employees. An October New York Times report said Huang had developed a "close relationship" with Alice Huang, a former tech executive whom US officials believe may have been passing information to China. China has denied the espionage claims , and the US Justice Department has not yet reached a conclusion on the matter. During the interview, Bessent also said Nvidia's board of directors should answer questions about the company's compliance with export regulations in the next 10 days. "Nvidia is a wonderful company. Jensen Huang is an incredible innovator, but that does not abrogate their duties to compliance," he said. In a statement, Nvidia said it would consider both internal and external candidates for the CEO role. Colette Kress , the company's chief financial officer, is serving as interim CEO. The board has not publicly discussed potential candidates , but some analysts and investors have shared their top picks. Others, meanwhile, are hoping that Nvidia's board reinstates Huang as CEO until an internal investigation into his affair is complete. There is a growing number of people in the tech industry who believe the allegations that Alice Huang is a spy might have been intentionally overblown by China hawks in the US looking to oust Huang. The former Nvidia CEO had been an advocate for supplying chips to China. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: I Built an AI Marketing Analyst. Then I Tested Whether It Actually Helped (Mostly, It Didn’t)
items.summary: The first benchmark showed almost no difference. The second showed where structured skills help AI agents, and where they still fail. In one of my test cases, September email revenue was up 11.2%. Every segment that existed in August was down by about a quarter. The entire increase came from a new VIP segment, and a dashboard showing only the total would have told exactly the wrong story. That gap is why I built Devil’s Analyst. Getting an AI model to produce an answer is easy. Getting it to challenge the assumptions behind that answer, separate evidence from explanation and recommend an action that holds up to scrutiny is much harder. Devil’s Analyst is an open-source collection of analytical skills for AI agents. It covers marketing metrics, attribution, experiments, research, pricing, channel performance, Power BI models and reporting. Once the skills, benchmark cases and graders were in place, I had one question: does giving an AI agent a structured body of analytical knowledge actually improve its work? I compared outputs with and without the relevant skills, using identical prompts and synthetic data. The results were mixed. One broad evaluation showed almost no difference. A smaller follow-up found better performance on some reporting and audit tasks, but also exposed failures that required changes to the skills. Neither result establishes a general performance improvement. But the experiment shows where the approach helped, where it didn’t, and what I still need to test. If you’re building skills, prompts or evaluations for AI agents, those details are the useful part. The problem: an answer is not an analysis Consider an ordinary marketing report. A dashboard shows that conversion rate has declined. Someone identifies a recent landing-page redesign as the likely explanation. A recommendation follows: revert the redesign. That chain hides three separate jobs: establish whether the decline is real, investigate what might explain it, and decide what action the evidence justifies. A correctly calculated metric does not establish its interpretation. A plausible explanation does not establish causality. An action based on an untested explanation remains untested. I wanted Devil’s Analyst to make the reasoning explicit: define the metric, validate the comparison, investigate competing explanations, examine the evidence and connect recommendations to something measurable. Figure 1. Analytical sequence from observation through validation, competing hypotheses, evidence and action. Invalid comparisons should return to data validation rather than proceed to diagnosis. Image by author. What I built Devil’s Analyst is an open-source collection of 16 agent skills and a session hook. The project contains 229 numbered analytical checks, alongside formulas, diagnostic playbooks, adversarial questions and review procedures. Its workflows cover metric definitions, movement decomposition, experimental design, evidence checks, diagnosis, recommendations and review of existing reports. The review workflows also examine whether correct work should remain unchanged. The intention is to make analytical reasoning easier to inspect and challenge. The skills should not make an agent produce longer reports or more warnings by default. Repository: https://github.com/C-Kapsalis/devils-analyst Figure 2. Devil’s Analyst architecture: session hook, routing skill, analytical skills, supporting knowledge and user-provided data. Image by author. Designing the comparison I compared two conditions: A: Claude Haiku with the relevant Devil’s Analyst skill B: Claude Haiku without the skill Both arms received the same task and identical input data for each case. I used synthetic marketing data because I needed to know what the correct answer should be. Each benchmark case contains deliberately constructed analytical problems, supporting exports and, where appropriate, decoys that should not be flagged. The repository contains 110 cases: 62 focused analytical traps, 36 draft reports with supporting exports, and 12 audits and reviews. Of these, 105 are generated by scripts that calculate expected answers; five early cases are hand-written. The first evaluation: breadth On 17 October 2026, I ran all 36 draft-report cases. Each case received three runs per arm, producing 216 runs in total. The model was Claude Haiku 5.5 in Claude Code. The evaluation used the default Claude plugin-evaluation judge, with three votes per grader and majority agreement determining the result. Subtle problem recall — with Devil’s Analyst: 100%; without: 99% Correct decision — with Devil’s Analyst: 97%; without: 95% No false alarms — with Devil’s Analyst: 80%; without: 81% All graders passed — with Devil’s Analyst: 77%; without: 78% Mean score — with Devil’s Analyst: 0.94; without: 0.93 The mean difference was 0.01. With three runs per case, that difference is too small to support a meaningful performance claim. The model without Devil’s Analyst already identified planted problems in 107 of 108 runs. These cases did not separate the two conditions very well on problem recall. Figure 3. Breadth evaluation (36 cases, three runs per case per arm): both configurations score almost identically, with a mean-score difference of 0.01. Image by author. The second evaluation: a closer inspection On 22 October 2026, I selected 17 cases: 13 focused analytical cases, two audit cases, one flawed report review and one clean report used as a control. Each arm received the same prompt and byte-identical fixture data. Arm A read the relevant skill and supporting references. Arm B received the same task without those materials. There was one run per arm per case. I graded the outputs myself against the predefined graders for each case. Graders passed — with Devil’s Analyst: 44/48; without: 35/48 Cases with every grader passed — with Devil’s Analyst: 13/17; without: 10/17 Focused analytical graders — with Devil’s Analyst: 34/36; without: 30/36 Audit and review graders — with Devil’s Analyst: 10/12; without: 5/12 This result is more encouraging, particularly for auditing and reviewing existing work. It is also a much smaller experiment. I wrote the skills, cases and graders, knew which arm I was evaluating, and ran each case only once. It is a promising observation, not proof of a general improvement. Figure 4. Grader pass rates in the 17-case evaluation, with raw counts. The largest gap is in audit and review graders (83.3% vs 41.7%), in a small, single-run evaluation. Image by author. Where the difference appeared Case 1: a marketing dashboard with a mix effect One case asked both agents to build a self-contained HTML dashboard comparing email performance in August and September 2026. The input contained 20 rows of synthetic email-send data, with one row per campaign send and segment. A new VIP repeat-buyer segment appeared in September. Its attributed revenue made total September revenue look higher, even though the two existing segments had declined. Newsletter subscribers — August revenue: 18,240; September revenue: 13,280; change: −4,960 Active customers — August revenue: 10,660; September revenue: 8,448; change: −2,212 VIP repeat buyers — August revenue: none (new segment); September revenue: 10,400; change: +10,400 Total — August revenue: 28,900; September revenue: 32,128; change: +3,228 Total revenue increased by 11.2%. The two comparable segments declined by 24.8%. Arm A passed all five graders. It produced a revenue bridge, showed blended and like-for-like rates, separated hypotheses from findings, and attached verification steps to its recommendations. Arm B passed two of the five graders. Its dashboard included some correct figures, but it did not make the distinction between the blended result and comparable segments sufficiently explicit. Figure 5. August–September revenue bridge (synthetic data): the new VIP segment adds 10,400 and turns two declining segments into an 11.2% blended increase, while like-for-like revenue falls 24.8%. Image by author. The synthetic input also contained repeated weekly figures that required investigation. The stronger output identified the concern and recommended checking the underlying export before treating the totals as reliable. Case 2: knowing when not to recommend changes I included a clean-control case: an existing report without the planted problems the review skill was designed to identify. An analytical reviewer that always finds something wrong creates unnecessary work and can undermine confidence in correct work. Arm A concluded that the report was ready to send and passed all three graders. Arm B proposed three changes and passed one grader. Figure 6. Clean-control case: with the skill, Haiku recommended sending the report unchanged (3/3 graders passed); without it, Haiku proposed three changes (1/3 passed). Image by author. Case 3: a failure in SEO diagnosis Both arms failed to distinguish declining market demand from a problem with the website’s SEO performance. The skill-assisted arm did not solve the case. I traced the failure to a missing diagnostic step. The instructions required the agent to rule out measurement problems before investigating behaviour, but did not explicitly ask whether the whole market had moved. I added a general rule: before diagnosing a decline as an organisation-specific problem, investigate whether the category or competitors experienced the same movement. The case was rerun with the revised skill, and the previously failing graders passed. This is useful engineering feedback, but not independent validation. I changed the instructions after seeing the failure, and the revised case was familiar to me. Figure 7. Revised SEO diagnostic flow, showing the market-level check added after the original failure. Image by author. What changed in the project Open rates were treated too confidently in an email decomposition: Added a rule to treat opens as a weak signal and never use them alone to verify an action SEO diagnosis missed a category-wide decline: Added a market-versus-organisation diagnostic step A review did not distinguish unresolved doubts from actual findings: Added a separate Not checked category for questions the available data cannot settle Audit priorities did not adequately account for upstream dependencies: Revised prioritisation to consider the order in which problems must be fixed I changed general rules rather than inserting case-specific answers. Otherwise, the benchmark would become a memorisation exercise. What the experiment does not prove The data is synthetic. The planted problems make correct answers easier to establish, but real marketing data is messier and often contains questions that cannot be resolved from an export alone. The first evaluation did not demonstrate a meaningful overall improvement. The 0.94 versus 0.93 mean score difference is too small to support that conclusion. The second evaluation was small: 17 cases and one run per arm. A single changed result can materially affect the comparison. I was also the judge. I wrote the cases, skills and graders, and knew which arm produced each answer. Another reviewer could disagree with some assessments. The experiment did not test the complete plugin-routing mechanism. Skill-assisted agents were directed to read relevant files. This did not test whether the session hook and routing mechanism would reliably select the right skill in an ordinary user session. Neither arm could execute code in the second evaluation. The skills recommend using code for calculations where appropriate, so this experiment did not test that part of the intended workflow. Finally, the results are specific to Claude Haiku in Claude Code. They do not establish that the same results will occur with other models, agents or platforms. What I want to test next The next evaluation should use more repetitions per case and arm to distinguish consistent behaviour from variation between runs. I also want independent grading. Another reviewer should assess anonymised outputs without knowing which arm produced them. The evaluation should separate whether the agent identified the problem, calculated correctly, avoided false alarms, distinguished observations from hypotheses, recommended an evidence-supported action and explained how to evaluate it. I also want cases created by people other than me. Finally, I want to test the complete agent workflow, including routing, data access and code execution. Five lessons if you’re building AI agent skills Check whether the baseline already passes. In my breadth evaluation, the model without skills caught the planted problems in 107 of 108 runs. A benchmark that can’t separate the two conditions can’t tell you whether your skills help. Include clean controls. A reviewer that always finds something wrong looks thorough but creates work. A case with nothing wrong tests whether the agent knows when to stop. Fix the rule, not the case. When the SEO case failed, I added a general diagnostic step rather than the specific answer. Otherwise the benchmark becomes a memory test. Grade the parts separately. Spotting a problem, calculating correctly, avoiding false alarms and recommending a testable action are different abilities. One blended score hides which of them moved. Don’t be your own only judge. If you wrote the skills, the cases and the graders, you aren’t neutral. Neither was I. The work between an answer and a decision We are giving AI agents access to more data systems, reporting tools and analytical workflows. Access to data does not automatically produce sound analytical judgement. An answer can rely on an unstable metric definition, an unfair comparison or an explanation the evidence does not support. I built Devil’s Analyst to make those assumptions more visible and give an agent a structured way to challenge them. The broad benchmark showed almost no difference. The smaller follow-up was encouraging on review tasks and exposed failures I have since fixed. I would rather publish an inconclusive result and explain what I learned than turn a small difference into a performance claim. The next step is to make the evaluation more independent, reproducible and difficult for my own assumptions to influence. If you work with marketing data, I could use your help. I’m looking for benchmark cases written by someone other than me, and for reviewers willing to grade anonymised outputs. Open an issue on the repository or leave a response here. Reproducing the work - Project: https://github.com/C-Kapsalis/devils-analyst - Benchmark methodology: https://github.com/C-Kapsalis/devils-analyst/blob/main/benchmarks/METHOD.md - Breadth evaluation: https://github.com/C-Kapsalis/devils-analyst/blob/main/benchmarks/results/2026-10-17-breadth.md - 17-case spot check: https://github.com/C-Kapsalis/devils-analyst/blob/main/benchmarks/results/2026-10-22-spot-check/README.md - Dashboard case and outputs: https://github.com/C-Kapsalis/devils-analyst/blob/main/benchmarks/results/2026-10-22-spot-check/dashboard-email.md - Clean-control case: https://github.com/C-Kapsalis/devils-analyst/blob/main/benchmarks/results/2026-10-22-spot-check/review-clean-control.md The benchmark uses synthetic data, not customer datasets. Results describe the specific models, prompts, environments and evaluation procedures documented above. Disclosure: I am the author of Devil’s Analyst. It is an independent personal project and is not affiliated with or endorsed by my employer. Christoforos (Chris) Kapsalis is a technical author and marketer with a passion for building open-source tools that will hopefully help businesses in disadvantaged parts of the world or run by members of disadvantaged communities improve their workflows and maximize the value generated by their marketing efforts. I Built an AI Marketing Analyst. Then I Tested Whether It Actually Helped (Mostly, It Didn’t) was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
