The first benchmark showed almost no difference. The second showed where structured skills help AI agents, and where they still fail.

In one of my test cases, September email revenue was up 11.2%. Every segment that existed in August was down by about a quarter. The entire increase came from a new VIP segment, and a dashboard showing only the total would have told exactly the wrong story.

That gap is why I built Devil’s Analyst. Getting an AI model to produce an answer is easy. Getting it to challenge the assumptions behind that answer, separate evidence from explanation and recommend an action that holds up to scrutiny is much harder.

Devil’s Analyst is an open-source collection of analytical skills for AI agents. It covers marketing metrics, attribution, experiments, research, pricing, channel performance, Power BI models and reporting.

Once the skills, benchmark cases and graders were in place, I had one question: does giving an AI agent a structured body of analytical knowledge actually improve its work?

I compared outputs with and without the relevant skills, using identical prompts and synthetic data. The results were mixed. One broad evaluation showed almost no difference. A smaller follow-up found better performance on some reporting and audit tasks, but also exposed failures that required changes to the skills.

Neither result establishes a general performance improvement. But the experiment shows where the approach helped, where it didn’t, and what I still need to test. If you’re building skills, prompts or evaluations for AI agents, those details are the useful part.

The problem: an answer is not an analysis

Consider an ordinary marketing report. A dashboard shows that conversion rate has declined. Someone identifies a recent landing-page redesign as the likely explanation. A recommendation follows: revert the redesign.

That chain hides three separate jobs: establish whether the decline is real, investigate what might explain it, and decide what action the evidence justifies.

A correctly calculated metric does not establish its interpretation. A plausible explanation does not establish causality. An action based on an untested explanation remains untested.

I wanted Devil’s Analyst to make the reasoning explicit: define the metric, validate the comparison, investigate competing explanations, examine the evidence and connect recommendations to something measurable.

Figure 1. Analytical sequence from observation through validation, competing hypotheses, evidence and action. Invalid comparisons should return to data validation rather than proceed to diagnosis. Image by author.What I built

Devil’s Analyst is an open-source collection of 16 agent skills and a session hook. The project contains 229 numbered analytical checks, alongside formulas, diagnostic playbooks, adversarial questions and review procedures.

Its workflows cover metric definitions, movement decomposition, experimental design, evidence checks, diagnosis, recommendations and review of existing reports. The review workflows also examine whether correct work should remain unchanged.

The intention is to make analytical reasoning easier to inspect and challenge. The skills should not make an agent produce longer reports or more warnings by default.

Repository: https://github.com/C-Kapsalis/devils-analyst

Figure 2. Devil’s Analyst architecture: session hook, routing skill, analytical skills, supporting knowledge and user-provided data. Image by author.Designing the comparison

I compared two conditions:

  • A: Claude Haiku with the relevant Devil’s Analyst skill
  • B: Claude Haiku without the skill

Both arms received the same task and identical input data for each case. I used synthetic marketing data because I needed to know what the correct answer should be. Each benchmark case contains deliberately constructed analytical problems, supporting exports and, where appropriate, decoys that should not be flagged.

The repository contains 110 cases: 62 focused analytical traps, 36 draft reports with supporting exports, and 12 audits and reviews. Of these, 105 are generated by scripts that calculate expected answers; five early cases are hand-written.

The first evaluation: breadth

On 17 October 2026, I ran all 36 draft-report cases. Each case received three runs per arm, producing 216 runs in total.

The model was Claude Haiku 5.5 in Claude Code. The evaluation used the default Claude plugin-evaluation judge, with three votes per grader and majority agreement determining the result.

  • Subtle problem recall — with Devil’s Analyst: 100%; without: 99%
  • Correct decision — with Devil’s Analyst: 97%; without: 95%
  • No false alarms — with Devil’s Analyst: 80%; without: 81%
  • All graders passed — with Devil’s Analyst: 77%; without: 78%
  • Mean score — with Devil’s Analyst: 0.94; without: 0.93

The mean difference was 0.01. With three runs per case, that difference is too small to support a meaningful performance claim. The model without Devil’s Analyst already identified planted problems in 107 of 108 runs. These cases did not separate the two conditions very well on problem recall.

Figure 3. Breadth evaluation (36 cases, three runs per case per arm): both configurations score almost identically, with a mean-score difference of 0.01. Image by author.The second evaluation: a closer inspection

On 22 October 2026, I selected 17 cases: 13 focused analytical cases, two audit cases, one flawed report review and one clean report used as a control.

Each arm received the same prompt and byte-identical fixture data. Arm A read the relevant skill and supporting references. Arm B received the same task without those materials.

There was one run per arm per case. I graded the outputs myself against the predefined graders for each case.

  • Graders passed — with Devil’s Analyst: 44/48; without: 35/48
  • Cases with every grader passed — with Devil’s Analyst: 13/17; without: 10/17
  • Focused analytical graders — with Devil’s Analyst: 34/36; without: 30/36
  • Audit and review graders — with Devil’s Analyst: 10/12; without: 5/12

This result is more encouraging, particularly for auditing and reviewing existing work. It is also a much smaller experiment. I wrote the skills, cases and graders, knew which arm I was evaluating, and ran each case only once. It is a promising observation, not proof of a general improvement.

Figure 4. Grader pass rates in the 17-case evaluation, with raw counts. The largest gap is in audit and review graders (83.3% vs 41.7%), in a small, single-run evaluation. Image by author.Where the difference appearedCase 1: a marketing dashboard with a mix effect

One case asked both agents to build a self-contained HTML dashboard comparing email performance in August and September 2026. The input contained 20 rows of synthetic email-send data, with one row per campaign send and segment.

A new VIP repeat-buyer segment appeared in September. Its attributed revenue made total September revenue look higher, even though the two existing segments had declined.

  • Newsletter subscribers — August revenue: 18,240; September revenue: 13,280; change: −4,960
  • Active customers — August revenue: 10,660; September revenue: 8,448; change: −2,212
  • VIP repeat buyers — August revenue: none (new segment); September revenue: 10,400; change: +10,400
  • Total — August revenue: 28,900; September revenue: 32,128; change: +3,228

Total revenue increased by 11.2%. The two comparable segments declined by 24.8%.

Arm A passed all five graders. It produced a revenue bridge, showed blended and like-for-like rates, separated hypotheses from findings, and attached verification steps to its recommendations.

Arm B passed two of the five graders. Its dashboard included some correct figures, but it did not make the distinction between the blended result and comparable segments sufficiently explicit.

Figure 5. August–September revenue bridge (synthetic data): the new VIP segment adds 10,400 and turns two declining segments into an 11.2% blended increase, while like-for-like revenue falls 24.8%. Image by author.

The synthetic input also contained repeated weekly figures that required investigation. The stronger output identified the concern and recommended checking the underlying export before treating the totals as reliable.

Case 2: knowing when not to recommend changes

I included a clean-control case: an existing report without the planted problems the review skill was designed to identify.

An analytical reviewer that always finds something wrong creates unnecessary work and can undermine confidence in correct work.

Arm A concluded that the report was ready to send and passed all three graders. Arm B proposed three changes and passed one grader.

Figure 6. Clean-control case: with the skill, Haiku recommended sending the report unchanged (3/3 graders passed); without it, Haiku proposed three changes (1/3 passed). Image by author.Case 3: a failure in SEO diagnosis

Both arms failed to distinguish declining market demand from a problem with the website’s SEO performance.

The skill-assisted arm did not solve the case. I traced the failure to a missing diagnostic step. The instructions required the agent to rule out measurement problems before investigating behaviour, but did not explicitly ask whether the whole market had moved.

I added a general rule: before diagnosing a decline as an organisation-specific problem, investigate whether the category or competitors experienced the same movement.

The case was rerun with the revised skill, and the previously failing graders passed. This is useful engineering feedback, but not independent validation. I changed the instructions after seeing the failure, and the revised case was familiar to me.

Figure 7. Revised SEO diagnostic flow, showing the market-level check added after the original failure. Image by author.What changed in the project
  • Open rates were treated too confidently in an email decomposition: Added a rule to treat opens as a weak signal and never use them alone to verify an action
  • SEO diagnosis missed a category-wide decline: Added a market-versus-organisation diagnostic step
  • A review did not distinguish unresolved doubts from actual findings: Added a separate Not checked category for questions the available data cannot settle
  • Audit priorities did not adequately account for upstream dependencies: Revised prioritisation to consider the order in which problems must be fixed

I changed general rules rather than inserting case-specific answers. Otherwise, the benchmark would become a memorisation exercise.

What the experiment does not prove

The data is synthetic. The planted problems make correct answers easier to establish, but real marketing data is messier and often contains questions that cannot be resolved from an export alone.

The first evaluation did not demonstrate a meaningful overall improvement. The 0.94 versus 0.93 mean score difference is too small to support that conclusion.

The second evaluation was small: 17 cases and one run per arm. A single changed result can materially affect the comparison.

I was also the judge. I wrote the cases, skills and graders, and knew which arm produced each answer. Another reviewer could disagree with some assessments.

The experiment did not test the complete plugin-routing mechanism. Skill-assisted agents were directed to read relevant files. This did not test whether the session hook and routing mechanism would reliably select the right skill in an ordinary user session.

Neither arm could execute code in the second evaluation. The skills recommend using code for calculations where appropriate, so this experiment did not test that part of the intended workflow.

Finally, the results are specific to Claude Haiku in Claude Code. They do not establish that the same results will occur with other models, agents or platforms.

What I want to test next

The next evaluation should use more repetitions per case and arm to distinguish consistent behaviour from variation between runs.

I also want independent grading. Another reviewer should assess anonymised outputs without knowing which arm produced them.

The evaluation should separate whether the agent identified the problem, calculated correctly, avoided false alarms, distinguished observations from hypotheses, recommended an evidence-supported action and explained how to evaluate it.

I also want cases created by people other than me. Finally, I want to test the complete agent workflow, including routing, data access and code execution.

Five lessons if you’re building AI agent skills
  1. Check whether the baseline already passes. In my breadth evaluation, the model without skills caught the planted problems in 107 of 108 runs. A benchmark that can’t separate the two conditions can’t tell you whether your skills help.
  2. Include clean controls. A reviewer that always finds something wrong looks thorough but creates work. A case with nothing wrong tests whether the agent knows when to stop.
  3. Fix the rule, not the case. When the SEO case failed, I added a general diagnostic step rather than the specific answer. Otherwise the benchmark becomes a memory test.
  4. Grade the parts separately. Spotting a problem, calculating correctly, avoiding false alarms and recommending a testable action are different abilities. One blended score hides which of them moved.
  5. Don’t be your own only judge. If you wrote the skills, the cases and the graders, you aren’t neutral. Neither was I.
The work between an answer and a decision

We are giving AI agents access to more data systems, reporting tools and analytical workflows. Access to data does not automatically produce sound analytical judgement.

An answer can rely on an unstable metric definition, an unfair comparison or an explanation the evidence does not support. I built Devil’s Analyst to make those assumptions more visible and give an agent a structured way to challenge them.

The broad benchmark showed almost no difference. The smaller follow-up was encouraging on review tasks and exposed failures I have since fixed.

I would rather publish an inconclusive result and explain what I learned than turn a small difference into a performance claim. The next step is to make the evaluation more independent, reproducible and difficult for my own assumptions to influence.

If you work with marketing data, I could use your help. I’m looking for benchmark cases written by someone other than me, and for reviewers willing to grade anonymised outputs. Open an issue on the repository or leave a response here.

Reproducing the work

- Project: https://github.com/C-Kapsalis/devils-analyst

- Benchmark methodology: https://github.com/C-Kapsalis/devils-analyst/blob/main/benchmarks/METHOD.md

- Breadth evaluation: https://github.com/C-Kapsalis/devils-analyst/blob/main/benchmarks/results/2026-10-17-breadth.md

- 17-case spot check: https://github.com/C-Kapsalis/devils-analyst/blob/main/benchmarks/results/2026-10-22-spot-check/README.md

- Dashboard case and outputs: https://github.com/C-Kapsalis/devils-analyst/blob/main/benchmarks/results/2026-10-22-spot-check/dashboard-email.md

- Clean-control case: https://github.com/C-Kapsalis/devils-analyst/blob/main/benchmarks/results/2026-10-22-spot-check/review-clean-control.md

The benchmark uses synthetic data, not customer datasets. Results describe the specific models, prompts, environments and evaluation procedures documented above.

Disclosure: I am the author of Devil’s Analyst. It is an independent personal project and is not affiliated with or endorsed by my employer.

Christoforos (Chris) Kapsalis is a technical author and marketer with a passion for building open-source tools that will hopefully help businesses in disadvantaged parts of the world or run by members of disadvantaged communities improve their workflows and maximize the value generated by their marketing efforts.

items.title: AI is set to change the graduate job market. Here’s how unis can respond
items.summary: Yan Krukau/Pexels, Kasto/Canva, The Conversation , CC BY-NC Globally, there have been concerns about the likelihood of artificial intelligence (AI) taking people’s jobs and reducing job opportunities for university graduates . AI software companies, such as OpenAI , Google DeepMind and Anthropic are pursuing AI systems capable of matching or exceeding human performance across a broad range of intellectual tasks. What does this mean for graduates and universities? Which jobs are most at risk? A federal government report , published in July, rated jobs typically involving cognitive tasks as those with the highest exposure to AI automation. This includes accountants, clerks and receptionists. Jobs that were rated as the lowest exposure to AI automation tended to be those requiring more physical work, such as tradies, carers and truck drivers. Much of the government narrative has been that jobs will more likely be changed or “augmented” by AI, rather than be cut by the technology. The report also found that as of February this year, AI had not had significant impacts on the Australian job market. This included job opportunities for graduate students, despite international concerns AI will reduce the number of entry-level roles. This article is part of a series on how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping higher education. We take a deeper look into how AI has disrupted degrees, how universities are responding to these new challenges and what the technology means for the sector’s future. You can find more stories here . However, things might be changing. This month the Reserve Bank of Australia noted there are already some signs younger workers in more AI-exposed industries are struggling to find work in Australia. The number of graduate jobs in some law firms has been slashed, with low-level tasks passed onto AI. Meanwhile, consulting firms have also cut graduate roles in recent years, but claim its not because of AI. Just last week, Qantas announced it will outsource 850 jobs to India while investing more in AI. What does this mean for desk jobs? AI models have been improving fast and can now automate many tasks in university-qualified jobs. Still, some experts argue reasoning and critical thinking skills are valuable for graduates in the AI job market. Research shows AI can still compete. In a 2024 study , researchers compared the reasoning skills of humans and AI language models (systems programmed to mimic human speech and writing) through a series of tests. The tests included maths puzzles designed to assess whether people and AI models could recognise that an answer, which seems right at first, is actually wrong. For example, a scarf costs 210€ more than a hat. The scarf and the hat cost 220€ in total. How much does the hat cost? The correct answer is 5€. People and AI models were then tested on how they reasoned their way to the correct answer. Researchers found earlier AI systems performed worse than human participants in the study’s reasoning test, while more recent AI models performed better. If this trend continues, AI could eventually outperform people on a much wider range of reasoning tasks. In one sign of that progress, an OpenAI model recently disproved a longstanding conjecture in geometry dating back to 1946. My own research reflects similar findings. We analysed AI’s responses on university criminal law exams in 2023 and 2025. We found its average exam scores improved from 52.5% in 2023 to 76.3% in 2025. The most striking finding was in critical thinking capabilities. Unlike the 2023 study, the 2025 models, on average, performed better than an average university student. These were specific tests and do not prove AI could displace humans and take over an entire profession. But the results challenge the assumption AI weaknesses will remain unchanged. What about trades? Physical work is a challenge for AI. But if a sufficiently capable AI could control reliable, affordable robots then electricians and plumbers could also face competition. We’re already seeing signs of this shift. Robotaxis carry passengers in a growing number of cities , delivery robots bring meals to customers and autonomous excavators dig on construction sites. Despite significant progress in robots’ ability to carry out complex physical tasks it’s still unclear how soon they will be able to do more of the work tradies do. For now, students who choose vocational pathways, such as apprenticeships, may face a lower risk of AI-related job disruption. Working with AI This doesn’t mean it’s over for white-collar workers. One likely possibility in an AI job market is that a person working with the technology will achieve a better result than AI alone. This is a form of AI augmentation, which can keep workers relevant and useful. But research shows collaborating with AI is not an easy skill. Getting useful results takes judgement. In a 2026 pilot study health-care professionals (mostly nurses) accepted half the deliberately wrong AI recommendations and passed over about one in six correct ones. And in a study looking at how the UK public uses AI for medical advice, researchers found people sometimes left out important details when consulting chatbots. As a result, the chatbots sometimes mixed useful suggestions with misleading ones. How can unis prepare graduates well? The possibility of humans working with AI should be central to how universities prepare students for the workforce. If a worker can’t improve the quality or efficiency of AI’s output, an employer may have little economic reason to involve them. To add value to the future workforce graduates may need to: understand what a good result looks like when using AI recognise when AI falls short have the knowledge and skills to improve AI’s output. They also need to learn how to collaborate with AI, how to direct it, question its output and persist until the result is better than what it produced initially. Universities can’t simply replace disciplinary knowledge with AI skills. Students will need the knowledge and skills their degrees have always required, as well as the ability to collaborate effectively with AI. The irony is that a technology designed to make our lives easier may actually require us to work harder to stay relevant in the job market. Armin Ashenberg (formerly published under Armin Alimardani) previously held a part-time contract with OpenAI as a consultant. The organisation had no input into this piece.

Yan Krukau/Pexels, Kasto/Canva, The Conversation, CC BY-NC

Globally, there have been concerns about the likelihood of artificial intelligence (AI) taking people’s jobs and reducing job opportunities for university graduates.

AI software companies, such as OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Anthropic are pursuing AI systems capable of matching or exceeding human performance across a broad range of intellectual tasks.

What does this mean for graduates and universities?

Which jobs are most at risk?

A federal government report, published in July, rated jobs typically involving cognitive tasks as those with the highest exposure to AI automation. This includes accountants, clerks and receptionists.

Jobs that were rated as the lowest exposure to AI automation tended to be those requiring more physical work, such as tradies, carers and truck drivers.

Much of the government narrative has been that jobs will more likely be changed or “augmented” by AI, rather than be cut by the technology.

The report also found that as of February this year, AI had not had significant impacts on the Australian job market. This included job opportunities for graduate students, despite international concerns AI will reduce the number of entry-level roles.

This article is part of a series on how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping higher education.

We take a deeper look into how AI has disrupted degrees, how universities are responding to these new challenges and what the technology means for the sector’s future. You can find more stories here.

However, things might be changing. This month the Reserve Bank of Australia noted there are already some signs younger workers in more AI-exposed industries are struggling to find work in Australia.

The number of graduate jobs in some law firms has been slashed, with low-level tasks passed onto AI. Meanwhile, consulting firms have also cut graduate roles in recent years, but claim its not because of AI.

Just last week, Qantas announced it will outsource 850 jobs to India while investing more in AI.

What does this mean for desk jobs?

AI models have been improving fast and can now automate many tasks in university-qualified jobs.

Still, some experts argue reasoning and critical thinking skills are valuable for graduates in the AI job market.

Research shows AI can still compete.

In a 2024 study, researchers compared the reasoning skills of humans and AI language models (systems programmed to mimic human speech and writing) through a series of tests.

The tests included maths puzzles designed to assess whether people and AI models could recognise that an answer, which seems right at first, is actually wrong. For example, a scarf costs 210€ more than a hat. The scarf and the hat cost 220€ in total. How much does the hat cost? The correct answer is 5€.

People and AI models were then tested on how they reasoned their way to the correct answer.

Researchers found earlier AI systems performed worse than human participants in the study’s reasoning test, while more recent AI models performed better.

If this trend continues, AI could eventually outperform people on a much wider range of reasoning tasks. In one sign of that progress, an OpenAI model recently disproved a longstanding conjecture in geometry dating back to 1946.

My own research reflects similar findings.

We analysed AI’s responses on university criminal law exams in 2023 and 2025. We found its average exam scores improved from 52.5% in 2023 to 76.3% in 2025. The most striking finding was in critical thinking capabilities. Unlike the 2023 study, the 2025 models, on average, performed better than an average university student.

These were specific tests and do not prove AI could displace humans and take over an entire profession. But the results challenge the assumption AI weaknesses will remain unchanged.

What about trades?

Physical work is a challenge for AI. But if a sufficiently capable AI could control reliable, affordable robots then electricians and plumbers could also face competition.

We’re already seeing signs of this shift. Robotaxis carry passengers in a growing number of cities, delivery robots bring meals to customers and autonomous excavators dig on construction sites.

Despite significant progress in robots’ ability to carry out complex physical tasks it’s still unclear how soon they will be able to do more of the work tradies do. For now, students who choose vocational pathways, such as apprenticeships, may face a lower risk of AI-related job disruption.

Working with AI

This doesn’t mean it’s over for white-collar workers.

One likely possibility in an AI job market is that a person working with the technology will achieve a better result than AI alone. This is a form of AI augmentation, which can keep workers relevant and useful.

But research shows collaborating with AI is not an easy skill. Getting useful results takes judgement.

In a 2026 pilot study health-care professionals (mostly nurses) accepted half the deliberately wrong AI recommendations and passed over about one in six correct ones. And in a study looking at how the UK public uses AI for medical advice, researchers found people sometimes left out important details when consulting chatbots. As a result, the chatbots sometimes mixed useful suggestions with misleading ones.

How can unis prepare graduates well?

The possibility of humans working with AI should be central to how universities prepare students for the workforce.

If a worker can’t improve the quality or efficiency of AI’s output, an employer may have little economic reason to involve them.

To add value to the future workforce graduates may need to:

  • understand what a good result looks like when using AI

  • recognise when AI falls short

  • have the knowledge and skills to improve AI’s output.

They also need to learn how to collaborate with AI, how to direct it, question its output and persist until the result is better than what it produced initially.

Universities can’t simply replace disciplinary knowledge with AI skills. Students will need the knowledge and skills their degrees have always required, as well as the ability to collaborate effectively with AI.

The irony is that a technology designed to make our lives easier may actually require us to work harder to stay relevant in the job market.

items.title: The Guardian view on civil service reform: AI cannot conjure a capable state on its own | Editorial
items.summary: Whitehall needs to change, but more technology isn’t enough. Opening routes to leadership would bring skills that are too often overlooked The cabinet secretary, Antonia Romeo, called for an overhaul of a “ reactive and risk-averse ” civil service in her speech last Tuesday. Ministers planned a “radical shift” of powers, resources and accountability to regional and local government, which she said would leave Whitehall “leaner and more strategic”. As 80% of civil servants already work outside London, devolution promises to alter what central government does, not simply where it operates. Reinvention is in the civil service’s blood – ever since it was founded as a permanent, impartial institution in 1854. Even departmental boundaries, Dame Antonia said, are on notice, asking do they “remain optimal in an era of cross‑cutting delivery?” This must be set against the civil service’s relative decline: it is ranked joint sixth internationally on one measure of public administration. To improve, Dame Antonia says the civil service must embrace AI. The efficacy of public service, she claimed, no longer has to be constrained by the limits of “ human bandwidth ”. That is an extraordinary claim. Technology can help speed up identifying someone at risk of homelessness – but it does not supply a home. Better administration and adequate resources need each other.

items.title: ChatGPT Can Now Buy Things for You. The Trust Belongs to the Bank, Not the Agent.
items.summary: OpenAI’s new Wallet hides your card behind a payment token and asks for Face ID on every purchase. That double lock is the right bar, and any company letting agents spend without it is taking a risk it cannot price. Cover image generated by the author. Agentic buying becomes serious the day the payment network carries the trust, not the agent. A payment token instead of the real card, plus a biometric proof for every purchase: that is the right bar. Any company that lets an AI agent spend money without that double lock is taking a risk it cannot price. I have argued this for a long time, and on November 13 OpenAI shipped a product that applies it almost line by line. Written with the help of AI tools; ideas, sources and final review by the author. The product is ChatGPT Wallet. OpenAI’s agents, called dots, can now help you decide what to buy and then complete the purchase on your behalf. You add a card once. Before each purchase, you review the items, the total and the card that will be charged, then approve with a security check such as Face ID or a fingerprint scan. The payment network then issues a payment token, a substitute card number with its own security code and expiration date. The merchant gets paid, but neither the agent nor the merchant ever sees your real card details. It is built with American Express, Mastercard and Visa. At launch, it is limited to ChatGPT Pro subscribers aged 18 and older in the US, with eligible US-issued cards. The interesting part is not the shopping. It is who OpenAI chose to put in charge of trust. The agent is the weakest link, so take the card away from it The naive version of agentic commerce is simple: give the agent your card number and let it fill in checkout forms. It works in a demo. In real life it means a piece of software that can be confused, manipulated by a malicious web page or simply wrong now holds a credential that works everywhere, for any amount, until you cancel the card. And agents are often wrong. On November 5, Visa published its Agentic Commerce Benchmark: 22 AI models from 12 labs, 15 realistic shopping scenarios such as buying a TV or a laptop. The models failed 42.8% of test runs. Only 34.2% of the time did a model pass all three attempts at the same scenario. Most telling of all, 54% of the failed runs still ended with the AI making a purchase. In other words, when an agent gets it wrong, it often does not stop. It buys the wrong thing. That single number is the whole argument. You cannot build a payment system on the assumption that the agent will behave. You build it so that the agent’s mistakes stay small, visible and reversible. A token does the first part: what the agent holds is not your card, and in OpenAI’s design it is issued by the network only after you approve. Biometrics do the second part: a human with a face or a fingerprint signs off on the exact basket and the exact total, and that approval creates a record of what the agent was authorized to buy. Why the bank, not OpenAI, should hold the trust Look at how OpenAI describes its own role. Users transact directly with businesses, which keep control of pricing, fulfillment, returns and customer service. Banks and networks bring their expertise to evaluating transactions. Card rewards stay, and so do the protections for eligible disputes, for example when an item is defective. That is the right division of labor, and it is the opposite of the instinct most AI companies have. The instinct is to own the whole flow: the agent, the checkout, the money. But the card networks already solved the hard problems of payment decades ago: fraud scoring, chargebacks, liability rules, tokenization. An AI lab that tries to rebuild that stack is asking customers to trust a far younger product with their money. An AI lab that plugs into it inherits a trust system that already works at the scale of billions of transactions. The networks clearly see it the same way. Mastercard launched Agent Pay in 2025 around what it calls agentic tokens: credentials tied to a verified agent and a specific user, with spending controls and proof of consent. In October 2026 it expanded that into the Agent Pay Trust Framework, adding identity, fraud and behavioral signals and a score that helps issuers judge whether an agent is legitimate. Visa Intelligent Commerce, its own portfolio for agentic commerce, combines tokenized credentials, authentication and spend controls, and Visa has announced a strategic partnership with OpenAI. Google’s Agent Payments Protocol, AP2, takes a related route: cryptographically signed mandates that prove what the user approved, both when the human is present and when the agent acts within pre-set limits. Different companies, different specifications, one shared conclusion: the proof of consent and the credential must live outside the agent. The demand is not there yet, and that is the point None of this means people are ready to hand their wallets to an AI. Visa’s Trust Index, released in September 2026, found that 72% of US consumers had used an AI assistant, but only 23% trusted AI to handle payment transactions on their behalf. TechCrunch notes that companies like DoorDash and Uber have so far reported low numbers of orders placed by AI agents, while Meta’s Muse, with more than 10 million users, has seen AI-assisted shopping become a top activity in its app. That gap between use and trust is exactly why the double lock matters. Consumers will not delegate spending because a model got smarter. They will delegate it when the downside is capped: the card cannot leak, every purchase leaves a signed record, and the dispute process they already know still applies. ChatGPT Wallet is not convincing because the dots are clever. It is convincing because it is boring in all the right places. OpenAI also says where it wants to go next: letting users pre-approve purchases within clear parameters such as spending limits, purchase categories or time periods, with enhanced safeguards built on today’s biometric checks and records of authorization. That is the moment to watch. Approving each purchase is easy to make safe. Approving a budget in advance is where weak designs will fail. The same rule applies inside companies This is not only a consumer story. Many companies are already giving agents the ability to spend: buying API credits, booking travel, renewing software, ordering supplies, paying invoices. Visa itself is piloting AI agents that pay supplier invoices with BILL and Billtrust. The question every finance team should ask is simple: if this agent makes the wrong purchase tomorrow, what stops it, who sees it, and who pays? If the answer is “the agent has a corporate card number in its configuration,” the company has no way to estimate its exposure. The loss is not limited by design, it is limited by luck. That is the risk I mean when I say it cannot be priced: not that it is large, but that nobody can say how large. What to do now For companies that let agents buy on their behalf: 1. Never give an agent a real card number. Use virtual or tokenized cards, one per agent or per task, with a hard limit, a merchant category restriction and an expiry date. If your bank cannot issue them, that is a reason to talk to your bank this month. 2. Require a human proof above a threshold. Small recurring purchases can be pre-approved within a budget. Anything above that limit should need an explicit approval from a named person, on a device they control, with the basket and the total in front of them. 3. Keep the record outside the agent. Every approval and every transaction should be logged by the payment system or the bank, not only in the agent’s own memory. That record is what you will need in a dispute or an audit. For merchants who want to sell to agents: 4. Stop blocking the agents you want. OpenAI’s Commerce Partner Playbook asks businesses to configure their CDN or firewall to recognize signed agent requests through Web Bot Auth, and warns that general security measures can block ChatGPT agents by accident. TechCrunch points out that Amazon, the largest retailer to ban AI agents, is steering users to its own assistant. Decide your own policy deliberately instead of by default. 5. Talk to your payment and fraud providers. OpenAI says Wallet’s tokens work with existing checkout flows, but risk systems may still flag legitimate agent purchases and decline them. It names Forter, Riskified, Sardine, Signifyd, Adyen, Checkout.com and Stripe among the partners working on this. Ask yours how they recognize these transactions. 6. Make your catalog readable. Accurate product data, current prices and stock, clear return terms. An agent that cannot understand your offer will simply buy elsewhere. Trust is infrastructure, not a feature The race in agentic commerce is often told as a race between models: which agent finds the best deal, which one understands you best. That race matters, but it will not decide adoption. Adoption will be decided by the plumbing nobody sees: tokens, signatures, biometric approvals, dispute rules. The companies that win will be the ones that let the bank do what the bank does best and keep the agent away from the money it does not need to see. Would you let an agent spend for your company today, and if so, what would stop it from making the wrong purchase? Follow me on Medium for the next analysis of how AI agents are changing the way companies decide, spend and lead. Sources OpenAI, “Introducing ChatGPT Wallet,” November 13, 2026 (includes the Commerce Partner Playbook): openai.com/index/introducing-chatgpt-wallet TechCrunch, Sarah Perez, “ChatGPT’s new Wallet lets AI agents shop and check out for you,” November 13, 2026: techcrunch.com Visa, “Visa Releases First-of-Its-Kind Industry Benchmark for AI Shopping; Almost Half of Test Runs Fail,” November 5, 2026 (also cites the Visa Trust Index): investor.visa.com Visa, “Visa Announces New AI, Stablecoin and Token Innovations to Power Intelligent, Programmable Commerce at Visa Payments Forum”: usa.visa.com Visa, BILL and Billtrust, “Visa, BILL, and Billtrust launch pilot for AI payments”: corporate.visa.com Mastercard, “Who’s behind the AI agent? Solving the identity challenge in agentic commerce,” October 8, 2026: mastercard.com Mastercard, “Agentic token framework: Driving trusted AI transactions,” 2025: mastercard.com Google Cloud, “Announcing Agent Payments Protocol (AP2)”: cloud.google.com ChatGPT Can Now Buy Things for You. The Trust Belongs to the Bank, Not the Agent. was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Different companies, different specifications, one shared conclusion: the proof of consent and the credential must live outside the agent.

The demand is not there yet, and that is the point

None of this means people are ready to hand their wallets to an AI. Visa’s Trust Index, released in September 2026, found that 72% of US consumers had used an AI assistant, but only 23% trusted AI to handle payment transactions on their behalf. TechCrunch notes that companies like DoorDash and Uber have so far reported low numbers of orders placed by AI agents, while Meta’s Muse, with more than 10 million users, has seen AI-assisted shopping become a top activity in its app.

That gap between use and trust is exactly why the double lock matters. Consumers will not delegate spending because a model got smarter. They will delegate it when the downside is capped: the card cannot leak, every purchase leaves a signed record, and the dispute process they already know still applies. ChatGPT Wallet is not convincing because the dots are clever. It is convincing because it is boring in all the right places.

OpenAI also says where it wants to go next: letting users pre-approve purchases within clear parameters such as spending limits, purchase categories or time periods, with enhanced safeguards built on today’s biometric checks and records of authorization. That is the moment to watch. Approving each purchase is easy to make safe. Approving a budget in advance is where weak designs will fail.

The same rule applies inside companies

This is not only a consumer story. Many companies are already giving agents the ability to spend: buying API credits, booking travel, renewing software, ordering supplies, paying invoices. Visa itself is piloting AI agents that pay supplier invoices with BILL and Billtrust. The question every finance team should ask is simple: if this agent makes the wrong purchase tomorrow, what stops it, who sees it, and who pays?

If the answer is “the agent has a corporate card number in its configuration,” the company has no way to estimate its exposure. The loss is not limited by design, it is limited by luck. That is the risk I mean when I say it cannot be priced: not that it is large, but that nobody can say how large.

What to do now

For companies that let agents buy on their behalf:

1. Never give an agent a real card number. Use virtual or tokenized cards, one per agent or per task, with a hard limit, a merchant category restriction and an expiry date. If your bank cannot issue them, that is a reason to talk to your bank this month.

2. Require a human proof above a threshold. Small recurring purchases can be pre-approved within a budget. Anything above that limit should need an explicit approval from a named person, on a device they control, with the basket and the total in front of them.

3. Keep the record outside the agent. Every approval and every transaction should be logged by the payment system or the bank, not only in the agent’s own memory. That record is what you will need in a dispute or an audit.

For merchants who want to sell to agents:

4. Stop blocking the agents you want. OpenAI’s Commerce Partner Playbook asks businesses to configure their CDN or firewall to recognize signed agent requests through Web Bot Auth, and warns that general security measures can block ChatGPT agents by accident. TechCrunch points out that Amazon, the largest retailer to ban AI agents, is steering users to its own assistant. Decide your own policy deliberately instead of by default.

5. Talk to your payment and fraud providers. OpenAI says Wallet’s tokens work with existing checkout flows, but risk systems may still flag legitimate agent purchases and decline them. It names Forter, Riskified, Sardine, Signifyd, Adyen, Checkout.com and Stripe among the partners working on this. Ask yours how they recognize these transactions.

6. Make your catalog readable. Accurate product data, current prices and stock, clear return terms. An agent that cannot understand your offer will simply buy elsewhere.

Trust is infrastructure, not a feature

The race in agentic commerce is often told as a race between models: which agent finds the best deal, which one understands you best. That race matters, but it will not decide adoption. Adoption will be decided by the plumbing nobody sees: tokens, signatures, biometric approvals, dispute rules. The companies that win will be the ones that let the bank do what the bank does best and keep the agent away from the money it does not need to see.

Would you let an agent spend for your company today, and if so, what would stop it from making the wrong purchase?

Follow me on Medium for the next analysis of how AI agents are changing the way companies decide, spend and lead.

items.title: A 2014 Xeon vs Two Mac Studios on a 125B Model: Who Wins?
items.summary: 128 GB of DDR3 on a Chinese X99 board against Apple’s M5 Max and M5 Ultra. The Macs are two to almost four times faster. The X99 costs a quarter to an eighth as much. Written with Claude (Anthropic), which also helped me run the tests. Who did what is at the end. A 2014 Xeon on an X99 board against two Mac Studios. Illustration generated with ChatGPT. This is the third part of a series about running very large language models on hardware nobody wants any more. In the first , a 2013 X79 workstation ran Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, a 125-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model, at 38 tokens per second. In the second , I needed two PCs on gigabit Ethernet to run its 4-bit version at a usable speed. This time I moved up one platform generation. The X99 board arrived on 11 November, I built the machine on the 13th, and on the morning of the 14th, with the lab nice and cool, I ran the whole test series on it: three models, the same engine, the same scripts. It runs the 4-bit model on its own as fast as the two PCs did together. And while I was reading Mac Studio reviews, I realized I had not seen anyone put a machine like this next to one. The machine and what it costs The board is a HUANANZHI X99-T8, one of the Chinese boards that run Intel’s 2014 server Xeons with DDR3 memory instead of DDR4. Mine came with a Xeon E5–2673 v3 already fitted: Haswell-EP, 12 cores and 24 threads at 2.4–3.1 GHz. Unlike the X79’s Ivy Bridge, it has AVX2 and FMA. Eight 16 GB DDR3–1600 registered ECC modules fill its four memory channels: 128 GB, with 51 GB/s of bandwidth on paper. The GPUs are an RTX 4070 and an RTX 3060, 12 GB each, both on PCIe 3.0 x16 slots, capped at 170 and 150 W. The X99 and what it cost. The board with its CPU, the RAM and the power supply are what I paid; the SSD, cooler, case and the two used GPUs are estimates of today’s prices. The platform without GPUs costs €638, less than one new RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB: the cheapest one on Amazon Italy costs €800 this week. The two GPUs, which I already owned, are 59% of the total. The 1 TB SSD is enough for all three models below: they take about 450 GB together. Three models, one morning All three runs used Strata 0.2.13, the open-source (MIT) engine I used in the previous articles. It keeps the most-used experts on the GPUs, keeps the rest in RAM where the CPU computes them, and drafts tokens ahead with the model’s own prediction layer (MTP). The models: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (125B parameters, 6B active per token) at 3.5 bits (IQ3_S) and at 4 bits (Unsloth’s UD-Q4_K_XL). DeepSeek V4.1-Flash , a much bigger mixture of experts (40 layers of 384 experts, six used per token), in Strata’s official 2-bit set. Its files take about 250 GB, including the 111 GB n-gram table. Three large models on the X99, measured on 14 November with Strata 0.2.13. Tokens/s is the median of six whole requests; the quality figures are Strata’s. “Tokens/s” is measured on the whole request, overhead included. “Decode only” is the engine’s own timing while it writes. I use the first one everywhere below, because it is what I wait for. The 3.5-bit model runs at 46 tokens per second. My main PC, with two RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB, a Ryzen 7 3700X and 64 GB of DDR4, does 56.5 under the same chat settings (256K context, vision on). The X99 gets 82% of it. The 4-bit model is the X99’s real result. Strata wants all 77 GB of its experts in RAM. My main PC has 64 GB, so it reads part of them from the SSD and runs at 16.2 tokens per second. In the previous article, two PCs together reached 28.6–30.7. The X99 alone does 28.9 , because 128 GB of DDR3 holds every expert. Here, RAM capacity mattered more than anything else, and it was also the cheapest part of the machine. DeepSeek runs at 9.3 tokens per second , just under the 10 I consider usable for real work. The day before, I tried it with an experimental branch of Strata that lets a second PC lend its GPU as an expert server over gigabit Ethernet. On that branch the X99 alone did 9.7. With my main PC holding 1,851 experts (15.9 GB) it reached 11.5 tokens per second, and 12.2 when the experts in VRAM were allowed to follow the conversation. On code, the 2-bit DeepSeek did at least as well as the two Qwen files. I gave each model twelve programming exercises with unit tests: an expression evaluator, Roman numerals, wildcard matching, date arithmetic and so on. The Qwen models ran them twice, DeepSeek once. DeepSeek failed only the expression evaluator, which every model failed. With twelve exercises, none of these differences is more than noise: not 18 against 19 between the two Qwen files, and not DeepSeek’s 11 out of 12 against them. The failures do differ: the 3.5-bit model got the Gregorian dates wrong and the wildcards right, the 4-bit model the opposite. Power I have no wall meter, so these are the components: the CPU package and the RAM from Intel RAPL, the GPUs from the NVIDIA driver. Component power on the X99, from Intel RAPL (CPU and RAM) and the NVIDIA driver (GPUs). Power at the wall was not measured. With a model loaded and nothing to do, the machine sits at 73–74 W, and at 90 W with DeepSeek. Almost half of the idle power is the RAM: eight registered DDR3 modules draw 33 W doing nothing. Adding the power supply’s losses and about 25 W for the board, disks and fans, I estimate about 320 W at the wall while generating, and about 100 W idle . The CPU never went above 47 °C. What a Mac Studio does with the same models Apple sells the Mac Studio as the machine for local AI, and on these models it is fast. I did not measure the Macs, and none of their numbers comes from the same test as mine: other prompts, other sampling, and on the Ultras another engine. The ratios below are approximate, and I give both ends wherever the choice of figure changes them. I found three sets of numbers I trust: M5 Max 128 GB: Strata’s own measurements ( MAC.md , DEEPSEEK_MAC.md ), with Strata’s Metal engine and the same quantizations I used. M5 Ultra 256 GB and M3 Ultra 512 GB: MacStories’ review , with the oMLX engine and a 4-bit MLX build of the same Qwen model. Prices: Italian list prices. The X99 against three Mac Studios. The Mac figures are not mine: Strata’s documentation for the M5 Max, MacStories for the two Ultras, from tests that differ from mine. How the tests differ: Strata measured the M5 Max on a 200-token story with greedy decoding. I took the story figure; on a short question the same Mac did 101.9 (3.5-bit) and 94.0 (4-bit). MacStories measured the Ultras at temperature 0 with thinking off. I took the 512-token answer after a 16K prompt; on short prompts the M5 Ultra did about 108 and the M3 Ultra about 70. The Mac figures are decode rates. Mine are whole requests: seven different prompts at temperature 0.7 with thinking on. My decode-only rates are 55.5 and 34.2. The first two choices flatter the X99 and the third flatters the Macs. What the table says: The M5 Max costs 3.8 times as much and is 2 to 2.6 times as fast , or up to 3.3 times at 4 bits on Strata’s short question. At 3.5 bits it reads prompts about as fast as the X99. At 4 bits it reads them 1.5 to 1.7 times faster. The M5 Ultra costs 8.1 times as much and is 3 times as fast at 4 bits , or 3.7 times on short prompts. It reads prompts 3.7 times faster. The base M5 Ultra (€6,699, 96 GB) cannot keep the 4-bit model in memory. Strata’s Mac page asks for about 91 GB resident and recommends a 128 GB Mac for this file. MacStories’ MLX build peaked at 155 GB of process memory. The 256 GB option adds €4,400, and the configuration MacStories tested, with the 80-core GPU, costs €12,529. The M3 Ultra is closer than I expected. It was Apple’s top machine for local AI until September. On the 4-bit model it writes 1.9 times as fast as the X99, or 2.4 times on short prompts, and reads prompts 1.5 times as fast. DeepSeek is where the gap is smallest. The M5 Max writes 15 to 16 tokens per second at 2 bits, 1.6 to 1.7 times the X99, and reads prompts about twice as fast. This model does not fit in the Mac’s memory: Strata keeps about 68 GB of its experts resident there and reads the rest from the SSD. Per euro, on the table’s figures, the X99 is 1.5 to 1.9 times better than the M5 Max and 2.7 times better than the M5 Ultra. With the Macs’ short-prompt figures, that narrows to 1.2 to 1.7 times and to 2.2 times. The electricity argument The usual answer is that the Mac pays for itself on the power bill. It does draw much less: Apple lists 7 W idle for the M5 Max and 9 W for the M5 Ultra, against my ~100 W. So I did the sums. Nothing in this section is measured. The X99’s wall power is my estimate, the Macs’ power while generating is my assumption, and the years below come from a simple scenario, not from a meter. They show the order of magnitude, not a result. Assumptions: Electricity price: €0.30 per kWh all-in. That is deliberately high, which favours the Mac. X99: about 320 W at the wall while generating and 100 W idle, my estimates. Macs while generating: 90 W for the M5 Max and 200 W for the M5 Ultra, against Apple’s maximums of 200 and 385 W. These are my assumptions. Model: the 4-bit Qwen, at the speeds in the table. How long the Mac’s lower power bill takes to cover its extra price, on the 4-bit model at €0.30 per kWh. A scenario built on estimated and assumed power, not a measurement. The Mac’s lower power draw pays back its price only if the machine generates around the clock for years. For anyone who uses a model the way I do, a few hours a day, it never does. This does not depend on my guesses for the Macs. If a Mac used no electricity at all, the X99’s whole bill in the first scenario would be about €225 a year: 19 years to pay back the M5 Max, 49 for the M5 Ultra. Generating nonstop, the X99’s electricity costs €0.93 per million tokens: about 5 years for the M5 Max and 13 for the Ultra. What the Mac does buy is real: two to almost four times the speed, depending on the Mac and the test; near silence; a box that fits on a desk; a warranty, new parts, and a resale value in five years; with the Ultra, prompts read 3.7 times faster. If you run coding agents all day and wait on every answer, that is worth paying for. If you want a 125B model to talk to, the X99 runs the same model at a quarter to half the speed, for an eighth to a quarter of the money. The cheap part, again At the end of the X79 article I wrote that the cheap part is the one nobody is looking for . The X99 says it again, louder: RAM: the 128 GB of DDR3 that made the 4-bit model possible cost €100. On a Mac, going from 96 to 256 GB costs €4,400. Board and CPU: both together cost €179. The expensive parts in this machine are the two GPUs, and they are mid-range cards from 2021 and 2023. The machine stays on my bench as a working computer: it already runs a copy of my daily chat, on the 3.5-bit model, with 128 GB of RAM behind it. Method Engine: Strata 0.2.13 with its own packaged engines, int8 KV cache, KV resident window of 32K, vision on, MTP drafting (4 draft tokens; 61–62% accepted on the Qwen models). The CPU’s sustained power limit was set to 105 W; the GPUs were capped at 170 W (RTX 4070) and 150 W (RTX 3060). The 3.5-bit run used the same configuration as my daily chat (256K context); the 4-bit and DeepSeek runs used 128K. Model files: ISTA-DASLab’s IQ3_S, Unsloth’s UD-Q4_K_XL (the original release that Strata pins; a 111 GB download, 77 GB of it routed experts) and Strata’s official DeepSeek V4.1-Flash 2.00 bpw set, all installed by Strata’s setup and checked against its hashes. Sizes are in decimal GB. The 3.5-bit files were on a SATA SSD; the others on an NVMe drive that this board connects at PCIe 2.0 x4 (1.5 GB/s). Start-up times depend on that. Speed: seven different prompts, 400 tokens each, thinking on, temperature 0.7. The first run is discarded to let the expert cache settle, and I report the median of the other six. Ranges: 39.7–50.6 (3.5-bit), 25.3–32.6 (4-bit), 7.8–9.9 (DeepSeek). “Decode only” is the engine’s own timing without request overhead. Long prompt: a 17,688-token log (16,293 for DeepSeek’s tokenizer) with a password hidden in it, not seen by the engine before. Coding test: twelve Python exercises with unit tests, temperature 0.2, thinking off, up to 3,000 tokens per answer; two rounds for the Qwen models, one for DeepSeek. Quality figures are Strata’s, not mine: QUANTS.md for Qwen (top-1 agreement with Q8_0) and DEEPSEEK41.md for DeepSeek (against the original model). Power: CPU package and DRAM energy from Intel RAPL counters over each phase; GPU power from nvidia-smi every second. Board, disks, fans and power-supply losses are not measured. The wall figures (components ÷ 0.9 + 25 W) are estimates. Main PC comparison: Ryzen 7 3700X, 64 GB DDR4, 2× RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB, the same Strata files; 3.5-bit at my chat settings, 4-bit measured alone for the previous article. Expert server test: 13 November, Strata’s experimental dsv41-vision-link branch built from source, my main PC as the expert server over gigabit Ethernet. Mac numbers: not measured by me. M5 Max, Qwen: Strata’s MAC.md (macOS 27.2, greedy, 200 generated tokens, MTP on, decode rate; engine version not recorded). Story: 94.7 (IQ3_S) and 73.7 (UD-Q4_K_XL). Short question: 101.9 and 94.0. Prompts: the warm rate on 4K and 32K prompts. That page reports contexts up to 32K. M5 Max, DeepSeek: Strata’s DEEPSEEK_MAC.md (2.00 bpw, engine 0.2.7.1, six experts per token): 15.2–16.2 tokens/s on short answers, 13.8–15.1 after a 14,000-token prompt, which it read at 479–512 tokens/s. Another model’s server was loaded on that Mac during the test, so an idle Mac may be faster. M5 Ultra 256 GB and M3 Ultra 512 GB: MacStories, oMLX 0.7.0, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next oQ4e, temperature 0, thinking off, multi-token prediction on. Writing speed is a 512-token answer after a 16K prompt; reading speed is on a 15,519-token prompt. Short-prompt prose: about 108 (M5 Ultra) and 70 (M3 Ultra). Mac power: Apple’s published idle and maximum figures, which Apple measured on a 36 GB M5 Max and a 512 GB M5 Ultra; the generating figures are my assumptions. Electricity: 4-bit speeds (28.9, 73.7 and 87.8 tokens/s). “The same work” means the Mac produces the tokens the X99 produces flat out, then idles. The first scenario gives both machines the same two hours of generation. Prices: what I paid for the board with the CPU, the RAM and the power supply; the GPU, SSD, cooler and case prices are my estimates of today’s market. The RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB price is the cheapest new card on Amazon Italy in mid-November 2026. Mac prices are Italian Apple list prices at launch: M5 Max with 128 GB and a 512 GB SSD €5,909 (€6,239 with 1 TB); M5 Ultra 96 GB €6,699; M5 Ultra with 36-core CPU, 80-core GPU, 256 GB and 1 TB €12,529. How this was made I built the machine and decided what to measure. Claude (Anthropic) worked with me on the tests and on the text. On the testing side, it helped me set up and run the test series on my machines and read the logs. On the editing side, it wrote the article from my notes and measurements, checked every number taken from Strata’s documentation, MacStories and Apple against its source, and recomputed the ratios and the electricity sums. I reviewed and edited the text. Every measurement of the X99 and of my main PC was run on my own machines. A 2014 Xeon vs Two Mac Studios on a 125B Model: Who Wins? was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

What a Mac Studio does with the same models

Apple sells the Mac Studio as the machine for local AI, and on these models it is fast. I did not measure the Macs, and none of their numbers comes from the same test as mine: other prompts, other sampling, and on the Ultras another engine. The ratios below are approximate, and I give both ends wherever the choice of figure changes them.

I found three sets of numbers I trust:

  • M5 Max 128 GB: Strata’s own measurements (MAC.md, DEEPSEEK_MAC.md), with Strata’s Metal engine and the same quantizations I used.
  • M5 Ultra 256 GB and M3 Ultra 512 GB: MacStories’ review, with the oMLX engine and a 4-bit MLX build of the same Qwen model.
  • Prices: Italian list prices.
The X99 against three Mac Studios. The Mac figures are not mine: Strata’s documentation for the M5 Max, MacStories for the two Ultras, from tests that differ from mine.

How the tests differ:

  • Strata measured the M5 Max on a 200-token story with greedy decoding. I took the story figure; on a short question the same Mac did 101.9 (3.5-bit) and 94.0 (4-bit).
  • MacStories measured the Ultras at temperature 0 with thinking off. I took the 512-token answer after a 16K prompt; on short prompts the M5 Ultra did about 108 and the M3 Ultra about 70.
  • The Mac figures are decode rates. Mine are whole requests: seven different prompts at temperature 0.7 with thinking on. My decode-only rates are 55.5 and 34.2.

The first two choices flatter the X99 and the third flatters the Macs.

What the table says:

  • The M5 Max costs 3.8 times as much and is 2 to 2.6 times as fast, or up to 3.3 times at 4 bits on Strata’s short question. At 3.5 bits it reads prompts about as fast as the X99. At 4 bits it reads them 1.5 to 1.7 times faster.
  • The M5 Ultra costs 8.1 times as much and is 3 times as fast at 4 bits, or 3.7 times on short prompts. It reads prompts 3.7 times faster.
  • The base M5 Ultra (€6,699, 96 GB) cannot keep the 4-bit model in memory. Strata’s Mac page asks for about 91 GB resident and recommends a 128 GB Mac for this file. MacStories’ MLX build peaked at 155 GB of process memory. The 256 GB option adds €4,400, and the configuration MacStories tested, with the 80-core GPU, costs €12,529.
  • The M3 Ultra is closer than I expected. It was Apple’s top machine for local AI until September. On the 4-bit model it writes 1.9 times as fast as the X99, or 2.4 times on short prompts, and reads prompts 1.5 times as fast.
  • DeepSeek is where the gap is smallest. The M5 Max writes 15 to 16 tokens per second at 2 bits, 1.6 to 1.7 times the X99, and reads prompts about twice as fast. This model does not fit in the Mac’s memory: Strata keeps about 68 GB of its experts resident there and reads the rest from the SSD.

Per euro, on the table’s figures, the X99 is 1.5 to 1.9 times better than the M5 Max and 2.7 times better than the M5 Ultra. With the Macs’ short-prompt figures, that narrows to 1.2 to 1.7 times and to 2.2 times.

The electricity argument

The usual answer is that the Mac pays for itself on the power bill. It does draw much less: Apple lists 7 W idle for the M5 Max and 9 W for the M5 Ultra, against my ~100 W. So I did the sums.

Nothing in this section is measured. The X99’s wall power is my estimate, the Macs’ power while generating is my assumption, and the years below come from a simple scenario, not from a meter. They show the order of magnitude, not a result.

Assumptions:

  • Electricity price: €0.30 per kWh all-in. That is deliberately high, which favours the Mac.
  • X99: about 320 W at the wall while generating and 100 W idle, my estimates.
  • Macs while generating: 90 W for the M5 Max and 200 W for the M5 Ultra, against Apple’s maximums of 200 and 385 W. These are my assumptions.
  • Model: the 4-bit Qwen, at the speeds in the table.
How long the Mac’s lower power bill takes to cover its extra price, on the 4-bit model at €0.30 per kWh. A scenario built on estimated and assumed power, not a measurement.

The Mac’s lower power draw pays back its price only if the machine generates around the clock for years. For anyone who uses a model the way I do, a few hours a day, it never does.

This does not depend on my guesses for the Macs. If a Mac used no electricity at all, the X99’s whole bill in the first scenario would be about €225 a year: 19 years to pay back the M5 Max, 49 for the M5 Ultra. Generating nonstop, the X99’s electricity costs €0.93 per million tokens: about 5 years for the M5 Max and 13 for the Ultra.

What the Mac does buy is real:

  • two to almost four times the speed, depending on the Mac and the test;
  • near silence;
  • a box that fits on a desk;
  • a warranty, new parts, and a resale value in five years;
  • with the Ultra, prompts read 3.7 times faster.

If you run coding agents all day and wait on every answer, that is worth paying for. If you want a 125B model to talk to, the X99 runs the same model at a quarter to half the speed, for an eighth to a quarter of the money.

The cheap part, again

At the end of the X79 article I wrote that the cheap part is the one nobody is looking for. The X99 says it again, louder:

  • RAM: the 128 GB of DDR3 that made the 4-bit model possible cost €100. On a Mac, going from 96 to 256 GB costs €4,400.
  • Board and CPU: both together cost €179.

The expensive parts in this machine are the two GPUs, and they are mid-range cards from 2021 and 2023.

The machine stays on my bench as a working computer: it already runs a copy of my daily chat, on the 3.5-bit model, with 128 GB of RAM behind it.

Method
  • Engine: Strata 0.2.13 with its own packaged engines, int8 KV cache, KV resident window of 32K, vision on, MTP drafting (4 draft tokens; 61–62% accepted on the Qwen models). The CPU’s sustained power limit was set to 105 W; the GPUs were capped at 170 W (RTX 4070) and 150 W (RTX 3060). The 3.5-bit run used the same configuration as my daily chat (256K context); the 4-bit and DeepSeek runs used 128K.
  • Model files: ISTA-DASLab’s IQ3_S, Unsloth’s UD-Q4_K_XL (the original release that Strata pins; a 111 GB download, 77 GB of it routed experts) and Strata’s official DeepSeek V4.1-Flash 2.00 bpw set, all installed by Strata’s setup and checked against its hashes. Sizes are in decimal GB. The 3.5-bit files were on a SATA SSD; the others on an NVMe drive that this board connects at PCIe 2.0 x4 (1.5 GB/s). Start-up times depend on that.
  • Speed: seven different prompts, 400 tokens each, thinking on, temperature 0.7. The first run is discarded to let the expert cache settle, and I report the median of the other six. Ranges: 39.7–50.6 (3.5-bit), 25.3–32.6 (4-bit), 7.8–9.9 (DeepSeek). “Decode only” is the engine’s own timing without request overhead.
  • Long prompt: a 17,688-token log (16,293 for DeepSeek’s tokenizer) with a password hidden in it, not seen by the engine before.
  • Coding test: twelve Python exercises with unit tests, temperature 0.2, thinking off, up to 3,000 tokens per answer; two rounds for the Qwen models, one for DeepSeek.
  • Quality figures are Strata’s, not mine: QUANTS.md for Qwen (top-1 agreement with Q8_0) and DEEPSEEK41.md for DeepSeek (against the original model).
  • Power: CPU package and DRAM energy from Intel RAPL counters over each phase; GPU power from nvidia-smi every second. Board, disks, fans and power-supply losses are not measured. The wall figures (components ÷ 0.9 + 25 W) are estimates.
  • Main PC comparison: Ryzen 7 3700X, 64 GB DDR4, 2× RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB, the same Strata files; 3.5-bit at my chat settings, 4-bit measured alone for the previous article.
  • Expert server test: 13 November, Strata’s experimental dsv41-vision-link branch built from source, my main PC as the expert server over gigabit Ethernet.
  • Mac numbers: not measured by me.
  • M5 Max, Qwen: Strata’s MAC.md (macOS 27.2, greedy, 200 generated tokens, MTP on, decode rate; engine version not recorded). Story: 94.7 (IQ3_S) and 73.7 (UD-Q4_K_XL). Short question: 101.9 and 94.0. Prompts: the warm rate on 4K and 32K prompts. That page reports contexts up to 32K.
  • M5 Max, DeepSeek: Strata’s DEEPSEEK_MAC.md (2.00 bpw, engine 0.2.7.1, six experts per token): 15.2–16.2 tokens/s on short answers, 13.8–15.1 after a 14,000-token prompt, which it read at 479–512 tokens/s. Another model’s server was loaded on that Mac during the test, so an idle Mac may be faster.
  • M5 Ultra 256 GB and M3 Ultra 512 GB: MacStories, oMLX 0.7.0, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next oQ4e, temperature 0, thinking off, multi-token prediction on. Writing speed is a 512-token answer after a 16K prompt; reading speed is on a 15,519-token prompt. Short-prompt prose: about 108 (M5 Ultra) and 70 (M3 Ultra).
  • Mac power: Apple’s published idle and maximum figures, which Apple measured on a 36 GB M5 Max and a 512 GB M5 Ultra; the generating figures are my assumptions.
  • Electricity: 4-bit speeds (28.9, 73.7 and 87.8 tokens/s). “The same work” means the Mac produces the tokens the X99 produces flat out, then idles. The first scenario gives both machines the same two hours of generation.
  • Prices: what I paid for the board with the CPU, the RAM and the power supply; the GPU, SSD, cooler and case prices are my estimates of today’s market. The RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB price is the cheapest new card on Amazon Italy in mid-November 2026. Mac prices are Italian Apple list prices at launch: M5 Max with 128 GB and a 512 GB SSD €5,909 (€6,239 with 1 TB); M5 Ultra 96 GB €6,699; M5 Ultra with 36-core CPU, 80-core GPU, 256 GB and 1 TB €12,529.
How this was made

I built the machine and decided what to measure. Claude (Anthropic) worked with me on the tests and on the text. On the testing side, it helped me set up and run the test series on my machines and read the logs. On the editing side, it wrote the article from my notes and measurements, checked every number taken from Strata’s documentation, MacStories and Apple against its source, and recomputed the ratios and the electricity sums. I reviewed and edited the text. Every measurement of the X99 and of my main PC was run on my own machines.

items.title: How a Chinese Energy Company Is Outpacing the U.S. on AI Power Technology
items.summary: Ulanqab, a city in China’s Inner Mongolia region, used to be known for its potatoes. Now it’s where a Chinese renewable energy firm is trying out a new way to plug in AI chips that shows China’s edge in the power systems that data centers need. Envision Energy has started using an 800-volt direct-current system to power computing workloads at its data center there, the Shanghai-based company said earlier this month. The setup, which wastes less electricity between the grid and the chips, is widely expected to become the standard way to power increasingly energy-hungry AI servers, and Envision says it is the first to run it in a functioning data center. Nvidia and its partners are still preparing the same kind of system for their next generation of AI hardware, due next year.

items.title: ‘SNL’ parodies Jensen Huang and other tech billionaires: ‘May I pleasure you in an industry secret?’
items.summary: The 'Saturday Night Live' cast as tech billionaires Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, and Peter Thiel. Saturday Night Live/NBC John Mulaney and the "Saturday Night Live" cast poked fun at the Nvidia scandal this week. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO last week after admitting to an affair. Former 'SNL' cast member Bowen Yang returned to play Huang: "It's me. Jensen 'hide your wife' Huang." This week's "Saturday Night Live" cold open was a who's-who of the AI revolution. Comedian John Mulaney kicked off the episode by playing a CIA officer conducting national security training for tech billionaires. Specifically, how to identify a spy. Mulaney's character is joined by Palantir cofounder Peter Thiel (James Austin Johnson), OpenAI CEO Sam Altman (Ben Marshall), Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei (Jane Wickline), Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg (Andrew Dismukes), and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk (Jeremy Culhane). "America needs you to learn the difference between a woman who actually wants to have sex with you, and a woman who is clearly a spy," Mulaney said. "You all saw how former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned this week after he was caught having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy." Last Sunday, Nvidia's board of directors said it would investigate whether Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort" on the same day he admitted to an extramarital affair in a memo to staff. Huang resigned from his position days later. On "Saturday Night Live," Mulaney's character empathized with the tech billionaires. "Look, I can't imagine how disorienting this has been for you. To go from these bug-eyed little weirdos to being gods," Mulaney said. "Never in the history of our species have people as pale and as strange as you, A: survived, and B: been given all the world's wealth and power." Mulaney asked the tech executives why someone "very beautiful" would be interested in them. "Because I have a good personality and normal, human mannerisms?" Marshall's Altman said. Zuckerberg, played by Dismukes, guessed it's because "she's comforted by my Meta glasses recording her at all times." Wickline's Amodei theorized it's because "she's using me... for my body." Mulaney then asked the group to pretend an attractive woman approached them at the bar and asked, "What are you working on?" Amodei and Zuckerberg weighed in. "I would say, Madam, what a pleasure to see you this evening. May I interest you in an industry secret?" Amodei said. Zuckerberg said he would "assume that she wanted to sleep with the man who created the Metaverse, as all women do." Near the end, former 'SNL' cast member Bowen Yang returned as Huang. "It's me. Jensen 'hide your wife' Huang," Yang says as he joins the other tech billionaires. "Ladies, when you invite Jensen over, you know what's about to go down. The S&P 500." He added, "That's right. I'm into BDSM: Breakin' da stock market." Nvidia lost more than $500 billion in market value over the last week. Yang's Huang cautioned his fellow tech executives against being like him. "Remember, women don't like guys like us. That's how we became guys like us," he said. In real life, some Nvidia loyalists are hoping the board will reinstate Huang . Nvidia's board of directors said it's considering internal and external candidates for the permanent CEO position . Read the original article on Business Insider
