items.title: You Will Understand 10 Years of LLMs
items.summary:
My new video, In 19 Minutes, You'll Understand 10 Years of LLMs , follows one question through every era of language models: "What is the capital of France?" This post is the developer version. It goes through every chapter of the video with the actual terms and numbers. Where the video shows a model's output, we ran an open model ourselves, so you get the code to reproduce it. pip install torch transformers accelerate All outputs below are what we got on an RTX 4070 Ti. Yours may differ slightly with hardware and precision. TL;DR timeline Year Milestone What it fixed What it left open 1948–51 Shannon's next-letter game "predict what comes next" as a measurable idea no machine could play it well 2013 word2vec words become vectors that capture meaning one vector per word, whatever the context 1997–2014 RNN, LSTM, seq2seq read sentences, translate one fixed-size summary per sentence 2014 attention (Bahdanau) the decoder looks back at every word still reads one word at a time 2017 the Transformer no recurrence: parallel training on GPUs writing is still one token at a time 2018–19 BERT, GPT-1, GPT-2 pretraining on raw text the model continues text, it doesn't answer 2020–22 scaling laws, GPT-3, Chinchilla predictable gains from size and data still not helpful 2022 InstructGPT / RLHF, ChatGPT a second training stage teaches it to answer serving at scale is expensive 2023–24 LLaMA, KV-cache sharing, mixture of experts cheaper, faster, longer contexts running out of human text 2024–25 o1, DeepSeek-R1 models learn to think before answering thinking helps, doesn't guarantee 2026 agents, hybrid attention plan, use tools, act 0. The quiz page (Experiment 1) Before chatbots, a language model's only job was to continue text. Ask GPT-2 XL (1.5B parameters, 2019): from transformers import AutoTokenizer , AutoModelForCausalLM import torch name = "openai-community/gpt2-xl" tok = AutoTokenizer . from_pretrained ( name ) model = AutoModelForCausalLM . from_pretrained ( name ) . eval ( ) ids = tok ( "What is the capital of France?" , return_tensors = "pt" ) . input_ids out = model . generate ( ids , max_new_tokens = 60 , do_sample = False , pad_token_id = tok . eos_token_id ) print ( tok . decode ( out [ 0 ] [ ids . shape [ 1 ] : ] ) ) The capital of France is Paris. What is the capital of the United States? The capital of the United States is Washington, D.C. What is the capital of the United Kingdom? The capital of the United Kingdom is London. What It's not answering; it's writing a quiz page. We'll come back to why. 1. Before 2017: the road to attention Shannon's game (1948, 1951) Claude Shannon asked how predictable English is. Letters don't come at random: counted in Pride and Prejudice , after a T comes an H 29% of the time; after a Q, a U 99.85% of the time. In 1948 he generated text that follows these odds with a book: pick a letter, open another page, find that letter, copy the one after it, repeat. Letter pairs give almost-words; word pairs give "The head and in frontal attack on an English writer that the character of this point…" Not English, but closer. The more context, the closer. In 1951 he made it a game with people: guess the next letter. On one passage they were right on the first try 79 times out of 102 . He estimated that a letter of English carries about 1 bit of new information, against about 4.75 bits if letters were random. That's the objective LLMs still train on: predict the next token. Words become vectors (2013) A word ID ( king = #4812 ) says nothing about meaning. word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) gives each word a vector of a few hundred numbers (300 in the classic setup), learned by predicting a word's neighbours over billions of words. Words used in similar contexts end up close, and the space has structure: king − man + woman ≈ queen (the nearest word, excluding the three inputs). The limit: one vector per word. The "bank" of a river and the bank with your money get the same vector. RNN, LSTM, seq2seq (1997–2014) A recurrent neural network reads one token at a time and updates a hidden state, a running memory. Two problems: the state is overwritten at every step, so early words fade; and in training, the error signal has to flow backwards through every step and shrinks on the way (vanishing gradients). The LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) adds a cell state, a memory lane that runs straight through every step, with gates that decide what to write, what to read and (since 2000) what to forget. By 2014, sequence to sequence translated with two of them: an encoder packs the English sentence into one fixed vector (8,000 numbers in Google's 4-layer version), and a decoder unpacks it into French, one word at a time. On basic encoder-decoders, quality dropped as sentences got longer: one fixed vector is a bottleneck. Attention (2014) Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio kept a vector for every source word, and at each output step let the decoder compute a weighted mix of all of them. To write "zone", it weighs "Area" most. Long sentences stopped falling apart. One problem remained: everything was still sequential. items.summary_html:
My new video, In 19 Minutes, You'll Understand 10 Years of LLMs, follows one question through every era of language models: "What is the capital of France?"

This post is the developer version. It goes through every chapter of the video with the actual terms and numbers. Where the video shows a model's output, we ran an open model ourselves, so you get the code to reproduce it.

pip install torch transformers accelerate

All outputs below are what we got on an RTX 4070 Ti. Yours may differ slightly with hardware and precision.

TL;DR timeline
Year Milestone What it fixed What it left open 1948–51 Shannon's next-letter game "predict what comes next" as a measurable idea no machine could play it well 2013 word2vec words become vectors that capture meaning one vector per word, whatever the context 1997–2014 RNN, LSTM, seq2seq read sentences, translate one fixed-size summary per sentence 2014 attention (Bahdanau) the decoder looks back at every word still reads one word at a time 2017 the Transformer no recurrence: parallel training on GPUs writing is still one token at a time 2018–19 BERT, GPT-1, GPT-2 pretraining on raw text the model continues text, it doesn't answer 2020–22 scaling laws, GPT-3, Chinchilla predictable gains from size and data still not helpful 2022 InstructGPT / RLHF, ChatGPT a second training stage teaches it to answer serving at scale is expensive 2023–24 LLaMA, KV-cache sharing, mixture of experts cheaper, faster, longer contexts running out of human text 2024–25 o1, DeepSeek-R1 models learn to think before answering thinking helps, doesn't guarantee 2026 agents, hybrid attention plan, use tools, act
0. The quiz page (Experiment 1)

Before chatbots, a language model's only job was to continue text. Ask GPT-2 XL (1.5B parameters, 2019):

from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM
import torch

name = "openai-community/gpt2-xl"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(name).eval()

ids = tok("What is the capital of France?", return_tensors="pt").input_ids
out = model.generate(ids, max_new_tokens=60, do_sample=False, pad_token_id=tok.eos_token_id)
print(tok.decode(out[0][ids.shape[1]:]))

The capital of France is Paris.

What is the capital of the United States?

The capital of the United States is Washington, D.C.

What is the capital of the United Kingdom?

The capital of the United Kingdom is London.

What

It's not answering; it's writing a quiz page. We'll come back to why.

1. Before 2017: the road to attention Shannon's game (1948, 1951)

Claude Shannon asked how predictable English is. Letters don't come at random: counted in Pride and Prejudice, after a T comes an H 29% of the time; after a Q, a U 99.85% of the time.

In 1948 he generated text that follows these odds with a book: pick a letter, open another page, find that letter, copy the one after it, repeat. Letter pairs give almost-words; word pairs give "The head and in frontal attack on an English writer that the character of this point…" Not English, but closer. The more context, the closer.

In 1951 he made it a game with people: guess the next letter. On one passage they were right on the first try 79 times out of 102. He estimated that a letter of English carries about 1 bit of new information, against about 4.75 bits if letters were random.

That's the objective LLMs still train on: predict the next token.

Words become vectors (2013)

A word ID (king = #4812) says nothing about meaning. word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) gives each word a vector of a few hundred numbers (300 in the classic setup), learned by predicting a word's neighbours over billions of words. Words used in similar contexts end up close, and the space has structure: king − man + woman ≈ queen (the nearest word, excluding the three inputs).

The limit: one vector per word. The "bank" of a river and the bank with your money get the same vector.

RNN, LSTM, seq2seq (1997–2014)

A recurrent neural network reads one token at a time and updates a hidden state, a running memory. Two problems: the state is overwritten at every step, so early words fade; and in training, the error signal has to flow backwards through every step and shrinks on the way (vanishing gradients).

The LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) adds a cell state, a memory lane that runs straight through every step, with gates that decide what to write, what to read and (since 2000) what to forget.

By 2014, sequence to sequence translated with two of them: an encoder packs the English sentence into one fixed vector (8,000 numbers in Google's 4-layer version), and a decoder unpacks it into French, one word at a time. On basic encoder-decoders, quality dropped as sentences got longer: one fixed vector is a bottleneck.

Attention (2014)

Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio kept a vector for every source word, and at each output step let the decoder compute a weighted mix of all of them. To write "zone", it weighs "Area" most. Long sentences stopped falling apart.

One problem remained: everything was still sequential. Step 50 needs the state from step 49, while GPUs are built to do thousands of operations at once.

2. 2017: the Transformer

"Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., Google, June 2017; author order random, the paper says so) kept attention and removed recurrence. Every token attends to every other token, all at once: self-attention.

What attention does (Experiment 2)

Google's example: "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired" (it = the animal) vs "…too wide" (it = the street). Each token produces a query; every token has a key and a value. Query-key matches (dot products, scaled, then softmax) give each token a share, and "it" takes in a weighted mix of the values.

You can watch this in BERT (12 layers × 12 heads = 144 heads). We searched for the head whose focus flips most between the two sentences: layer 7, head 11 (index 6 and 10 in code):

from transformers import AutoModel

btok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")
bert = AutoModel.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased", output_attentions=True).eval()

for end in ["tired", "wide"]:
    s = f"The animal didn't cross the street because it was too {end}."
    enc = btok(s, return_tensors="pt")
    toks = btok.convert_ids_to_tokens(enc.input_ids[0])
    with torch.no_grad():
        att = bert(**enc).attentions[6][0, 10]        # layer 7, head 11
    it = toks.index("it")
    print(end, {w: round(att[it, toks.index(w)].item(), 3) for w in ["animal", "street"]})

tired {'animal': 0.284, 'street': 0.067}
wide {'animal': 0.012, 'street': 0.59}

We picked this head because it flips the most; other heads learn other links (the previous word, the next word, sentence boundaries). Running many heads side by side is multi-head attention.

The whole machine (Experiment 3)

Text is cut into tokens, pieces from a fixed vocabulary (byte-pair encoding; 50,257 pieces for GPT-2):

gtok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("openai-community/gpt2")
for text in ["The capital of France is Paris.", "unbelievably", "strawberry", " strawberry"]:
    print(repr(text), [gtok.decode([i]) for i in gtok(text).input_ids])

'The capital of France is Paris.' ['The', ' capital', ' of', ' France', ' is', ' Paris', '.']
'unbelievably' ['un', 'bel', 'iev', 'ably']
'strawberry' ['st', 'raw', 'berry']
' strawberry' [' strawberry']

Then:

  • each token becomes an embedding vector (word2vec's idea, learned with the model) plus a positional encoding, since attention alone has no notion of order;
  • each layer has an attention block (tokens share information) and a feed-forward block (each token processed on its own);
  • the 2017 model stacks 6 encoder layers (read the English) and 6 decoder layers (write the French);
  • the output is a probability for every possible next token.
Why it won: parallel training

In training, the whole target sentence is known, so the model learns from every position at once and the GPUs are fully used. The big model trained in 3.5 days on one machine with 8 P100 GPUs and set records (BLEU 28.4 English–German, 41.8 English–French) at a fraction of the previous training cost.

Writing stayed sequential: the next token doesn't exist until it's chosen.

3. 2018–2019: reading vs writing

The blueprint split in two.

  • BERT (Google, 2018): encoder only. Training game: mask a word and predict it from both sides. Great at understanding, can't generate.
  • GPT (OpenAI): decoder only, with causal masking. Training game: Shannon's, predict the next token from the left.

Next-token prediction needs no labels: any text is a lesson. That's pretraining, and it turns the internet into training data.

  • GPT-1 (2018): about 117M parameters, 12 layers, 7,000 unpublished books.
  • GPT-2 (2019): same objective, 1.5B parameters, 48 layers, 8 million web pages. OpenAI initially held back the full model citing "concerns about malicious applications".

Experiment 1 now makes sense: GPT-2 continues documents, and on the web a question is often followed by its answer, then another question. It could also do untrained tasks by prompt alone: add TL;DR: after an article and it writes a rough summary.

4. 2020–2022: scale

Scaling laws (Kaplan et al., OpenAI, January 2020): train many models from tiny to large, and on log-log axes, loss falls along straight lines as parameters, data and compute grow. Not a law of nature, but a pattern you can plan around.

GPT-3 (2020): nearly the same architecture as GPT-2, but 175B parameters, 96 layers, trained on 300B tokens. It showed in-context learning: give a few examples in the prompt and it continues the pattern.

Experiment 4: in-context learning, already in GPT-2 
def p_next(prompt, word=" Paris"):
    ids = tok(prompt, return_tensors="pt").input_ids
    with torch.no_grad():
        probs = torch.softmax(model(ids).logits[0, -1].float(), -1)
    return probs[tok.encode(word)[0]].item()

zero = "Q: What is the capital of France?\nA:"
few = ("Q: What is the capital of Germany?\nA: Berlin\n"
       "Q: What is the capital of Italy?\nA: Rome\n"
       "Q: What is the capital of France?\nA:")
print(f"zero-shot: {p_next(zero):.2f}   few-shot: {p_next(few):.2f}")   # GPT-2 XL from experiment 1

zero-shot: 0.57   few-shot: 0.99

Chinchilla (DeepMind, 2022) showed the balance was off: models were too big for their data. Chinchilla (70B parameters, 1.4T tokens) beat Gopher (280B, 300B tokens) almost everywhere. Data started to matter as much as size.

5. 2022: teaching it to help

Scale didn't fix behaviour. OpenAI's own example: prompt GPT-3 with "Explain the moon landing to a 6 year old in a few sentences" and it may continue with "Explain the theory of gravity to a 6 year old…"

InstructGPT (January 2022) added a second training stage:

  1. Supervised fine-tuning: people write good answers; the model imitates them.
  2. Reward model: the model writes several answers, people rank them, and a second model learns to predict the ranking.
  3. Reinforcement learning: the language model is optimized against the reward model.

That's RLHF. People preferred a 1.3B InstructGPT model to the 175B GPT-3.

Experiment 5: the two stages in one small model 
name = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct"
ctok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
chat_model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(name).eval()
q = "What is the capital of France?"

chat = ctok.apply_chat_template([{"role": "user", "content": q}], add_generation_prompt=True, return_tensors="pt")
out = chat_model.generate(chat, max_new_tokens=80, do_sample=False)
print("CHAT:", ctok.decode(out[0][chat.shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True))

raw = ctok(q, return_tensors="pt").input_ids
out = chat_model.generate(raw, max_new_tokens=60, do_sample=False)
print("RAW:", ctok.decode(out[0][raw.shape[1]:]))

CHAT: The capital of France is Paris.
RAW:  The capital of France is Paris.

To verify this, I will use a simple Python code snippet to confirm ...

With the chat template, it answers and stops. Without it, it rambles. Knowledge comes from pretraining; manners come from the second stage.

On November 30, 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT, trained this way. A million users in five days, and serving these models at scale became the next problem.

6. 2023–2024: bigger, cheaper, longer

GPT-4 (March 2023): its report "contains no further details about the architecture (including model size)". The frontier went closed; open models like Meta's LLaMA (2023) show what changed inside the 2017 block:

  • RoPE: positions as rotations applied inside attention, instead of added vectors;
  • RMSNorm and SwiGLU: leaner normalization and feed-forward blocks;
  • FlashAttention: the same attention, computed to fit the GPU's fastest memory.

Two harder problems:

Memory: the KV cache. During generation, each new token attends to all previous ones, so the model caches every past token's keys and values in every layer. The cache grows with context length and, for long conversations, can outgrow the model's own weights. Fixes: grouped-query attention (groups of heads share one set of keys/values) and DeepSeek's multi-head latent attention (store a compressed summary). Smaller caches are part of how context windows went from a few thousand tokens to about a million.

Compute: mixture of experts. Every token normally goes through every parameter. A MoE layer splits the feed-forward block into many experts and a router sends each token to just a few. DeepSeek-V3 (December 2024): 671B parameters stored, 37B used per token.

7. 2024–2025: thinking

In December 2024, Ilya Sutskever said at NeurIPS: "Pre-training as we know it will unquestionably end" and "We have but one internet." Epoch AI estimates models will have used up the public human text somewhere between 2026 and 2032.

Gains moved to inference time. Kojima et al. (2022) found that adding "Let's think step by step" took one maths benchmark (MultiArith) from 18% to 79%. A model spends roughly the same compute per token, so writing out steps buys more forward passes, and each step is easier than the whole jump.

  • o1 (OpenAI, September 2024): trained with reinforcement learning to reason before answering; accuracy rose with thinking time. On the AIME 2024 maths competition: GPT-4o 12%, o1 74%.
  • DeepSeek-R1 (January 2025), recipe published: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (maths with known answers, code with tests), rewarding only correct outcomes. R1-Zero's responses grew from about 500 to 9,500 tokens over training, and it started checking its own work: "Wait, wait. Wait. That's an aha moment I can flag here."
Experiment 6: a small model that thinks

DeepSeek also released distilled students of R1. The 1.5B one, with the model card's sampling settings:

name = "deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B"
rtok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
rmodel = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(name, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16).eval()

q = "How many r letters are in the word strawberry?"
chat = rtok.apply_chat_template([{"role": "user", "content": q}], add_generation_prompt=True, return_tensors="pt")
out = rmodel.generate(chat, max_new_tokens=900, do_sample=True, temperature=0.6, top_p=0.95)
print(rtok.decode(out[0][chat.shape[1]:]))

On the capital question, it thought for 255 to 659 tokens and answered "Paris" four times out of five. On strawberry, across five runs: 3, 2, 3, 3, and once 8. Remember experiment 3: " strawberry" is one token, so the model never sees the letters. Thinking helps; it doesn't guarantee. Many models now decide for themselves whether to think, and for how long.

8. Now: senses and agents

Images and audio can be tokenized too, so the same architecture handles them: GPT-4o (2024) took text, images and audio in one network.

Agents run the model in a loop: plan, call a tool (search, code execution, file edits), read the result, repeat. METR measures the length of tasks (in human working time) that agents complete with 50% success, mostly on software tasks: GPT-2 a few seconds, GPT-4 (2023) about four minutes, early 2025 about an hour, and by April 2026 around 17 hours, beyond what their test suite measures reliably.

The architecture keeps moving too. Full attention costs more as context grows, so many new open models keep it in only some layers and use cheaper, recurrent-style layers in between, the RNN idea made trainable in parallel. And in September 2026, DeepSeek described a new model as a "causal encoder-decoder". Nine years later, the encoder is back.

9. 2017 vs today
2017 Transformer Today Structure encoder + decoder mostly decoder-only Positions added sinusoidal stamps rotations inside attention (RoPE) Attention memory every head its own keys/values shared (GQA) or compressed (MLA) Feed-forward one block per layer many experts with a router (MoE) Attention coverage every layer often only some layers Training supervised translation pretraining on trillions of tokens, then human preferences, then reasoning and tool use

Almost every part has been replaced. Two things remain: attention, in some layers at least, and the objective: predict the next token, Shannon's game from 1948.

▶ What happens inside one model when it answers: What Actually Happens When You Press Enter on ChatGPT

items.title: Cramming a New Framework Feels Faster. Your Brain Disagrees.
items.summary: Your brain holds on to what it nearly lost. That sounds backwards. It's also one of the oldest, best-replicated findings in memory research, and most of us code against it every time we pick up something new. Here's the usual pattern. A new framework drops, or the team decides to move to Rust, or there's an interview in two weeks. So you block out a Saturday. Ten hours of docs, tutorials and a toy project. By Sunday night it all makes sense. By the following Thursday you're back on the docs page for the same hook, the same lifetime rule, the same CLI flag. You didn't fail to learn it. You learned it in a shape your brain doesn't keep. Four psychologists, 300 words, nine years The most stubborn test of this came from one family. In the 1980s the psychologist Harry Bahrick, his wife Phyllis and their daughters Lorraine and Audrey, all psychologists, started an experiment on themselves that would run for nine years. Each of them learned 300 foreign-language word pairs, split into sets. Some sets were reviewed 13 times, some 26 times. The gaps between review sessions were 14, 28 or 56 days. Then they stopped, and tested themselves one, two, three and five years later. The wide gaps were slightly worse while they were learning. Words came back less easily at each session. But the long-term numbers flipped. The paper, published in Psychological Science in 1993, reports that 13 sessions spaced 56 days apart gave about the same five-year retention as 26 sessions spaced 14 days apart. Half the study time. Same result. The only thing that changed was the calendar. Four people is a tiny sample, and they were all experts in memory, so I wouldn't stop there. Luckily nobody else did either. The spacing effect, at scale In 2006 Nicholas Cepeda, Harold Pashler and colleagues pulled together the spacing literature in Psychological Bulletin : 317 experiments from 184 articles. Spreading study out beat massing it together, again and again. Two years later, the same group ran the big one. More than 1,350 people learned a set of obscure facts online. After a gap of up to three and a half months they got one review. Then a final test, up to a year later. The best gap depended on how long you wanted to remember. For a test one week away, the sweet spot was roughly 20 to 40 percent of that week. For a test a year away it fell to about 5 to 10 percent of the year, which still means waiting weeks or months before the review. Cepeda also told York University's news office that a gap that's too short hurts far more than one that's a bit too long. So if you want to remember something for a year, reviewing it the next morning and calling it done is the expensive mistake. Coming back a month later is the cheap win. Why it feels like cramming works This is the cruel bit. Nate Kornell, then at Williams College, had people learn GRE-style vocabulary with flashcards on a web app. In one condition they studied one big stack, so each card came back after a long wait. In the other they worked through small stacks, so each card came back quickly. Across his experiments, spacing beat massing for 90 percent of participants. In one experiment the spaced words were recalled 54 percent of the time against 21 percent for massed ones. And yet after the first session, 72 percent of people said massing had worked better. That's the trap every developer knows. When you reread a tutorial straight after reading it, everything feels fluent. Fluent feels like learned. It isn't the same thing. The ease is coming from the fact that the information is still sitting in short-term memory, not from a durable trace. What your brain is doing in the gap Why would a gap help? One old idea, the study-phase retrieval hypothesis, says the second exposure only does real work if you have to reach back and pull up the first one. If the first is still fresh, there's nothing to reach for. In 2019 Gui Xue's lab at Beijing Normal University tested this with EEG, published in the Journal of Neuroscience (Feng et al.). Participants saw words repeated either back to back or with other items in between, while the team measured how similar the brain's electrical pattern was each time a given word came round. Spaced repetitions produced more similar patterns over right frontal sites, about half a second to three quarters of a second after the word appeared. The more the pattern matched, the better the word was remembered later, and that matching partly explained the spacing benefit. Massed repeats showed the opposite signature: the brain's response shrank, as if it registered "seen that" and moved on. The memory gain in that study was modest. High-confidence hits went from about 40 percent with massed repeats to about 45 percent with longer spacing. But the mechanism is the interesting part. A gap forces your brain to rebuild the original pattern, and rebuilding is what strengthens it. Forgetting a little, in other words, is part of the deal. It gives the next review something to do. Try this on the next thing you learn Take whatever you're picking up this month. A new ORM, Kubernetes basics, the parts of TypeScript generics you always look up. Do your first proper session. Then, before you close the laptop, write five questions you should be able to answer without looking. "What does satisfies check that a type annotation doesn't?" That kind of thing. Answer them tomorrow from memory. Then in about four days. Then in a couple of weeks. Then roughly a month later. Don't reread first. Try, check, fix the misses. It'll feel worse than a marathon weekend. Some answers will be gone, and you'll be annoyed. That's the moment the Feng study is describing, your brain digging the old pattern back up, and it's the part that makes it stick. If you're prepping for something with a date on it, use Cepeda's rough rule: first review somewhere around a fifth of the way to the deadline, not the next day. Where Recl fits I kept losing things I'd learned from conference talks and long docs this exact way, so I built Recl around the idea. You save a video or article, it pulls out the key takeaways, and it brings each one back later as a quick recall question, with the gaps stretching when you get it right. You don't need an app for any of this, though. A text file of questions and a calendar reminder will get you most of the way. The point is the gap. Learn it once. Then let yourself almost forget it, and go get it back. Asutosh writes about memory and how brains learn, and builds Recl , an app for remembering what you watch and read. References Bahrick, H. P., Bahrick, L. E., Bahrick, A. S., & Bahrick, P. E. (1993). Maintenance of foreign language vocabulary and the spacing effect. Psychological Science, 4 (5), 316–321. https://digitalcommons.fiu.edu/psychology_fac/50/ Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132 (3), 354–380. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16719566/ Cepeda, N. J., Vul, E., Rohrer, D., Wixted, J. T., & Pashler, H. (2008). Spacing effects in learning: A temporal ridgeline of optimal retention. Psychological Science, 19 (11), 1095–1102. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19076480/ York University (2007). Cramming damages long-term retention: York U study. https://news.yorku.ca/2007/11/12/cramming-damages-long-term-retention-york-u-study/ Kornell, N. (2009). items.title: Find Duplicate and Near-Duplicate Pages Across Your Sitemap with Python (Standard Library Only): Content Hashing, difflib Similarity, CSV Report
items.summary: Most duplicate pages are not copied on purpose. A CMS keeps serving the old URL after a page is renamed. A newsletter link with a tracking parameter ends up in the sitemap. A print view, a demo copy of the home page, or a set of city pages built from one template quietly becomes a second (or fifth) version of the same content. Each page loads fine on its own. You only see the problem when you compare pages with each other. This post builds a small duplicate finder in Python using only the standard library ( urllib , html.parser , xml.etree , hashlib , difflib , csv , concurrent.futures ). It reads a sitemap or sitemap index, fetches every page, strips the shared template, and compares pages three ways: identical HTML, identical main content, and near-identical main content scored with difflib . Matching pages are grouped into clusters, each cluster gets a canonical check and a suggested keeper URL, and the result is a CSV, a console summary and an exit code that works in CI. Google Search Central's What is canonicalization (showing "Last updated 2026-08-20 UTC"), How to specify a canonical URL with rel="canonical" and other methods (showing "Last updated 2026-07-10 UTC") and Fix canonicalization issues (showing "Last updated 2026-08-21 UTC") were opened on 14 Nov 2026, and every Google statement below comes from those three pages. Appie free-tool descriptions are as of 14 Nov 2026, checked on the tool pages that day. The script was tested on Python 3.13.5 against a local fixture site with planted duplicates; the output below is real, from a run on 14 Nov 2026. Disclosure: Appie.run publishes this article. Two free tools mentioned near the end are ours. The script does not depend on them. Where this fits This is another script in a small standard-library series. An earlier post audited canonical tags and noindex directives across a sitemap , which checks what each page says its canonical is. Another found missing and duplicate H1 tags . This one asks the question underneath both: which pages actually are the same, judged by their content, and do their canonical signals agree about which one should win? What Google actually says (and what it does not) The canonicalization overview defines the result of the process: "a canonical URL is the URL of a page that Google chose as the most representative from a set of duplicate pages." It then lists common reasons a site ends up with duplicates, which double as a checklist for what to plant in a test fixture: "Region variants: for example, separate USA and UK URLs with hreflang, but essentially the same content in the same language" "Device variants: for example, a page with both a mobile and a desktop version" "Protocol variants: for example, the HTTP and HTTPS versions of a site" "Site functions: for example, the results of sorting and filtering functions of a category page" "Accidental variants: for example, the demo version of the site is accidentally left accessible to crawlers" The same page is clear that duplicates are not a penalty in themselves: "Some duplicate content on a site is normal and it's not a violation of Google's spam policies." The reasons it gives for caring are practical. Having the same content at many URLs "can be a bad user experience" and "may make it harder for you to track how your content performs in search results." It also describes how Google handles them, and this is the part the script imitates. Google determines "the primary content (or centerpiece) of each page," and "If Google finds multiple pages that seem to be the same or the primary content very similar, it clusters them together." It then picks one page as canonical, and "duplicates are crawled less frequently." Your own signals help but do not decide: "indicating a canonical preference is a hint, not a rule." The page on specifying a canonical URL ranks the signals "in order of how strongly they can influence canonicalization": Redirects: "A strong signal that the target of the redirect should become canonical." rel="canonical" link annotations: "A strong signal that the specified URL should become canonical." Sitemap inclusion: "A weak signal that helps the URLs that are included in a sitemap become canonical." Two of its best practices map directly onto checks in the script: "Don't specify different URLs as canonical for the same page using different canonicalization techniques (for example, don't specify one URL in a sitemap, but a different URL for that same page using rel="canonical")," and "When linking within your site, link to the canonical URL rather than a duplicate URL." It also says "We don't recommend using noindex to prevent selection of a canonical page within a single site," and that none of these methods are required: "your site will likely do just fine without specifying a canonical preference." The troubleshooting page adds the fix for near-duplicates you want kept separate: it "boils down to ensuring that the pages that are clustered together are sufficiently different," and notes that "Google might hold pages in a duplicate cluster for up to two weeks" after you change them. What none of the three pages give is a similarity percentage. Google does not say how similar two pages must be to be clustered, so the script's --threshold (default 0.90) is a triage line for finding pairs worth a look, not Google's number. URL Inspection in Search Console is where you see which canonical Google actually chose. How the comparison works For each page the script keeps only the main content : text inside , or role="main" if the page has one, and everything outside , , and top-level / if it does not. Then, after all pages are fetched, any text block that appears on at least half of them (and on at least three) is dropped as template. That second step removes a "Start your free trial" box that sits inside on every page and would otherwise make unrelated short pages look alike. Pages are then compared in three passes, cheapest first: exact_html : SHA-256 of the raw response bytes. Identical hashes mean the server returned the same file for two URLs. This is the old URL still serving, or a query-string variant the CMS ignores. same_content : SHA-256 of the normalized main-content words (lowercased, whitespace collapsed). Different templates, same body. Print views and AMP-style copies land here. near_duplicate : difflib.SequenceMatcher(...).ratio() on the two word lists, at or above --threshold . Template pages with a city name swapped land here. difflib is accurate but slow, and comparing every pair is O(n²). So the near-duplicate pass first builds an inverted index of 5-word shingles and only sends a pair to difflib if their shingle Jaccard similarity is at least --prefilter (default 0.30). Shingles that appear on more than 50 pages are ignored, because a phrase on 50 pages says nothing about any two of them. Pages under --min-words (default 50) skip this pass, since two short pages can score high on very little text. The prefilter is deliberately loose. Changing one number in a sentence breaks every shingle that touches it, so Jaccard drops much faster than difflib 's ratio. On the fixture below, two pricing pages with a difflib ratio of 0.89 had a shingle Jaccard of 0.35, so a prefilter of 0.5 would have hidden them. Every match is an edge, and a small union-find groups connected pages into clusters . If A matches B and B matches C, all three are one cluster even if A and C fall just under the threshold. What the script flags Within each cluster it reads every page's canonical ( first, then a Link: <...>; rel="canonical" HTTP header) and checks whether the signals agree: competing_self_canonicals : Meaning: Two or more pages in the cluster each declare themselves canonical; What to check: Either they are meant to be different (make them more different) or one should point to the other canonicals_disagree : Meaning: Pages in the cluster point to more than one canonical target; What to check: Pick one target for the whole cluster no_canonical : Meaning: A clustered page has no canonical at all; What to check: Add one pointing to the keeper, or redirect sitemap_lists_non_canonical : Meaning: The sitemap lists a URL whose own canonical points elsewhere; What to check: Google's "don't specify one URL in a sitemap, but a different URL" case; list the canonical instead canonical_not_in_sitemap : Meaning: The canonical target is not in the sitemap; What to check: Often the target is missing, renamed or a 404 url_variant : Meaning: The URL differs from another member only by query string, trailing slash, index.html , www or case; What to check: Usually a tracking or filter parameter; fix the link or the sitemap generator noindex : Meaning: A clustered page has noindex (informational); What to check: Google recommends rel="canonical" over noindex for duplicates on one site http_error / fetch_failed / not_html / redirected : Meaning: The sitemap URL did not load as an HTML page; What to check: Fix it or remove it from the sitemap Each clustered row also gets a suggested keeper : the URL most members already name as canonical, preferring URLs in the sitemap, then URLs without a query string, then the shortest. It is a starting point for a decision, not the decision. The script Save as dup_pages.py . No pip install needed. #!/usr/bin/env python3 """Find duplicate and near-duplicate pages across a sitemap. Exact HTML hashes, main-content hashes, shingle prefilter + difflib similarity, duplicate clusters, canonical checks per cluster, CSV report. Standard library only. """ import argparse import concurrent . futures as cf import csv import difflib import gzip import hashlib import re import sys import urllib . error import urllib . parse import urllib . request import xml . etree . By default SequenceMatcher treats very common items as junk once a sequence is longer than 200 elements, and in a word list that means words like "the" and "and". Turning it off makes ratios on long pages stable at some cost in speed, which the shingle prefilter pays back. Similarity is on words, not characters. Markup, whitespace and punctuation changes do not count; a changed price or city name does. Only pages that load as HTML with status 200 are compared. Redirected URLs are compared using the page they land on and flagged redirected . Exit codes: 0 when there are no clusters and no fetch errors, 1 when there is at least one cluster or failed URL, 2 when the sitemap cannot be read. Memory is modest. Each page keeps its word list and shingle hashes. For sites over a few tens of thousands of URLs, run one child sitemap at a time with --limit for a first pass. ,http://127.0.0.1:8773/blog/old-webinar-recap,,,,,,http_error Notes on that result: All five planted clusters were found, and nothing else. The four unrelated pages share the same header, footer and trial box, and none of them clustered, because that text was dropped as template (it appeared on 16 of the 17 HTML pages, above the 8.5-page cutoff). The utm_source URL is exact_html , url_variant and sitemap_lists_non_canonical . The page's canonical is right; the sitemap is wrong. The fix is in whatever generates the sitemap, not on the page. /features/reports is the same story without the parameter. Both URLs return the same file and the canonical already names /features/reporting . Google's guidance for retiring a duplicate is a permanent redirect: "Use this only when deprecating a duplicate page." The print view has a different title and no template , so its HTML hash differs, but its main content hashes the same. A byte-level comparison alone would have missed it. The demo copy scored 0.97. One extra sentence ("Demo mode. Data resets every night.") is enough to change the content hash, which is why the difflib pass exists. The city cluster shows three different canonical targets for three near-identical pages. Berlin and Munich each claim to be canonical, Hamburg points to a page that is not in the sitemap (and in this fixture does not exist). The suggested keeper is Berlin only because it ties with Munich and sorts first. Whether these pages should exist separately is a content decision: if they should, the troubleshooting page's advice is to make them "sufficiently different." The old pricing page scored 0.890 , just under the 0.90 threshold, and appears in the "closest pairs" list rather than as a cluster. It has different prices and limits, so it is not a duplicate in the sense of identical content, but it is very likely a page nobody meant to keep live. That last pair is why the threshold is a judgment call, not a rule. Rerunning with --threshold 0.85 pulls it in as a sixth cluster: 18 sitemap URLs; 17 HTML pages compared; template blocks = text on >= 8.5 pages 6 duplicate clusters covering 13 URLs; 1 URLs not fetched as HTML ... cluster 6: 2 pages (near_duplicate) http://127.0.0.1:8773/pricing http://127.0.0.1:8773/pricing-2025 The CSV marks both pricing pages competing_self_canonicals and suggests /pricing as the keeper. Lower thresholds find more real problems and more false alarms; on a site with many pages built from one template, start at the default and read the "closest pairs" list before lowering it. When the sitemap URL is wrong, the script exits early: Could not read sitemap: http://127.0.0.1:8773/missing.xml returned 404 exit code: 2 Running it on your own sitemap Point the script at your sitemap, start with a low worker count, and use --limit for a first pass on a large site: python3 dup_pages.py https://example.com/sitemap.xml --out duplicate_pages.csv --workers 2 --limit 200 Sort the CSV by cluster , then read each cluster as a group. The match column tells you how they matched, and the canonical and suggested_keeper columns tell you whether the site already agrees with itself. Expect some clusters you meant to have. Product, tool or integration pages built from one template often share most of their text, and the script will cluster them. That is not an error in the script; it is the same thing Google's overview describes when it says it clusters pages whose "primary content" is "very similar." If those pages are meant to rank separately, the fix is more page-specific content, not a lower threshold. If you want to check one suspect pair by eye first, two free tools on our site can help. The Sitemap URL Extractor takes a sitemap URL or pasted XML and returns one URL per line (for a sitemap index it lists the child sitemaps, so you run it again on each child), which is a quick way to see whether parameter URLs or old paths are in the file at all. Convert a Webpage to Markdown fetches a public page's main content as Markdown, leaving out navigation and scripts, so you can paste two pages into any diff viewer and see what actually differs. Both ask for a captcha before each run and work one URL at a time; the script is what you want for a whole site. Fixing what it finds Retire true duplicates with a permanent redirect. For exact_html and same_content clusters where one URL is simply old ( /features/reports ), redirect it to the keeper. Google lists redirects as the strongest signal and says to use them "when you want to get rid of existing duplicate pages." Point every member at one canonical. For duplicates that must stay reachable (print views, parameter URLs, demo copies), add with an absolute URL, and a self-referencing canonical on the keeper. Google says "Use absolute paths rather than relative paths with the rel="canonical" link element." List only canonical URLs in the sitemap. Every sitemap_lists_non_canonical row is a mixed signal Google's page asks you to avoid. Fix the generator, not the individual entries. Link to the keeper. Update internal links and campaign templates so they use the canonical URL. Tracking parameters in a newsletter are fine; tracking parameters in the sitemap or the navigation are the problem. Make near-duplicates different, or merge them. For template clusters you want to keep, add content that is specific to each page. If they do not each serve a purpose, merge them into one page and redirect the rest. Expect Google to take time to re-evaluate: the troubleshooting page mentions "up to two weeks." Do not use robots.txt or noindex for this. Google's page says "Don't use the robots.txt file for canonicalization purposes" and does not recommend noindex for choosing a canonical within one site. Check what Google chose. Run the keeper and one duplicate through URL Inspection in Search Console. Your canonical is a hint; Google's choice is what shows in results. Rerun after the fix. Keep it in CI so a template change that duplicates a section fails the build. Extending it Cross-host checks. Pass several sitemaps (for example www and a docs subdomain) by concatenating them into one list before fetching, and the variant_key function already treats www and non- www as the same host. Hreflang awareness. Google's overview says regional variants in the same language should "use both canonicalization and hreflang." If your site has those, read in PageParser and skip pairs that are declared alternates of each other. Faster near-duplicate search. For very large sites, replace the inverted index with MinHash over the same shingles, still standard library ( hashlib with a few salts), and only send the top candidates to difflib . Diff runs. Save the CSV per deploy and compare cluster membership. A cluster that grows from 2 to 40 pages after a release is a template change worth catching early. FAQ Does Google penalize duplicate content? Google's canonicalization overview says "Some duplicate content on a site is normal and it's not a violation of Google's spam policies." Google groups duplicates and picks one URL to show. The reasons to fix duplicates are the ones Google gives: user confusion, split tracking, and crawl time spent on copies. What similarity score does Google use? None of the three Search Central pages give one. The 0.90 default is a starting point for review. Pages with different prices, dates or names can still score high, so read the cluster before acting. Why not just compare titles or H1s? Different URLs often share a title and have different content (paginated archives), and true duplicates sometimes have different titles (the print view in the fixture). Comparing main content catches both cases; the H1 post linked above covers headings on their own. Why does the script ignore my header and footer? Because they are on every page. Text inside , , and top-level / is dropped by structure, and any block that appears on half or more of the pages is dropped by repetition. Without that, every short page on a site would look like every other one. Can I run it in CI? Yes. It exits 1 when it finds a cluster or a URL that failed to load, 0 when clean and 2 when the sitemap cannot be read. If you have template clusters you have decided to keep, filter them out of the CSV before failing the build. Wrap-up Duplicate pages are usually a by-product of how a site is built: an old URL that still answers, a parameter that leaked into the sitemap, a print view, a demo copy, a template filled in once per city. Each one looks fine alone. Comparing main content across the whole sitemap finds them, grouping them into clusters shows which URLs belong together, and checking canonicals per cluster shows whether your redirects, tags and sitemap all name the same winner. Run it after a migration or a template change, start with the exact_html and same_content clusters, and decide for each near-duplicate cluster whether to merge the pages or make them different. RG, Founder, Appie.run
items.summary_html:
Most duplicate pages are not copied on purpose. A CMS keeps serving the old URL after a page is renamed. A newsletter link with a tracking parameter ends up in the sitemap. A print view, a demo copy of the home page, or a set of city pages built from one template quietly becomes a second (or fifth) version of the same content. Each page loads fine on its own. You only see the problem when you compare pages with each other.

This post builds a small duplicate finder in Python using only the standard library (urllib, html.parser, xml.etree, hashlib, difflib, csv, concurrent.futures). It reads a sitemap or sitemap index, fetches every page, strips the shared template, and compares pages three ways: identical HTML, identical main content, and near-identical main content scored with difflib. Matching pages are grouped into clusters, each cluster gets a canonical check and a suggested keeper URL, and the result is a CSV, a console summary and an exit code that works in CI.

Google Search Central's What is canonicalization (showing "Last updated 2026-08-20 UTC"), How to specify a canonical URL with rel="canonical" and other methods (showing "Last updated 2026-07-10 UTC") and Fix canonicalization issues (showing "Last updated 2026-08-21 UTC") were opened on 14 Nov 2026, and every Google statement below comes from those three pages. Appie free-tool descriptions are as of 14 Nov 2026, checked on the tool pages that day. The script was tested on Python 3.13.5 against a local fixture site with planted duplicates; the output below is real, from a run on 14 Nov 2026.

Disclosure: Appie.run publishes this article. Two free tools mentioned near the end are ours. The script does not depend on them.

Where this fits

This is another script in a small standard-library series. An earlier post audited canonical tags and noindex directives across a sitemap, which checks what each page says its canonical is. Another found missing and duplicate H1 tags. This one asks the question underneath both: which pages actually are the same, judged by their content, and do their canonical signals agree about which one should win?

What Google actually says (and what it does not)

The canonicalization overview defines the result of the process: "a canonical URL is the URL of a page that Google chose as the most representative from a set of duplicate pages." It then lists common reasons a site ends up with duplicates, which double as a checklist for what to plant in a test fixture:

  • "Region variants: for example, separate USA and UK URLs with hreflang, but essentially the same content in the same language"
  • "Device variants: for example, a page with both a mobile and a desktop version"
  • "Protocol variants: for example, the HTTP and HTTPS versions of a site"
  • "Site functions: for example, the results of sorting and filtering functions of a category page"
  • "Accidental variants: for example, the demo version of the site is accidentally left accessible to crawlers"

The same page is clear that duplicates are not a penalty in themselves: "Some duplicate content on a site is normal and it's not a violation of Google's spam policies." The reasons it gives for caring are practical. Having the same content at many URLs "can be a bad user experience" and "may make it harder for you to track how your content performs in search results."

It also describes how Google handles them, and this is the part the script imitates. Google determines "the primary content (or centerpiece) of each page," and "If Google finds multiple pages that seem to be the same or the primary content very similar, it clusters them together." It then picks one page as canonical, and "duplicates are crawled less frequently." Your own signals help but do not decide: "indicating a canonical preference is a hint, not a rule."

The page on specifying a canonical URL ranks the signals "in order of how strongly they can influence canonicalization":

  1. Redirects: "A strong signal that the target of the redirect should become canonical."
  2. rel="canonical" link annotations: "A strong signal that the specified URL should become canonical."
  3. Sitemap inclusion: "A weak signal that helps the URLs that are included in a sitemap become canonical."

Two of its best practices map directly onto checks in the script: "Don't specify different URLs as canonical for the same page using different canonicalization techniques (for example, don't specify one URL in a sitemap, but a different URL for that same page using rel="canonical")," and "When linking within your site, link to the canonical URL rather than a duplicate URL." It also says "We don't recommend using noindex to prevent selection of a canonical page within a single site," and that none of these methods are required: "your site will likely do just fine without specifying a canonical preference."

The troubleshooting page adds the fix for near-duplicates you want kept separate: it "boils down to ensuring that the pages that are clustered together are sufficiently different," and notes that "Google might hold pages in a duplicate cluster for up to two weeks" after you change them.

What none of the three pages give is a similarity percentage. Google does not say how similar two pages must be to be clustered, so the script's --threshold (default 0.90) is a triage line for finding pairs worth a look, not Google's number. URL Inspection in Search Console is where you see which canonical Google actually chose.

How the comparison works

For each page the script keeps only the main content: text inside , or role="main" if the page has one, and everything outside , , and top-level / if it does not. Then, after all pages are fetched, any text block that appears on at least half of them (and on at least three) is dropped as template. That second step removes a "Start your free trial" box that sits inside on every page and would otherwise make unrelated short pages look alike.

Pages are then compared in three passes, cheapest first:

  1. exact_html: SHA-256 of the raw response bytes. Identical hashes mean the server returned the same file for two URLs. This is the old URL still serving, or a query-string variant the CMS ignores.
  2. same_content: SHA-256 of the normalized main-content words (lowercased, whitespace collapsed). Different templates, same body. Print views and AMP-style copies land here.
  3. near_duplicate: difflib.SequenceMatcher(...).ratio() on the two word lists, at or above --threshold. Template pages with a city name swapped land here.

difflib is accurate but slow, and comparing every pair is O(n²). So the near-duplicate pass first builds an inverted index of 5-word shingles and only sends a pair to difflib if their shingle Jaccard similarity is at least --prefilter (default 0.30). Shingles that appear on more than 50 pages are ignored, because a phrase on 50 pages says nothing about any two of them. Pages under --min-words (default 50) skip this pass, since two short pages can score high on very little text.

The prefilter is deliberately loose. Changing one number in a sentence breaks every shingle that touches it, so Jaccard drops much faster than difflib's ratio. On the fixture below, two pricing pages with a difflib ratio of 0.89 had a shingle Jaccard of 0.35, so a prefilter of 0.5 would have hidden them.

Every match is an edge, and a small union-find groups connected pages into clusters. If A matches B and B matches C, all three are one cluster even if A and C fall just under the threshold.

What the script flags

Within each cluster it reads every page's canonical ( first, then a Link: <...>; rel="canonical" HTTP header) and checks whether the signals agree:

  • competing_self_canonicals: Meaning: Two or more pages in the cluster each declare themselves canonical; What to check: Either they are meant to be different (make them more different) or one should point to the other
  • canonicals_disagree: Meaning: Pages in the cluster point to more than one canonical target; What to check: Pick one target for the whole cluster
  • no_canonical: Meaning: A clustered page has no canonical at all; What to check: Add one pointing to the keeper, or redirect
  • sitemap_lists_non_canonical: Meaning: The sitemap lists a URL whose own canonical points elsewhere; What to check: Google's "don't specify one URL in a sitemap, but a different URL" case; list the canonical instead
  • canonical_not_in_sitemap: Meaning: The canonical target is not in the sitemap; What to check: Often the target is missing, renamed or a 404
  • url_variant: Meaning: The URL differs from another member only by query string, trailing slash, index.html, www or case; What to check: Usually a tracking or filter parameter; fix the link or the sitemap generator
  • noindex: Meaning: A clustered page has noindex (informational); What to check: Google recommends rel="canonical" over noindex for duplicates on one site
  • http_error / fetch_failed / not_html / redirected: Meaning: The sitemap URL did not load as an HTML page; What to check: Fix it or remove it from the sitemap

Each clustered row also gets a suggested keeper: the URL most members already name as canonical, preferring URLs in the sitemap, then URLs without a query string, then the shortest. It is a starting point for a decision, not the decision.

The script

Save as dup_pages.py. No pip install needed.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Find duplicate and near-duplicate pages across a sitemap.

Exact HTML hashes, main-content hashes, shingle prefilter + difflib
similarity, duplicate clusters, canonical checks per cluster, CSV report.
Standard library only.
"""
import argparse
import concurrent.futures as cf
import csv
import difflib
import gzip
import hashlib
import re
import sys
import urllib.error
import urllib.parse
import urllib.request
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
from html.parser import HTMLParser

UA = "dup-pages-audit/1.0 (+https://example.com/bot)"
SM_NS = "{http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9}"
SKIP = {"script", "style", "noscript", "template", "svg", "iframe", "head"}
CHROME = {"nav", "aside", "form", "header", "footer"}
MAIN = {"main", "article"}
BLOCK = {"p", "li", "h1", "h2", "h3", "h4", "h5", "h6", "td", "th",
         "blockquote", "pre", "dd", "dt", "figcaption", "div", "section"}
VOID = {"area", "base", "br", "col", "embed", "hr", "img", "input",
        "link", "meta", "source", "track", "wbr"}
WORD = re.compile(r"[^\W_]+(?:['’-][^\W_]+)*", re.UNICODE)

def fetch(url, timeout=20):
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": UA,
                                               "Accept-Encoding": "gzip"})
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=timeout) as resp:
            body = resp.read()
            if resp.headers.get("Content-Encoding") == "gzip":
                body = gzip.decompress(body)
            return (resp.status, resp.geturl(),
                    resp.headers.get("Content-Type", ""),
                    resp.headers.get("Link", ""), body)
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
        return e.code, url, "", "", b""
    except Exception as e:  # DNS, timeout, TLS
        return None, url, str(e), "", b""

def read_sitemap(url, seen=None):
    seen = seen if seen is not None else set()
    if url in seen:
        return []
    seen.add(url)
    status, _, _, _, body = fetch(url)
    if status != 200:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{url} returned {status}")
    if body[:2] == b"\x1f\x8b":
        body = gzip.decompress(body)
    root = ET.fromstring(body)
    if root.tag == SM_NS + "sitemapindex":
        urls = []
        for loc in root.iter(SM_NS + "loc"):
            urls += read_sitemap(loc.text.strip(), seen)
        return urls
    return [loc.text.strip() for loc in root.iter(SM_NS + "loc") if loc.text]

class PageParser(HTMLParser):
    """Collects title, canonical, robots meta and text blocks by context."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(convert_charrefs=True)
        self.stack = []
        self.title, self.canonical, self.robots = "", "", ""
        self.blocks = []          # (text, in_main, in_chrome)
        self.has_main = False
        self.buf = []

    def flush(self):
        text = " ".join("".join(self.buf).split())
        self.buf = []
        if text:
            in_main = any(m for _, _, m in self.stack)
            in_chrome = any(c for _, c, _ in self.stack)
            self.blocks.append((text, in_main, in_chrome))

    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
        a = {k: (v or "") for k, v in attrs}
        if tag == "link" and "canonical" in a.get("rel", "").lower().split():
            self.canonical = self.canonical or a.get("href", "").strip()
        if tag == "meta" and a.get("name", "").lower() in ("robots", "googlebot"):
            self.robots += " " + a.get("content", "").lower()
        if tag in VOID:
            return
        if tag in BLOCK or tag in MAIN or tag in CHROME:
            self.flush()
        role = a.get("role", "").lower()
        is_main = tag in MAIN or role == "main"
        self.has_main = self.has_main or is_main
        inside_main = any(m for _, _, m in self.stack)
        chrome = (tag in {"nav", "aside", "form"}
                  or (tag in {"header", "footer"} and not inside_main)
                  or role in {"navigation", "banner", "contentinfo"})
        self.stack.append((tag, chrome, is_main))

    def handle_endtag(self, tag):
        if tag in VOID:
            return
        if tag in BLOCK or tag in MAIN or tag in CHROME:
            self.flush()
        for i in range(len(self.stack) - 1, -1, -1):
            if self.stack[i][0] == tag:
                del self.stack[i:]
                break

    def handle_data(self, data):
        tags = [t for t, _, _ in self.stack]
        if "title" in tags:
            self.title += data
            return
        if any(t in SKIP for t in tags):
            return
        self.buf.append(data)

def norm_block(text):
    return " ".join(text.lower().split())

def analyse(url):
    status, final, ctype, link_hdr, body = fetch(url)
    row = {"url": url, "status": status if status else "fetch_failed",
           "final_url": final, "issues": []}
    if status != 200:
        row["issues"].append("http_error" if status else "fetch_failed")
        return row
    if final != url:
        row["issues"].append("redirected")
    if "html" not in ctype.lower():
        row["issues"].append("not_html")
        return row
    p = PageParser()
    p.feed(body.decode("utf-8", "replace"))
    p.flush()
    canon = p.canonical
    m = re.search(r'<([^>]+)>\s*;\s*rel="?canonical"?', link_hdr or "")
    if m and not canon:
        canon = m.group(1)
    row.update({
        "html_hash": hashlib.sha256(body).hexdigest()[:12],
        "title": " ".join(p.title.split()),
        "canonical": urllib.parse.urljoin(final, canon) if canon else "",
        "noindex": "noindex" in p.robots or "none" in p.robots.split(","),
        "blocks": [b for b, in_main, chrome in p.blocks
                   if not chrome and (in_main or not p.has_main)],
    })
    return row

def variant_key(u):
    """Same key for URLs that differ only by protocol, www, case,
    trailing slash, index.html or query string."""
    s = urllib.parse.urlsplit(u)
    host = s.netloc.lower().removeprefix("www.")
    path = re.sub(r"/(index\.html?)?$", "", s.path.lower()) or "/"
    return host + path

class DSU:
    def __init__(self):
        self.parent = {}

    def find(self, x):
        self.parent.setdefault(x, x)
        while self.parent[x] != x:
            self.parent[x] = self.parent[self.parent[x]]
            x = self.parent[x]
        return x

    def union(self, a, b):
        self.parent[self.find(a)] = self.find(b)

def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    ap.add_argument("sitemap")
    ap.add_argument("--out", default="duplicate_pages.csv")
    ap.add_argument("--threshold", type=float, default=0.90,
                    help="difflib ratio that counts as near_duplicate")
    ap.add_argument("--prefilter", type=float, default=0.30,
                    help="5-word shingle Jaccard needed before running difflib")
    ap.add_argument("--min-words", type=int, default=50,
                    help="pages with fewer main words skip the near check")
    ap.add_argument("--workers", type=int, default=4)
    ap.add_argument("--limit", type=int, default=0)
    args = ap.parse_args()

    try:
        urls = list(dict.fromkeys(read_sitemap(args.sitemap)))
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Could not read sitemap: {e}")
        return 2
    if args.limit:
        urls = urls[:args.limit]
    in_sitemap = set(urls)
    with cf.ThreadPoolExecutor(args.workers) as pool:
        rows = list(pool.map(analyse, urls))
    pages = [r for r in rows if "blocks" in r]

    # Template by repetition: block text on >= half the pages (min 3)
    df = Counter(b for r in pages for b in {norm_block(x) for x in r["blocks"]})
    cutoff = max(3, len(pages) / 2)
    for r in pages:
        text = " ".join(b for b in r["blocks"] if df[norm_block(b)] < cutoff)
        r["words"] = [w.lower() for w in WORD.findall(text)]
        r["content_hash"] = hashlib.sha256(
            " ".join(r["words"]).encode()).hexdigest()[:12]

    dsu, edges = DSU(), {}

    def link(a, b, kind, score):
        key = tuple(sorted((a, b)))
        if key not in edges or edges[key][1] < score:
            edges[key] = (kind, score)
        dsu.union(a, b)

    # 1 and 2: identical bytes, then identical main content
    for field, kind in (("html_hash", "exact_html"), ("content_hash", "same_content")):
        groups = defaultdict(list)
        for r in pages:
            if r["words"]:
                groups[r[field]].append(r["url"])
        for members in groups.values():
            for other in members[1:]:
                link(members[0], other, kind, 1.0)

    # 3: near duplicates. Inverted shingle index finds candidate pairs,
    # difflib confirms them on the word sequence.
    by_url = {r["url"]: r for r in pages}
    sh = {}
    for r in pages:
        w = r["words"]
        if len(w) >= args.min_words:
            sh[r["url"]] = {hash(" ".join(w[i:i + 5])) for i in range(len(w) - 4)}
    index = defaultdict(list)
    for u, s in sh.items():
        for h in s:
            index[h].append(u)
    shared = Counter()
    for posting in index.values():
        if len(posting) > 50:      # a phrase on 50+ pages says nothing
            continue
        for i, a in enumerate(posting):
            for b in posting[i + 1:]:
                shared[tuple(sorted((a, b)))] += 1
    near_misses = []
    for (a, b), n in shared.items():
        jac = n / len(sh[a] | sh[b])
        if jac < args.prefilter or (a, b) in edges:
            continue
        ratio = difflib.SequenceMatcher(None, by_url[a]["words"],
                                        by_url[b]["words"], autojunk=False).ratio()
        if ratio >= args.threshold:
            link(a, b, "near_duplicate", ratio)
        else:
            near_misses.append((ratio, a, b))

    # Clusters
    clusters = defaultdict(list)
    for u in {u for pair in edges for u in pair}:
        clusters[dsu.find(u)].append(u)
    ordered = sorted(clusters.values(), key=lambda m: (-len(m), min(m)))
    out_rows = []
    for cid, members in enumerate(ordered, 1):
        members.sort()
        canon_of = {u: by_url[u]["canonical"] for u in members}
        targets = Counter(c for c in canon_of.values() if c)
        self_canon = [u for u in members if canon_of[u] == u]
        # Keeper: most-used canonical target, preferring sitemap URLs,
        # then clean, short URLs. A starting point, not a decision.
        keeper = min(set(members) | set(targets), key=lambda u: (
            -targets[u], u not in in_sitemap, "?" in u, len(u), u))
        vkeys = Counter(variant_key(u) for u in members)
        for u in members:
            r = by_url[u]
            kinds = [edges[k] for k in edges if u in k]
            kind, score = max(kinds, key=lambda e: (e[1], e[0]))
            issues = list(r["issues"])
            if not canon_of[u]:
                issues.append("no_canonical")
            elif canon_of[u] not in in_sitemap:
                issues.append("canonical_not_in_sitemap")
            if len(self_canon) > 1 and u in self_canon:
                issues.append("competing_self_canonicals")
            if len(targets) > 1:
                issues.append("canonicals_disagree")
            if canon_of[u] and canon_of[u] != u:
                issues.append("sitemap_lists_non_canonical")
            if vkeys[variant_key(u)] > 1 and u != keeper:
                issues.append("url_variant")
            if r["noindex"]:
                issues.append("noindex")
            out_rows.append({
                "cluster": cid, "size": len(members), "url": u,
                "match": kind, "similarity": f"{score:.2f}",
                "words": len(r["words"]), "canonical": canon_of[u],
                "suggested_keeper": keeper, "issues": ";".join(issues),
                "title": r["title"]})
    errors = [r for r in rows if "blocks" not in r]
    for r in errors:
        out_rows.append({"cluster": "", "size": "", "url": r["url"],
                         "match": "", "similarity": "", "words": "",
                         "canonical": "", "suggested_keeper": "",
                         "issues": ";".join(r["issues"]), "title": ""})

    with open(args.out, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=list(out_rows[0]) if out_rows else ["url"])
        w.writeheader()
        w.writerows(out_rows)

    dup_urls = sum(len(m) for m in ordered)
    print(f"{len(rows)} sitemap URLs; {len(pages)} HTML pages compared; "
          f"template blocks = text on >= {cutoff:g} pages")
    print(f"{len(ordered)} duplicate clusters covering {dup_urls} URLs; "
          f"{len(errors)} URLs not fetched as HTML")
    for cid, members in enumerate(ordered, 1):
        kinds = Counter(edges[k][0] for k in edges if k[0] in members)
        print(f"  cluster {cid}: {len(members)} pages ({', '.join(sorted(kinds))})")
        for u in members:
            print(f"      {u}")
    if near_misses:
        print(f"Closest pairs below --threshold {args.threshold}:")
        for ratio, a, b in sorted(near_misses, reverse=True)[:5]:
            print(f"  {ratio:.3f}  {a}  ~  {b}")
    counts = Counter(i for r in out_rows for i in r["issues"].split(";") if i)
    for name, n in counts.most_common():
        print(f"  {name:<28} {n}")
    print(f"Report: {args.out}")
    return 1 if ordered or errors else 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

A few design choices worth knowing:

  • autojunk=False matters. By default SequenceMatcher treats very common items as junk once a sequence is longer than 200 elements, and in a word list that means words like "the" and "and". Turning it off makes ratios on long pages stable at some cost in speed, which the shingle prefilter pays back.
  • Similarity is on words, not characters. Markup, whitespace and punctuation changes do not count; a changed price or city name does.
  • Only pages that load as HTML with status 200 are compared. Redirected URLs are compared using the page they land on and flagged redirected.
  • Exit codes: 0 when there are no clusters and no fetch errors, 1 when there is at least one cluster or failed URL, 2 when the sitemap cannot be read.
  • Memory is modest. Each page keeps its word list and shingle hashes. For sites over a few tens of thousands of URLs, run one child sitemap at a time with --limit for a first pass.
Testing it against a local fixture

To get output you can check line by line, I built a small fictional site ("Ledgerly", a bookkeeping app) with 16 routes and an 18-URL sitemap, and planted one example of each duplicate type Google lists, plus controls:

  • Old URL still serving the same file: URLs: /features/reporting, /features/reports (both canonical to /features/reporting); Expected: exact_html, sitemap lists the non-canonical
  • Tracking parameter in the sitemap (a "site functions" variant): URLs: /blog/close-the-books-faster and ?utm_source=newsletter; Expected: exact_html, url_variant
  • Print view with a different template, no canonical: URLs: /guides/month-end-checklist and /print; Expected: same_content, no_canonical
  • Demo copy of the home page (Google's "accidental variant") with one extra line: URLs: / and /demo/; Expected: near_duplicate, no_canonical
  • City pages from one template: URLs: /locations/berlin, /munich (self-canonical), /hamburg (canonical to an unlisted /locations/germany); Expected: one cluster, canonicals disagree
  • Old pricing page with different prices and limits: URLs: /pricing, /pricing-2025; Expected: just below the threshold
  • Unrelated pages: URLs: /about, /blog/, /blog/reconcile-bank-feeds, /privacy; Expected: not clustered
  • Dead URL in the sitemap: URLs: /blog/old-webinar-recap; Expected: http_error

Every page shares a header, footer and a "Start your free trial" box inside . Like many CMSs, the fixture server ignores the query string when routing, which is how the utm_source URL ends up serving the same bytes. The handler is short:

import http.server, json, pathlib, urllib.parse
HERE = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent / "fixture"
ROUTES = json.loads((HERE / "routes.json").read_text())  # path -> HTML

class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        path = urllib.parse.urlsplit(self.path).path  # query string ignored
        if path == "/sitemap.xml":
            body, ctype = (HERE / "sitemap.xml").read_bytes(), "application/xml"
        elif path in ROUTES:
            body, ctype = ROUTES[path].encode(), "text/html; charset=utf-8"
        else:
            self.send_response(404); self.end_headers(); return
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", ctype)
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body)

http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8773), H).serve_forever()
