items.title: The race to build autonomous war robots faces a problem that self-driving cars don't. There are no rules of the road.
items.summary: War robots have to be able to function in environments without proper roads or rules, but with plenty of chaos. Andrew Kravchenko/Bloomberg via Getty Images Militaries are increasingly using ground robots, and manufacturers want to make them more autonomous. But battlefields present challenges that self-driving cars don't face. There are no reliable roads or traffic rules, and battlefield conditions constantly change. War robots are becoming a growing presence on modern battlefields, and defense manufacturers are pushing to make them more autonomous to further reduce the risks to soldiers . But making uncrewed ground vehicles that can drive themselves into battle presents a challenge that self-driving cars don't. The number of robots in military arsenals is soaring, particularly in Ukraine, where they fire weapons, attack positions, and carry wounded soldiers , all while their operators remain farther from danger. Greater autonomy would allow fewer soldiers to operate more vehicles, let troops stay farther from the front, and allow robots to keep going when communications are disrupted. A chaotic battlefield, however, is far different from safe, well-mapped roadways. Robots have to navigate muddy tracks, forests, and dangerous terrain while facing enemy attacks. Terrain, conditions, and targets change constantly. And there are no rules. No speed limits, no predictable traffic, and no guarantee of safety. Robots work under constant threat of attack. Yan Dobronosov/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images German defense technology company ARX Robotics makes GEREON robots, autonomous systems that have been used by Ukraine and procured by the UK. David Roberts, CEO of the company's British arm, told Business Insider that, when it comes to making self-driving vehicles, companies working on civilian roads face a less challenging environment. "Roads are structured," he said. "They've got rules. Roads are wide enough for cars to drive down. They have markings to tell a vehicle what to do and when to do it." In war, "there are no real rules," Roberts continued. "You don't quite know if someone's going to step out in front of you or be in the long grass in front. It's a very challenging environment in the first place to build autonomy." Mike McGinty, the CEO of British firm Digital Concepts Engineering (DCE), whose X-series ground robots have been procured by the British Army, also spelled out the differences. A street is "flat, of a guaranteed surface. It's marked. It's a track. It has a left and a right. It's signed," he said. And it's unchanging. "The same street's there tomorrow." "True autonomy is an extremely hard problem on cross-country ground," he said. "If you see a line on the ground, is it a hole, a log, a burn mark, a shadow, a crocodile, a person?" Robots are becoming a growing presence in conflicts, especially in Ukraine. Dmytro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images That doesn't mean it's easy to develop a self-driving car or taxi. "The truth is it's still extremely difficult," McGinty said, but developing autonomous uncrewed ground vehicles for war is a much more daunting task. The push for battlefield autonomy Autonomy can mean anything from following preset routes to independently navigating to a destination. Capabilities in Ukraine have grown, with AI helping robots navigate when Russian electronic warfare cuts communications. Ukraine's robots have limited but growing autonomy. Yevhen Titov/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Autonomy remains limited. Roberts said that most robots in Ukraine are simply remote-controlled, with autonomy in "very niche areas," such as following waypoints if they lose their operator connection. He said autonomy needs to evolve beyond what has been demonstrated in Ukraine. The GEREON robots that ARX Robotics makes run on Mithra, a software layer that connects their sensors, AI, and autonomy functions. The "supervised autonomy allows a single soldier to task and oversee multiple systems simultaneously, delivering more mission output with fewer personnel," the company says. Roberts said the "ability to tell a vehicle to go to a certain place on the battlefield is very much where we are working at the moment." ARX's robots can already follow waypoints, detect people, avoid collisions, and make safety stops, he said. The next step is at the mission level, and he predicted that, within the next year or two, battlefield management systems will be able to tell vehicles where to go. "I don't think that this is something that anyone has actually got deployed yet, but I think there are a number of companies who are working on that sort of problem set." McGinty said Ukraine's current level of autonomy typically allows operators to control robots remotely, calling this the level of autonomy that DCE had "mastered." "Full autonomy is still a very difficult technological step," he said. "So someone will take it, but it won't be us because we're not the software company doing that." ARX Robotics' GEREON robot is used by Ukraine's forces. Angelika Warmuth/REUTERS DCE's robots can be fitted with a Marionette kit, which enables remote control and supports autonomous features, including software developed by other companies. Oleksandr Yabchanka, head of robotic systems for Ukraine's Da Vinci Wolves Battalion, told Business Insider that ground robot autonomy in Ukraine "is still in the early stages of development," but units want more to protect their soldiers. "The future of both aerial drones and unmanned ground systems lies in the development of autonomy." Multiple projects are underway. Ukraine's state-backed innovation platform Brave1's grant program, for instance, calls for "autonomous logistics" robots that can independently return to base and move autonomously if communications are lost. Ukraine has integrated AI into aerial drones , which have been more prominent in this war, as well as fixed weapons, and it is increasingly being incorporated into ground robots as the country pushes for greater autonomy in its uncrewed warfighting systems. items.summary_html:
War robots have to be able to function in environments without proper roads or rules, but with plenty of chaos.

Andrew Kravchenko/Bloomberg via Getty Images

  • Militaries are increasingly using ground robots, and manufacturers want to make them more autonomous.
  • But battlefields present challenges that self-driving cars don't face.
  • There are no reliable roads or traffic rules, and battlefield conditions constantly change.

War robots are becoming a growing presence on modern battlefields, and defense manufacturers are pushing to make them more autonomous to further reduce the risks to soldiers.

But making uncrewed ground vehicles that can drive themselves into battle presents a challenge that self-driving cars don't.

The number of robots in military arsenals is soaring, particularly in Ukraine, where they fire weapons, attack positions, and carry wounded soldiers, all while their operators remain farther from danger. Greater autonomy would allow fewer soldiers to operate more vehicles, let troops stay farther from the front, and allow robots to keep going when communications are disrupted.

A chaotic battlefield, however, is far different from safe, well-mapped roadways. Robots have to navigate muddy tracks, forests, and dangerous terrain while facing enemy attacks.

Terrain, conditions, and targets change constantly. And there are no rules. No speed limits, no predictable traffic, and no guarantee of safety.

Robots work under constant threat of attack.

Yan Dobronosov/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images

German defense technology company ARX Robotics makes GEREON robots, autonomous systems that have been used by Ukraine and procured by the UK. David Roberts, CEO of the company's British arm, told Business Insider that, when it comes to making self-driving vehicles, companies working on civilian roads face a less challenging environment.

"Roads are structured," he said. "They've got rules. Roads are wide enough for cars to drive down. They have markings to tell a vehicle what to do and when to do it."

In war, "there are no real rules," Roberts continued. "You don't quite know if someone's going to step out in front of you or be in the long grass in front. It's a very challenging environment in the first place to build autonomy."

Mike McGinty, the CEO of British firm Digital Concepts Engineering (DCE), whose X-series ground robots have been procured by the British Army, also spelled out the differences.

A street is "flat, of a guaranteed surface. It's marked. It's a track. It has a left and a right. It's signed," he said. And it's unchanging. "The same street's there tomorrow."

"True autonomy is an extremely hard problem on cross-country ground," he said. "If you see a line on the ground, is it a hole, a log, a burn mark, a shadow, a crocodile, a person?"

Robots are becoming a growing presence in conflicts, especially in Ukraine.

Dmytro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images

That doesn't mean it's easy to develop a self-driving car or taxi. "The truth is it's still extremely difficult," McGinty said, but developing autonomous uncrewed ground vehicles for war is a much more daunting task.

The push for battlefield autonomy

Autonomy can mean anything from following preset routes to independently navigating to a destination. Capabilities in Ukraine have grown, with AI helping robots navigate when Russian electronic warfare cuts communications.

Ukraine's robots have limited but growing autonomy.

Yevhen Titov/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images

Autonomy remains limited. Roberts said that most robots in Ukraine are simply remote-controlled, with autonomy in "very niche areas," such as following waypoints if they lose their operator connection.

He said autonomy needs to evolve beyond what has been demonstrated in Ukraine.

The GEREON robots that ARX Robotics makes run on Mithra, a software layer that connects their sensors, AI, and autonomy functions. The "supervised autonomy allows a single soldier to task and oversee multiple systems simultaneously, delivering more mission output with fewer personnel," the company says.

Roberts said the "ability to tell a vehicle to go to a certain place on the battlefield is very much where we are working at the moment." ARX's robots can already follow waypoints, detect people, avoid collisions, and make safety stops, he said.

The next step is at the mission level, and he predicted that, within the next year or two, battlefield management systems will be able to tell vehicles where to go. "I don't think that this is something that anyone has actually got deployed yet, but I think there are a number of companies who are working on that sort of problem set."

McGinty said Ukraine's current level of autonomy typically allows operators to control robots remotely, calling this the level of autonomy that DCE had "mastered."

"Full autonomy is still a very difficult technological step," he said. "So someone will take it, but it won't be us because we're not the software company doing that."

ARX Robotics' GEREON robot is used by Ukraine's forces.

Angelika Warmuth/REUTERS

DCE's robots can be fitted with a Marionette kit, which enables remote control and supports autonomous features, including software developed by other companies.

Oleksandr Yabchanka, head of robotic systems for Ukraine's Da Vinci Wolves Battalion, told Business Insider that ground robot autonomy in Ukraine "is still in the early stages of development," but units want more to protect their soldiers. "The future of both aerial drones and unmanned ground systems lies in the development of autonomy."

Multiple projects are underway.

Ukraine's state-backed innovation platform Brave1's grant program, for instance, calls for "autonomous logistics" robots that can independently return to base and move autonomously if communications are lost.

Ukraine has integrated AI into aerial drones, which have been more prominent in this war, as well as fixed weapons, and it is increasingly being incorporated into ground robots as the country pushes for greater autonomy in its uncrewed warfighting systems.

The aim is to enable a single soldier to oversee multiple pieces of equipment simultaneously.

items.title: AI and Open Banking: Building Smarter Financial Experiences
items.summary: How artificial intelligence and secure financial data sharing are transforming traditional banking into a more personalized, intelligent, and connected financial ecosystem. Imagine opening your banking application and finding more than just your account balance. It tells you where your money goes, predicts upcoming expenses, identifies unusual transactions, and recommends ways to improve your financial habits. It may even help you compare financial products based on your spending patterns and financial goals. This is no longer just a vision of future banking. The combination of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Open Banking is making these experiences increasingly possible. ChatGPT Generated Image Traditional banking has largely operated around isolated financial systems, where customer information remains within individual institutions. Open Banking changes this approach by allowing customers to securely share their financial information with authorized third-party providers through Application Programming Interfaces (APIs). When AI enters this ecosystem, financial data becomes more valuable because it can be analyzed, interpreted, and converted into actionable insights. Together, these technologies are creating a smarter and more connected financial environment. Understanding the Connection Between AI and Open Banking Open Banking gives customers greater control over their financial information while enabling authorized providers to access relevant data with appropriate consent. AI uses this information to identify patterns, automate processes, and generate personalized recommendations. For example, a customer who connects multiple bank accounts to a financial management platform can view their overall financial position in one place. AI can analyze income, spending habits, recurring payments, and savings patterns to provide a clearer picture of their financial health. The technologies serve different but complementary purposes: Open Banking: Enables secure, consent-based financial data sharing between banks and authorized third-party providers. Artificial Intelligence: Analyzes financial information, identifies patterns, predicts outcomes, and supports intelligent decision-making. APIs: Establish communication between financial institutions, fintech platforms, and authorized service providers. Data Analytics: Converts financial information into meaningful insights that support better customer experiences. The real opportunity lies in combining these capabilities to deliver financial services that are more responsive, accessible, and personalized. Personalized Banking Experiences Customers increasingly expect financial services to understand their individual needs rather than provide identical experiences to everyone. AI-powered Open Banking applications can analyze transaction histories, income patterns, spending categories, and financial commitments to develop personalized recommendations. Consider someone who regularly spends more than expected on subscriptions, food delivery, and entertainment. An AI-powered financial application can identify these patterns and suggest realistic spending limits. Similarly, it can recommend savings targets based on income and recurring expenses. Personalization can support: Customized budgeting and savings recommendations. Spending analysis across multiple bank accounts. Financial product suggestions based on customer requirements. Personalized notifications about upcoming payments. Insights into changing financial habits. This approach transforms banking applications from simple transaction platforms into intelligent financial assistants. Smarter Fraud Detection and Risk Management Financial fraud continues to challenge banks, payment providers, and digital financial platforms. Traditional fraud detection systems often depend on predefined rules and historical patterns, which may struggle to identify sophisticated or rapidly changing threats. AI introduces more adaptive fraud detection capabilities. By analyzing transaction behavior, device information, payment patterns, and other permitted data, machine learning models can identify activities that appear inconsistent with normal customer behavior. For instance, if a customer usually makes small transactions within a particular region but suddenly experiences multiple unusual high-value transactions, an AI-powered system may flag the activity for additional verification. Open Banking can provide a broader financial picture when customers authorize relevant data sharing. This additional context may help institutions assess suspicious activity more effectively. Important applications include: Real-time transaction monitoring. Unusual spending pattern identification. Behavioral analysis and anomaly detection. Risk-based authentication. Automated alerts and investigation support. However, AI-generated alerts should not automatically be treated as proof of fraud. Human oversight, explainability, and appropriate investigation remain essential. Faster and More Intelligent Lending Decisions Traditional lending processes often require customers to submit extensive documentation, including bank statements, salary information, and other financial records. Open Banking can simplify this process by allowing customers to authorize lenders to access relevant financial information directly from participating institutions. AI can then analyze income consistency, existing financial obligations, transaction history, and spending behavior to support credit assessments. For example, a self-employed individual with irregular monthly income may find it difficult to demonstrate financial stability through conventional documentation. With authorized access to relevant banking data, lenders may gain a more detailed understanding of their cash flow. This can contribute to: Faster loan application processing. More informed credit assessments. Improved cash-flow analysis. Better identification of repayment risks. Potentially broader access to suitable credit products. Nevertheless, AI-based lending decisions must address bias, data quality, transparency, and applicable fair-lending requirements. Alternative data should improve assessment quality, not create unfair disadvantages. AI-Powered Financial Management and Forecasting Managing personal finances becomes challenging when customers maintain multiple accounts, credit cards, loans, and investment relationships. Open Banking helps consolidate authorized financial information, while AI makes it easier to understand and act on that information. Instead of manually reviewing transactions, customers can receive automated financial summaries and forecasts. For example, an AI-powered application might identify that a customer has several upcoming bill payments and predict a potential shortage in their account balance. It could then recommend adjusting discretionary spending or transferring funds between eligible accounts. Some valuable capabilities include: Predicting monthly cash-flow requirements. Identifying unnecessary recurring subscriptions. Tracking financial goals. Recommending savings opportunities. Providing automated spending summaries. These capabilities can help customers make informed decisions before financial problems arise. Improving Customer Support Through Intelligent Automation Customer experience is another area where AI and Open Banking can work together. Traditional banking support often involves long waiting times, repetitive questions, and manual information retrieval. AI-powered chatbots and virtual assistants can improve these interactions by providing faster responses and assisting customers with routine financial tasks. When integrated with authorized Open Banking data, these assistants may provide contextual support. For example, customers could ask why their spending increased last month or whether a particular payment has been processed. The application could analyze relevant authorized information and provide an understandable response. Potential benefits include: 24/7 customer assistance. Faster transaction-related queries. Personalized financial explanations. Automated account insights. Reduced pressure on customer support teams. Financial institutions must still protect sensitive information and ensure that AI assistants do not disclose account details without proper authentication and authorization. Challenges That Financial Institutions Must Address Despite its potential, integrating AI with Open Banking is not without challenges. Financial institutions must establish strong foundations before deploying these technologies at scale. Data privacy and customer consent: Customers must understand what information they are sharing, why it is required, and how it will be used. Consent should be transparent and appropriately managed. Cybersecurity threats: APIs, connected applications, and financial data exchanges introduce additional security considerations. Strong authentication, encryption, access controls, and continuous monitoring are essential. Data quality and interoperability: Inconsistent data formats and differences between banking systems can affect AI accuracy. Standardized APIs and reliable data management practices are important. Algorithmic bias: AI models trained on incomplete or unrepresentative datasets may produce unfair outcomes, particularly in lending and risk assessment. Regulatory compliance: Financial institutions must follow applicable data protection, banking, consumer protection, and Open Banking requirements in the markets where they operate. Addressing these challenges requires collaboration between banks, fintech companies, technology providers, regulators, and cybersecurity specialists. The Future: Moving Towards Intelligent, Connected Banking The future of banking will increasingly depend on how effectively financial institutions combine secure data sharing with intelligent automation. Emerging technologies such as generative AI, predictive analytics, and advanced API ecosystems could make financial services more conversational, proactive, and accessible. Customers may eventually interact with AI-powered financial assistants that help them understand complex financial decisions, manage recurring expenses, compare suitable products, and monitor financial goals through a single interface. For businesses, these technologies could improve cash-flow visibility, automate financial reporting, simplify account reconciliation, and support more informed financial planning. However, successful adoption will depend on trust. Customers must remain in control of their data, understand automated recommendations, and have access to appropriate human support when necessary. Conclusion AI and Open Banking are not simply two emerging fintech trends operating independently. Together, they represent a significant shift in how financial services are developed, delivered, and experienced. Open Banking creates opportunities for secure, consent-based financial connectivity, while AI transforms connected information into useful insights, predictions, and automated services. From personalized financial management and smarter lending to fraud detection and intelligent customer support, their combined capabilities can make banking more efficient and customer-focused. The institutions that succeed will not necessarily be those adopting the most advanced technology. They will be the ones that combine innovation with transparency, security, responsible AI practices, and customer trust. items.summary_html:
How artificial intelligence and secure financial data sharing are transforming traditional banking into a more personalized, intelligent, and connected financial ecosystem.

Imagine opening your banking application and finding more than just your account balance. It tells you where your money goes, predicts upcoming expenses, identifies unusual transactions, and recommends ways to improve your financial habits. It may even help you compare financial products based on your spending patterns and financial goals.

This is no longer just a vision of future banking. The combination of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Open Banking is making these experiences increasingly possible.

ChatGPT Generated Image

Traditional banking has largely operated around isolated financial systems, where customer information remains within individual institutions. Open Banking changes this approach by allowing customers to securely share their financial information with authorized third-party providers through Application Programming Interfaces (APIs). When AI enters this ecosystem, financial data becomes more valuable because it can be analyzed, interpreted, and converted into actionable insights.

Together, these technologies are creating a smarter and more connected financial environment.

Understanding the Connection Between AI and Open Banking

Open Banking gives customers greater control over their financial information while enabling authorized providers to access relevant data with appropriate consent. AI uses this information to identify patterns, automate processes, and generate personalized recommendations.

For example, a customer who connects multiple bank accounts to a financial management platform can view their overall financial position in one place. AI can analyze income, spending habits, recurring payments, and savings patterns to provide a clearer picture of their financial health.

The technologies serve different but complementary purposes:

  • Open Banking: Enables secure, consent-based financial data sharing between banks and authorized third-party providers.
  • Artificial Intelligence: Analyzes financial information, identifies patterns, predicts outcomes, and supports intelligent decision-making.
  • APIs: Establish communication between financial institutions, fintech platforms, and authorized service providers.
  • Data Analytics: Converts financial information into meaningful insights that support better customer experiences.

The real opportunity lies in combining these capabilities to deliver financial services that are more responsive, accessible, and personalized.

Personalized Banking Experiences

Customers increasingly expect financial services to understand their individual needs rather than provide identical experiences to everyone.

AI-powered Open Banking applications can analyze transaction histories, income patterns, spending categories, and financial commitments to develop personalized recommendations.

Consider someone who regularly spends more than expected on subscriptions, food delivery, and entertainment. An AI-powered financial application can identify these patterns and suggest realistic spending limits.

Similarly, it can recommend savings targets based on income and recurring expenses.

Personalization can support:

  • Customized budgeting and savings recommendations.
  • Spending analysis across multiple bank accounts.
  • Financial product suggestions based on customer requirements.
  • Personalized notifications about upcoming payments.
  • Insights into changing financial habits.

This approach transforms banking applications from simple transaction platforms into intelligent financial assistants.

Smarter Fraud Detection and Risk Management

Financial fraud continues to challenge banks, payment providers, and digital financial platforms. Traditional fraud detection systems often depend on predefined rules and historical patterns, which may struggle to identify sophisticated or rapidly changing threats.

AI introduces more adaptive fraud detection capabilities.

By analyzing transaction behavior, device information, payment patterns, and other permitted data, machine learning models can identify activities that appear inconsistent with normal customer behavior.

For instance, if a customer usually makes small transactions within a particular region but suddenly experiences multiple unusual high-value transactions, an AI-powered system may flag the activity for additional verification.

Open Banking can provide a broader financial picture when customers authorize relevant data sharing. This additional context may help institutions assess suspicious activity more effectively.

Important applications include:

  • Real-time transaction monitoring.
  • Unusual spending pattern identification.
  • Behavioral analysis and anomaly detection.
  • Risk-based authentication.
  • Automated alerts and investigation support.

However, AI-generated alerts should not automatically be treated as proof of fraud. Human oversight, explainability, and appropriate investigation remain essential.

Faster and More Intelligent Lending Decisions

Traditional lending processes often require customers to submit extensive documentation, including bank statements, salary information, and other financial records.

Open Banking can simplify this process by allowing customers to authorize lenders to access relevant financial information directly from participating institutions.

AI can then analyze income consistency, existing financial obligations, transaction history, and spending behavior to support credit assessments.

For example, a self-employed individual with irregular monthly income may find it difficult to demonstrate financial stability through conventional documentation. With authorized access to relevant banking data, lenders may gain a more detailed understanding of their cash flow.

This can contribute to:

  • Faster loan application processing.
  • More informed credit assessments.
  • Improved cash-flow analysis.
  • Better identification of repayment risks.
  • Potentially broader access to suitable credit products.

Nevertheless, AI-based lending decisions must address bias, data quality, transparency, and applicable fair-lending requirements. Alternative data should improve assessment quality, not create unfair disadvantages.

AI-Powered Financial Management and Forecasting

Managing personal finances becomes challenging when customers maintain multiple accounts, credit cards, loans, and investment relationships.

Open Banking helps consolidate authorized financial information, while AI makes it easier to understand and act on that information.

Instead of manually reviewing transactions, customers can receive automated financial summaries and forecasts.

For example, an AI-powered application might identify that a customer has several upcoming bill payments and predict a potential shortage in their account balance. It could then recommend adjusting discretionary spending or transferring funds between eligible accounts.

Some valuable capabilities include:

  • Predicting monthly cash-flow requirements.
  • Identifying unnecessary recurring subscriptions.
  • Tracking financial goals.
  • Recommending savings opportunities.
  • Providing automated spending summaries.

These capabilities can help customers make informed decisions before financial problems arise.

Improving Customer Support Through Intelligent Automation

Customer experience is another area where AI and Open Banking can work together.

Traditional banking support often involves long waiting times, repetitive questions, and manual information retrieval. AI-powered chatbots and virtual assistants can improve these interactions by providing faster responses and assisting customers with routine financial tasks.

When integrated with authorized Open Banking data, these assistants may provide contextual support.

For example, customers could ask why their spending increased last month or whether a particular payment has been processed. The application could analyze relevant authorized information and provide an understandable response.

Potential benefits include:

  • 24/7 customer assistance.
  • Faster transaction-related queries.
  • Personalized financial explanations.
  • Automated account insights.
  • Reduced pressure on customer support teams.

Financial institutions must still protect sensitive information and ensure that AI assistants do not disclose account details without proper authentication and authorization.

Challenges That Financial Institutions Must Address

Despite its potential, integrating AI with Open Banking is not without challenges. Financial institutions must establish strong foundations before deploying these technologies at scale.

Data privacy and customer consent: Customers must understand what information they are sharing, why it is required, and how it will be used. Consent should be transparent and appropriately managed.

Cybersecurity threats: APIs, connected applications, and financial data exchanges introduce additional security considerations. Strong authentication, encryption, access controls, and continuous monitoring are essential.

Data quality and interoperability: Inconsistent data formats and differences between banking systems can affect AI accuracy. Standardized APIs and reliable data management practices are important.

Algorithmic bias: AI models trained on incomplete or unrepresentative datasets may produce unfair outcomes, particularly in lending and risk assessment.

Regulatory compliance: Financial institutions must follow applicable data protection, banking, consumer protection, and Open Banking requirements in the markets where they operate.

Addressing these challenges requires collaboration between banks, fintech companies, technology providers, regulators, and cybersecurity specialists.

The Future: Moving Towards Intelligent, Connected Banking

The future of banking will increasingly depend on how effectively financial institutions combine secure data sharing with intelligent automation.

Emerging technologies such as generative AI, predictive analytics, and advanced API ecosystems could make financial services more conversational, proactive, and accessible.

Customers may eventually interact with AI-powered financial assistants that help them understand complex financial decisions, manage recurring expenses, compare suitable products, and monitor financial goals through a single interface.

For businesses, these technologies could improve cash-flow visibility, automate financial reporting, simplify account reconciliation, and support more informed financial planning.

However, successful adoption will depend on trust. Customers must remain in control of their data, understand automated recommendations, and have access to appropriate human support when necessary.

Conclusion

AI and Open Banking are not simply two emerging fintech trends operating independently. Together, they represent a significant shift in how financial services are developed, delivered, and experienced.

Open Banking creates opportunities for secure, consent-based financial connectivity, while AI transforms connected information into useful insights, predictions, and automated services.

From personalized financial management and smarter lending to fraud detection and intelligent customer support, their combined capabilities can make banking more efficient and customer-focused.

The institutions that succeed will not necessarily be those adopting the most advanced technology. They will be the ones that combine innovation with transparency, security, responsible AI practices, and customer trust.

items.title: 10 challenges facing the real estate industry in 2026, according to young leaders
items.summary: Business Insider's 2026 Rising Stars of real estate share the biggest challenges facing real estate. Alyssa Powell Business Insider has announced its 2026 class of Rising Stars of Real Estate. We asked 10 about the biggest challenges facing residential and commercial real estate. From AI to high interest rates and economic uncertainty, here's what they had to say. The real estate market has felt anything but normal in 2026. High interest rates and home prices have turned off many would-be buyers , even in some of the country's previously hottest markets . New taxes affecting high-end properties , coupled with broader economic uncertainty , have also prompted wealthy buyers to question whether it still makes sense to buy or invest in real estate in their cities — or look elsewhere , even overseas . These challenges are likely to carry into next year. But Business Insider's 2026 Rising Stars of Real Estate say it's not all doom and gloom. Some rising stars see a bigger role for agents as buyers and sellers try to make sense of a complicated market. Others are experimenting with AI to manage and grow their businesses. And in some markets, like Miami and New York, they say demand is picking up again. Here are what 10 of this year's rising stars say are the biggest issues facing real estate and how they think the industry will adapt. Agents can't get by just knowing the basics. Photo Courtesy of Joey Ben-Zvi Joey Ben-Zvi, founder of the real-estate firm Ben-Zvi Group, says technology has made data and information more accessible, leading some buyers and sellers to believe they can navigate a transaction on their own, without an agent. "Consumers have more access to information than ever before, which is ultimately a good thing, but access to information isn't the same as being in the trenches on a daily basis and staying deeply connected to the product and consumers, along with having the experience, judgment, and relationships necessary to navigate a complicated transaction," Ben-Zvi told Business Insider. While Ben-Zvi believes agents remain fundamental to the homebuying and selling experience, he says knowing the basics is no longer enough. "I think the industry is going through a necessary evolution," Ben-Zvi said. "Agents can no longer rely solely on access to listings or information. They have to demonstrate real value through their expertise, creativity, negotiation skills, and ability to solve problems." Data will become even more critical. Photo Courtesy of Saharsh Chordia Saharsh Chordia, the 33-year-old vice president of strategy and analytics at Cortland, said that data will become much more important. The challenge, he said, is turning the vast amount of data generated by physical assets into actionable insight. "Real estate is fundamentally a business built around physical assets, yet much of the industry's data remains fragmented and underutilized," Chordia said. "AI will play an important role, but the organizations that create a meaningful advantage will be the ones that can effectively collect, structure, and learn from information generated across their portfolios." Business Insider's 2026 Rising Stars of real estate share the biggest challenges facing real estate.

Alyssa Powell

  • Business Insider has announced its 2026 class of Rising Stars of Real Estate.
  • We asked 10 about the biggest challenges facing residential and commercial real estate.
  • From AI to high interest rates and economic uncertainty, here's what they had to say.

The real estate market has felt anything but normal in 2026. High interest rates and home prices have turned off many would-be buyers, even in some of the country's previously hottest markets.

New taxes affecting high-end properties, coupled with broader economic uncertainty, have also prompted wealthy buyers to question whether it still makes sense to buy or invest in real estate in their cities — or look elsewhere, even overseas.

These challenges are likely to carry into next year. But Business Insider's 2026 Rising Stars of Real Estate say it's not all doom and gloom.

Some rising stars see a bigger role for agents as buyers and sellers try to make sense of a complicated market. Others are experimenting with AI to manage and grow their businesses. And in some markets, like Miami and New York, they say demand is picking up again.

Here are what 10 of this year's rising stars say are the biggest issues facing real estate and how they think the industry will adapt.

Agents can't get by just knowing the basics.

Photo Courtesy of Joey Ben-Zvi

Joey Ben-Zvi, founder of the real-estate firm Ben-Zvi Group, says technology has made data and information more accessible, leading some buyers and sellers to believe they can navigate a transaction on their own, without an agent.

"Consumers have more access to information than ever before, which is ultimately a good thing, but access to information isn't the same as being in the trenches on a daily basis and staying deeply connected to the product and consumers, along with having the experience, judgment, and relationships necessary to navigate a complicated transaction," Ben-Zvi told Business Insider.

While Ben-Zvi believes agents remain fundamental to the homebuying and selling experience, he says knowing the basics is no longer enough.

"I think the industry is going through a necessary evolution," Ben-Zvi said. "Agents can no longer rely solely on access to listings or information. They have to demonstrate real value through their expertise, creativity, negotiation skills, and ability to solve problems."

Data will become even more critical.

Photo Courtesy of Saharsh Chordia

Saharsh Chordia, the 33-year-old vice president of strategy and analytics at Cortland, said that data will become much more important. The challenge, he said, is turning the vast amount of data generated by physical assets into actionable insight.

"Real estate is fundamentally a business built around physical assets, yet much of the industry's data remains fragmented and underutilized," Chordia said. "AI will play an important role, but the organizations that create a meaningful advantage will be the ones that can effectively collect, structure, and learn from information generated across their portfolios."

Data centers could hurt some types of properties.

Photo Courtesy of Michael Dillon

Michael Dillon, a 31-year-old vice president at Prime Finance, said data centers and power-adjacent properties could drive changes in what traditional property types benefit and suffer. He noted that it's unclear how an AI-driven economy could position certain asset types over the long term.

"For a lender, that means underwriting not just the building today, but folding those questions into our view of durable demand for that specific property over a ten-year horizon," Dillon said.

AI is "Our biggest challenge but also our newest advantage."

Photo Courtesy of Alex Dobosh

Alex Dobosh, an associate director at HKS Real Estate Advisors, sees artificial intelligence as real estate's biggest challenge, and potentially one of its greatest opportunities.

It's not hard to see why. Americans are turning to platforms like ChatGPT for real-estate advice, home-construction guidance, and help with the buying and selling process.

Business Insider has even written about homebuyers who have successfully used AI as their real-estate agent.

Dobosh doesn't see AI as a reason for agents to panic. He says it can be a powerful tool for professionals willing to embrace it. His firm is already doing so.

"Our biggest challenge is also our newest advantage, which is AI," Dobosh said. "It can be overwhelming to see how it's changing our world. We are leveraging it every single day to source business and help our clients, but also because we refuse to fall behind."

The wealth gap will continue to grow.

Photo Courtesy of Landy Liu

Landy Liu, the 33-year-old founder of Foyer, a "401(k) for homeownership," expects 2027 to be another year of affordability concerns.

"We are facing a structural squeeze on consumers that is leading to a dramatic evolution of the homebuying experience," Liu said.

Liu, who founded Foyer to give first-time homebuyers more support throughout the process, said a lack of affordable homes has widened the wealth gap.

"The industry needs to fundamentally change to better support younger Americans and other consumers at a lower cost," he said.

There's a housing shortage and an affordability crisis.

Photo Courtesy of Katherine McGrath

Katherine McGrath, whose work at lobbying firm Kasirer deals with land use projects, believes the lack of affordable homes — and of homes in general — is a major challenge, especially in her city of New York.

"Demand continues to rise across all five boroughs, but land, construction, labor, and financing costs make it extremely difficult to build projects with a meaningful share of affordable units," McGrath told Business Insider.

McGrath said that mixed-income development is one of the most effective ways to combat both supply and affordability in one blow. But developers need assistance from their local governments.

"Developers can't close that gap alone," she said. "They need incentive programs that reflect real-world costs, a faster approvals process, and continued zoning reform. If we want more affordable homes, we have to make it feasible to build them."

The lack of quality buildings is slowing down transaction velocity.

Photo Courtesy of Nigel Alfred

Cordelia Meserow, a vice president of asset management at real estate investment and management firm Harbor Group International, said that while interest rate volatility has had an effect on pricing commercial buildings in Manhattan, the city's leasing market has never been stronger. The problem is that there's not enough good office space to go around.

"There seems to be no ceiling for what tenants will spend on desirable space," Meserow told Business Insider. "The biggest challenge in New York is that the market is actually running out of Class A space."

Because of the shortage of Class A buildings, transaction velocity will be constrained.

"Velocity will certainly slow down because of the lack of availability," she said.

Real estate agents need to regain clients' trust and show their worth.

Photo Courtesy of Steven Rivera

After the structural changes to commissions, real estate agent Steven Rivera thinks agents need to win back their clients' trust to succeed.

"Since the commission settlement, buyers sign an agreement with their agent before touring a home and rightly ask what they are paying for," Rivera told Business Insider. "That is healthy for the industry, but it raises the bar: agents now have to demonstrate their value, not simply claim it."

Rivera said he gives his clients a high level of service to instill trust in the final result.

"If you cannot explain what you do for the fee, the market will ask," he said.

The real estate industry needs to start catering to younger generation.

Photo Courtesy of Selin Sonmez

"Real Estate is built for a world that no longer exists," cofounder of Snag, Selin Sonmez, told Business Insider. "Its biggest challenge is adapting to the new economic reality of the rising generation."

Sonmez's startup Snag is geared toward younger renters looking to sublet their spots using a social-media-like approach to listing. She's recognized that consumers are getting younger, and thinks the rest of the industry should try to cater to the next generation.

"Young people are expected to rent for 20 years, have multiple jobs, and not be permanent," she said. "How is real estate adapting to this new reality? Most industries shifted to bite-size, approachable, scalable units, from media to investments," she said.

Real estate professionals need to adapt their use of land to meet people's needs.

Photo Courtesy of James Williams Jr.

James Williams Jr., a shareholder in the real estate group at the law firm Gunster, believes real estate professionals need to adapt their plans to meet the changing needs for housing, employment, and services.

"That means looking at whether a property's existing use still serves the community's needs — and, if not, what it could become," Williams Jr. told Business Insider.

But he said the work doesn't stop once you identify a more optimal use for a building; there are a lot of hurdles — like zoning or funding — that need to be overcome to make it happen.

"Existing zoning may not permit the proposed development, infrastructure may need significant upgrades, and the cost of those improvements may make an otherwise promising project financially unworkable," he said. "The challenge is addressing those obstacles while ensuring that the development fits its surroundings and delivers meaningful benefits to the community."

items.title: Gemini 4 Carbon Isn’t in Google AI Pro: 5 Ways to Use It
items.summary: Gemini 4 Carbon isn’t in Google AI Pro or Plus. 5 ways to use it now, what each costs, and when Argon is enough. Google AI Pro stops at Argon. Ultra has Carbon, and there are three more routes in between. Google released Gemini 4 Carbon to the public on November 10. If you pay $19.99 a month for Google AI Pro, you probably opened the Gemini app, tapped Carbon, and got an upgrade screen asking for $99.99 a month. That’s not a slow rollout. Carbon is a Google AI Ultra model for now. Google’s Varun Mohan wrote on X on November 11 that the team is still figuring out “broader rollout”, and until then “you can access it if you are an Ultra user”. No date for Pro. Short answer: Gemini 4 Carbon isn’t available on Google AI Pro or Google AI Plus. You can use it right now in five ways: upgrade to Ultra, use a multi-model app that already includes it, pay per token in Google AI Studio, pay per token through OpenRouter, or stay on Argon until a task actually needs Carbon. If you’re not sure you need Carbon at all, I ran a Gemini 4 Carbon vs Argon test on a 60-page report before writing this. Upgrade to Google AI Ultra Use Gemini 4 Carbon in a multi-model app that already includes it Use Carbon in Google AI Studio with a paid API key Use Gemini 4 Carbon through OpenRouter Stay on Gemini 4 Argon, and know when to switch The five routes side by side. Gemini 4 Carbon pricing at a glance Google AI Ultra: $99.99 a month and up, $80 more than Pro. Multi-model apps: some include Carbon in their paid plans, usually at a higher credit cost per message than Argon. Gemini API in AI Studio: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens until November 30, then $4 and $20. OpenRouter: Google’s API rates, paid from credit you load in advance. Argon on Google AI Pro: $0 extra. Is Gemini 4 Carbon available on Google AI Pro? No. As of November 12, Google AI Pro gets Gemini 4 Argon but not Carbon, Google AI Plus gets neither, and Carbon is Ultra only in the Gemini app, AI Mode in Search and Antigravity. The AI Studio plans page says the same thing for developers: Carbon “requires an AI Ultra plan in AI Studio (not available on the Free or AI Pro plans)”. The paid Gemini API and Gemini for business do have Carbon. The free tier doesn’t. Carbon access in Google. 1. Upgrade to Google AI Ultra The official route. $99.99 a month gets you Carbon everywhere Google offers it, including the Gemini app, AI Mode in Search, Antigravity and AI Studio, with higher limits than any third-party app will give you. If Gemini is the only model you use, this is the cleanest answer. The catch is the jump. You’re paying $80 more a month than Pro, mostly for one model. And Carbon is slow. Google’s own docs note that it spends more thinking tokens per turn , and on launch day one Hacker News commenter reported a 60-second wait before the first token. Even an Ultra subscriber in that thread wasn’t sure Carbon “will make sense for most activities”. If you only need it a few times a week, that math is rough. 2. Use Gemini 4 Carbon in a multi-model app I personally use HaloMate, a multi-model AI workspace, for most of my daily work, and Carbon showed up in its model picker next to Argon and models from OpenAI, Anthropic and others. It’s already in the paid plans, so I could try it without setting up an API key or a separate bill. When you switch models in a chat, none of that goes anywhere. You can regenerate the last answer with Carbon and compare it side by side with Argon, or just switch and keep going. Carbon and Argon in the same picker. Gemini 3.1 Pro is still in the list too. That’s how I compared the two. I put a 60-page Stanford report into a Project once and did the reading and fact-checking on Argon. Then I gave both models the same one-line request: turn the findings into a short animation for a meeting. Argon made a cramped slide deck and recorded its own play buttons into the video. Carbon made one I’d actually play in the room. Same prompt, same data. Argon’s player bar ended up inside its video. Carbon kept one point per screen. Full test, all three rounds: Is Gemini 4 Carbon Better Than Argon? Tested on Real Work Now the limits. Carbon uses more credits per message than Argon, so on a lower plan you’d switch to it for the hard step, not leave it on all day. Expensive models are expensive everywhere. I’m on the Max plan, which costs about the same as Google AI Ultra, and if Gemini were the only model I used, Ultra would give me more Carbon. What I’m paying for is choosing across providers when models move or get retired ( as GPT-4o and Opus 4.5 did ), without rebuilding my context each time. HaloMate isn’t the only app putting several providers under one subscription. Whichever one you look at, check two things: whether Carbon is in the plan or billed on top, and whether your files and instructions carry over when you switch models. 3. Use Carbon in Google AI Studio with a paid API key This is the route most guides skip, and it’s confusing enough to spell out. If you sign in to Google AI Studio with your Pro subscription, Carbon isn’t selectable. Subscription benefits in AI Studio only cover what your plan includes. But if you create an API key and turn on Cloud Billing, you can call Carbon in the same interface and pay per request. Pricing is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens until November 30, then $4 and $20 ( Google ). Carbon thinks longer than Argon and thinking tokens count as output, so long answers cost more than they look. The bigger point: this is money on top of the $19.99 you already pay for Pro. And you get a developer console, not a workspace. Nothing carries between sessions unless you wire it up yourself. 4. Use Gemini 4 Carbon through OpenRouter OpenRouter added Carbon on launch day, served through Google AI Studio and Vertex at Google’s API rates. You load credit and pay per token. If you already pair OpenRouter with a chat client, it’s the fastest way to try Carbon for a few dollars with zero monthly commitment. If you don’t, you have to set up a client first, and like AI Studio, every run is billed on top of your existing subscriptions with no shared project memory. It does the job for quick experiments. It isn’t built for keeping real work organized over weeks. 5. Stay on Gemini 4 Argon, and know when to switch This is the option nobody selling an upgrade leads with, though Google comes close. Its launch post says Argon “remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work”, while Carbon is built for tasks “that test the limits of a model’s intelligence”. Benchmarks split the same way. Carbon jumps ahead on Artificial Analysis’s overall Intelligence Index (60 vs 50), driven by hard coding and reasoning tasks, yet on long-context document reasoning the two are practically tied at 79.3% and 79.0%. My own test landed in the same place. Argon read every chart bar accurately and reached the same conclusion as Carbon. Carbon only pulled ahead when the job was a finished deliverable. If your work is reading, extracting and summarizing, Pro is already enough. Run your hard task on Argon first, and if it holds up, you just saved $80 a month. And since Google says it’s still working out a broader rollout, waiting is a reasonable plan too. Other routes, briefly Perplexity: Carbon is available inside Perplexity Computer on Perplexity’s Pro and Max plans, and in regular search on Max only. Cursor: Carbon has been in Cursor since launch day, if you code there already. GitHub Copilot: Carbon is in Copilot , with Business and Enterprise admins controlling access. Scientists and researchers: Google is taking applications for six months of free access through Antigravity’s top tier, subject to selection. If you got Google AI Pro bundled through Jio, you’re a tier below regular Pro right now, which is a separate fight . The real problem isn’t Carbon Look at what else happened around November 10. As Carbon rolled out, the Gemini app started removing Gemini 3.1 Pro . If 3.1 Pro was the model you’d tuned your prompts around, it’s disappearing from the picker. Jio’s bundled Pro users found out that “Pro” means different things depending on how you paid. And Anthropic is about to run its own version of this with Fable on Claude Pro on November 17. None of this is unusual anymore. Plans change every month. The strongest model moves up a tier, the one you relied on gets retired, and the people burned worst are the ones who built daily work inside a single vendor’s app. So the question isn’t really how to get Carbon. It’s whether the work you depend on should be tied to one company’s pricing page. I’d rather keep my instructions, files and context in one place and treat the model as the part that changes, because it will change again, probably before the end of the month. FAQ Is Gemini 4 Carbon available on Google AI Pro? No. As of November 12, 2026, Google AI Pro includes Gemini 4 Argon but not Carbon, and Google AI Plus includes neither. In the Gemini app, AI Mode in Search, Antigravity and AI Studio, Carbon requires Google AI Ultra. Will Gemini 4 Carbon come to Google AI Pro? Maybe, but there’s no date. Google’s Varun Mohan said on November 11 that Google is still figuring out “broader rollout”, and for now Carbon is for Ultra users. How much does Gemini 4 Carbon cost? In Google’s consumer apps, Carbon requires Google AI Ultra at $99.99 a month and up. In the Gemini API, it costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens until November 30, 2026, then $4 and $20. Some multi-model apps include it in their plans. Can I use Gemini 4 Carbon for free? Not through Google’s consumer or developer free tiers. The only no-cost option Google lists is a selective six-month access program for scientists and researchers in Google Antigravity. Why can’t I select Gemini 4 Carbon in Google AI Studio with Pro? AI Studio access follows your consumer plan, so Ultra gets Carbon and Pro gets Argon. To use Carbon in AI Studio without Ultra, attach an API key with Google Cloud Billing turned on and pay per token. Is Gemini 4 Carbon better than Argon? For finished deliverables, hard coding and multi-step tasks, yes. For reading long PDFs, pulling numbers from charts and everyday reasoning, Argon matched Carbon in my test and answered faster. Is Gemini 4 Carbon cheaper than Claude Fable 5.2? On the API, yes. Fable 5.2 costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, so Carbon is a quarter of that until November 30 and half after it, according to VentureBeat ’s price comparison. I write field notes on how I actually use AI at work: workflows, experiments, and what breaks. More at angied.me or on Medium . Gemini 4 Carbon Isn’t in Google AI Pro: 5 Ways to Use It was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Benchmarks split the same way. Carbon jumps ahead on Artificial Analysis’s overall Intelligence Index (60 vs 50), driven by hard coding and reasoning tasks, yet on long-context document reasoning the two are practically tied at 79.3% and 79.0%.

My own test landed in the same place. Argon read every chart bar accurately and reached the same conclusion as Carbon. Carbon only pulled ahead when the job was a finished deliverable. If your work is reading, extracting and summarizing, Pro is already enough. Run your hard task on Argon first, and if it holds up, you just saved $80 a month. And since Google says it’s still working out a broader rollout, waiting is a reasonable plan too.

Other routes, briefly
  • Perplexity: Carbon is available inside Perplexity Computer on Perplexity’s Pro and Max plans, and in regular search on Max only.
  • Cursor: Carbon has been in Cursor since launch day, if you code there already.
  • GitHub Copilot: Carbon is in Copilot, with Business and Enterprise admins controlling access.
  • Scientists and researchers: Google is taking applications for six months of free access through Antigravity’s top tier, subject to selection.

If you got Google AI Pro bundled through Jio, you’re a tier below regular Pro right now, which is a separate fight.

The real problem isn’t Carbon

Look at what else happened around November 10. As Carbon rolled out, the Gemini app started removing Gemini 3.1 Pro. If 3.1 Pro was the model you’d tuned your prompts around, it’s disappearing from the picker. Jio’s bundled Pro users found out that “Pro” means different things depending on how you paid. And Anthropic is about to run its own version of this with Fable on Claude Pro on November 17.

None of this is unusual anymore. Plans change every month. The strongest model moves up a tier, the one you relied on gets retired, and the people burned worst are the ones who built daily work inside a single vendor’s app.

So the question isn’t really how to get Carbon. It’s whether the work you depend on should be tied to one company’s pricing page. I’d rather keep my instructions, files and context in one place and treat the model as the part that changes, because it will change again, probably before the end of the month.

FAQIs Gemini 4 Carbon available on Google AI Pro?

No. As of November 12, 2026, Google AI Pro includes Gemini 4 Argon but not Carbon, and Google AI Plus includes neither. In the Gemini app, AI Mode in Search, Antigravity and AI Studio, Carbon requires Google AI Ultra.

Will Gemini 4 Carbon come to Google AI Pro?

Maybe, but there’s no date. Google’s Varun Mohan said on November 11 that Google is still figuring out “broader rollout”, and for now Carbon is for Ultra users.

How much does Gemini 4 Carbon cost?

In Google’s consumer apps, Carbon requires Google AI Ultra at $99.99 a month and up. In the Gemini API, it costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens until November 30, 2026, then $4 and $20. Some multi-model apps include it in their plans.

Can I use Gemini 4 Carbon for free?

Not through Google’s consumer or developer free tiers. The only no-cost option Google lists is a selective six-month access program for scientists and researchers in Google Antigravity.

Why can’t I select Gemini 4 Carbon in Google AI Studio with Pro?

AI Studio access follows your consumer plan, so Ultra gets Carbon and Pro gets Argon. To use Carbon in AI Studio without Ultra, attach an API key with Google Cloud Billing turned on and pay per token.

Is Gemini 4 Carbon better than Argon?

For finished deliverables, hard coding and multi-step tasks, yes. For reading long PDFs, pulling numbers from charts and everyday reasoning, Argon matched Carbon in my test and answered faster.

Is Gemini 4 Carbon cheaper than Claude Fable 5.2?

On the API, yes. Fable 5.2 costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, so Carbon is a quarter of that until November 30 and half after it, according to VentureBeat’s price comparison.
