items.title: This Comic Kills Technofascists
items.summary: Dave Maass has been writing about comics for more than 20 years, and now he also writes comics. By day, he teaches tech investigative techniques at the University of Nevada, Reno Reynolds School of Journalism and researches surveillance at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. If I was the manager of a comic book store, I’d create a section for “journalism nerdcore.” It’s where I would stock Transmetropolitan, DMZ, and Abbott – comics that place fictional journalists in the center of genre stories, be it science fiction, action or horror. Despite their daylight jobs, Spider-Man and Superman wouldn’t be allowed there, but DC’s Lois Lane would find a home of her own. On the end-of-shelf display, with a big fat, Sharpie-written “Employee Pick of 2026” sign: Exploit , the new comic series from Laura Hudson and Tim Leong and illustrator Emiliana Pinna, which was just published last month by Mad Cave Studios in its collected trade paperback volume . It doesn’t get more journalism nerdcore than its tag line: “Don’t Bury The Lede. Bury Your Enemies!” Exploit is an action thriller inspired by the battle raging right now between the tech oligarchy and the independent press. Editorial intern Kirby Kuo is trying to score her first byline in RIOT! , a WIRED -style print magazine, before the newsroom is wiped out by its soon-to-be new owner, a thin-skinned Alex Karp-flavored cyberlibertarian-turned-technofascist. But when the subject of her reporting is assassinated on a live stream, Kirby finds herself facing the blame, on the run and forced to place her trust in agoraphobic hacker Lenox and Cold War-alum cybermercenary Ipsum. Creators Hudson and Leong shared the masthead at WIRED (senior editor and director of digital design, respectively), but long before that they ran Comic Foundry , where they were “the team that changed comics journalism forever,” as ComicsBeat put it . Their careers have dovetailed between comics and journalism for years, with Hudson putting time at The Verge and ComicsAlliance and logging bylines in The Guardian, The New York Times, and Slate , and Leong holding creative roles at Fortune and Entertainment Weekly, while also writing and designing the Super Graphic series . All that experience shows. Between the chase sequences and heist-planning, there are plot points based on real episodes in tech and cybersecurity uncovered in publications like 404 Media, WIRED , and The Markup. But the panels radiate with the earnest love for scrappy, independent journalism–especially print journalism–and a molten fury for those who threaten it. I asked Hudson some questions to learn more about the heart and rage she poured into this series. The following has been edited for length and to avoid spoilers. Exploit explores the perils journalists face when handling leaked data. Dave Maass: Comics love an origin story. Take me through the back story of Exploit . Laura Hudson: We've been working on Exploit since we met up in a diner in LA in 2019, pre-pandemic. I don't live in LA but I was there working on a TV show, and it was the first time we'd lived in the same city since mid-aughts New York. Tim fucking LOVES print, and we'd both spent the last decade watching print journalism collapse from the inside. There are definitely scenes in the comic, and a few darlings we had to cut, that were ripped directly from real life whether anyone believes us or not. We arrived just after the good times had ended, in time to hear all the stories about how amazing it had been, and watch it get worse and worse. And of course, the generation just after us only experiences the wreckage. Tim had an idea for a comic set at a print magazine in New York, and I started imagining how I would feel, starting out as a journalist now. It always makes me think of donut blocks, from Super Mario Bros 3 on. They're the round, cakey-looking blocks in the game that start shaking when you step on them, and then fall down. So if you're going to walk across them, you better run, or you're gonna die. If you stop, you're gonna die. So, you can't stop. Ever. I understand that feeling intimately, and I knew I could write from there. And hell, I've wanted to make comics for over 30 years and now I'm finally doing it at 45? Fuck me. Exploit’ s main protagonist is a journalist (technically an intern) working for a magazine that specializes in tech investigations. It’s a WIRED meets Mother Jones kind of affair, but also if VICE’s Motherboard had been a standalone, hard-copy publication. Why choose a tech journalist as your hero? It probably says something about me that this question baffles me. Maybe I've just known too many good tech journalists, because to me it feels so obvious. Technology and the internet have played, are playing, and will play transformative roles in our lives, often in ways that few people fully understand. We're still governed by a gerontocracy where many of our leaders conceptualize the internet as a bewildering series of tubes, possibly now filled with AI. Our technology has surpassed our ability to legislate it or address it ethically to such an extreme degree that some tech leaders are actually asking to be stopped . The internet (or at least its infrastructure) is a hyperobject in the Mortonian sense of the word , something so massive, complex and distributed that people struggle to comprehend it fully. We can see pieces of it, and effects of it, but it's impossible to perceive or experience it as a whole, even and especially when we are inside it. But as Morton has written in reference to climate change, apocalyptic framing around hyperobjects can lead to hopelessness and inaction in situations when things genuinely can be addressed: "You are closing down the future. You are making your reader submit to tyrannical despair." Recognizing the enormity of something, in both the classic and popular sense, doesn't have to mean giving up. People who refuse to accept that something is too vast, too complicated, or too powerful to challenge are pretty compelling to me. That's what the best tech journalists do. Now let’s talk about the dual villains–both techbro executives at a start-up that is not only a government contractor, but aims to take over key government functions. Now the last comparable comic I read like this was 2014’s Hacktivist (written by of all people actor Alyssa Milano with Jackson Lanzing and Collin Kelly), and it also featured two very similar tech bros–but they were the heroes, moonlighting as digital freedom fighters. That was a time where people were inspired by larger-than-life figures like Jack Dorsey and Elon Musk. That's not so much the case anymore. How would you say that Exploit ’s antagonists reflect the shift in the public perception, and activities, of the “founder” class in our society? We want to believe that there is someone coming to save us, and since billionaires were the ones powerful enough to fuck up human civilization, it makes sense that we'd look for someone of equal power to save us. It makes sense to want that. But this is a fairytale we tell ourselves, which I say as someone who once wanted to believe it was at least possible. But no one is coming to save us. Let me say it one more time, because this is important: NO ONE IS COMING TO SAVE US. Billionaires least of all. Tech billionaires, by and large, are much better at destroying than fixing, and have advertised this fact for decades. They like to move fast and break things, and leave them broken. Many of them struggle to understand human beings socially even as they run social networks. They are prone to massive ego, can have anything they want at any time, and exist in bubble worlds where they are never told no. These are the people we're putting in charge of the future? I wouldn't put them in charge of a Dairy Queen. And I personally believe that some of them would be willing to accept the deaths of millions or even billions of people as the cost of advancing humanity in whatever sci-fi way they have imagined. Their obscene wealth requires them to exist at a scope that most humans are not built for, like images stretched out over miles. It distorts them as individuals, and it can distort their morality, insofar as it ever existed beyond the desire to advance and profit. This has become more evident as more tech leaders have chosen to behave as open buffoons in an age of buffoonery. But this is who they always were. In 2008, Exploit authors Laura Hudson and Tim Leong circa 2008 co-ran Comic Foundry. Courtesy: Laura Hudson From the first pages of the book, we’re introduced to the very real, extreme asymmetrical conflict between tech billionaires. Even a poorly paid journalist can threaten a billionaire (or at least his ego), but a billionaire has so much money, it’s easy to crush a publication. It immediately made me think of Jeff Bezos buying the Washington Post , Peter Thiel bankrolling the attacks on Gawker, and cases where surveillance companies have threatened news outlets. Am I wrong to think that’s the overarching theme of the whole series? Nope. I feel an anger about it so deep that I almost intuitively dissociate when it comes up. Not because I don't think I should be angry, but because I have learned I cannot be angry all the time without deleterious effects. Sometimes you just have to play the Yakety-Sax song in your head until the feeling passes, because you have to get things done today. It's worth noting that Kirby and Lenox (and Ipsum) [Note: Lenox is a young hacker and Ipsum is an old-school cybermercenary] undertake their mission with full knowledge that it will probably ruin their lives. That's part of the benefit package of being a billionaire. People can't challenge you without possibly ruining their lives. Now Exploit isn’t meant to be a realistic treatment of tech journalism, but I do think there’s a lot of truth in how you portray the perils faced by journalists who deal with hackers and leakers. This is running in a publication that specializes in that, but a lot of other journalists have been burned pretty bad, some even ending up in jail. How did reality affect the way you handled the relationship between your protagonist and the various hackers who enter her orbit? We've all seen things go very wrong for journalists, even those who meant well. Kirby has lived more life than the average intern, and done some journalistic work, but never at this level and never with these kinds of sources. She's green, and we wanted to show that. Before the big lead comes in, we have her pitching stories from sources that clearly have their own agenda, and her pitches get slapped down. That kind of pushback is essential, and what helps you learn before you're in a position to make serious mistakes. Kirby is pushed into a very big story before she is probably ready, but she's the only one in a position to do it. We wanted it to be clear that she's able to do what she does not just because she's smart and brave, but because she has an experienced group around her. Dealing with hackers, leakers, and sensitive sources requires dealing with two competing impulses as a journalist. Good journalism requires rigorous skepticism as a discipline. There's that journo saying that if your mother says she loves you, check it out. But developing a relationship with a source requires trust on both sides, and risk on both sides. One of the things Kirby learns is that a source is not necessarily an ally, even when they have valuable information. Their goals may overlap in places, but they can be different in invisible and dangerous ways. It's not something anyone should approach lightly or without care. A quarter of the way into the book, you introduce an assassination drone–and I initially expected it to be a sort of “Chekhov’s gun” that would play a huge role later on. But, it actually wasn’t. It turned out the most frightening thing still is people –specifically the mobs of doxxers who worship tech demagogues. Does this mirror your own experiences with online harassment? One of the things people used to say a lot, to dismiss or ignore the nightmarish world of online harassment, is that it was "only" online. You could just close your computer and go outside, so really, wasn't it all in your head? This line of convenient fiction collapsed pretty quickly, as doxxing, swatting, stalking, assaulting, raping, and molesting people through the internet became, shall we say, super popular? You can't dismiss the internet as a fake, unreal place where nothing of consequence matters. We know it matters now, that it's dangerous. But now it almost feels too late to care. These systems and the people who run them have certainly shown they don't care, and there's no Band-Aid you can put on it now to fix it. We could have built the internet and its social architecture very differently, in a way that prioritized dialogue over the right to abuse. But the trolls thought it was funny, and the companies wanted more money, so here we are living in the cursed labyrinth of their lols. One thing about an assassination drone, though: everyone understands it as a weapon. A tool of sorts, but one designed explicitly to cause damage. Its goals and impacts are not opaque. Social media platforms were pitched as a way to connect people, to give them the power to reach out and touch anyone from anywhere. Giving this power away to anyone who wanted it with little to no accountability was described by tech companies at the time as inherently good. It took longer—some would say too long—for everyone to realize the scope of the damage it could cause. Or that this incredible communications technology could double as a custom-made playground for grifters, bullies and predators of every stripe. So yeah, people are the scary part. But people get a lot scarier when they are given great power with zero accountability. RIOT magazine’s editor still has fucks left to give about investigative reporting. Zines play a major plot point in the book. But you also made a promotional zine for San Diego Comic-Con, which included a lot of digital security advice. How do you see physical media reemerging in political life? Tim designed that, by the way, and I can't believe how much it looks like an actual riot grrrl zine. Zines have long been linked to comics culture, and you can see the overlap in a lot of indie comics spaces and events. But zines—or as they once called them, pamphlets—have been powerful political tools for over 500 years. They have defeated churches and kings. And they're a very compelling tool right now, as a form of dissent that exists outside of the internet and its platforms. You can't hack a printed page. And we don't think about it this way anymore, but writing on paper is a communications technology—perhaps the greatest in the history of the world—and we should regard it as such. A lot of obsolete or antiquated tech can have value today because accessibility is also vulnerability, and obsolescence is its own kind of security feature. There are some impressive Gen Z zine enthusiasts, and a great WIRED article about the scene. But I'd love to see more people pick up that torch, for both creative and political reasons. No one can stop you. What do you hope people will take away from Exploit? How do you hope it will make them feel? In the year of our Lord 2026, I would be happy just to give people a bit of distraction from the horrors. But if you feel like your life has been suffused by the feeling that you showed up after the party was over, and that it's only downhill from here, then we made this, in part, for you. It's a grim feeling we know well, a sort of miasmic dread that flattens the future and makes you feel helpless and paralyzed. And that's exactly how a lot of terrible people want you to feel. They want you to lie down and allow the terrible machine to function smoothly around you. Both Kirby and Lenox come up with their own imperfect coping mechanisms for that reality and feeling, but they do cope. They do move forward and fight, and they don't do it alone. They can't, and neither can we.

A quarter of the way into the book, you introduce an assassination drone–and I initially  expected it to be a sort of “Chekhov’s gun” that would play a huge role later on.  But, it actually wasn’t. It turned out the most frightening thing still is people–specifically the mobs of doxxers who worship tech demagogues. Does this mirror your own experiences with online harassment?

One of the things people used to say a lot, to dismiss or ignore the nightmarish world of online harassment, is that it was "only" online. You could just close your computer and go outside, so really, wasn't it all in your head? This line of convenient fiction collapsed pretty quickly, as doxxing, swatting, stalking, assaulting, raping, and molesting people through the internet became, shall we say, super popular? You can't dismiss the internet as a fake, unreal place where nothing of consequence matters. We know it matters now, that it's dangerous. But now it almost feels too late to care. These systems and the people who run them have certainly shown they don't care, and there's no Band-Aid you can put on it now to fix it. We could have built the internet and its social architecture very differently, in a way that prioritized dialogue over the right to abuse. But the trolls thought it was funny, and the companies wanted more money, so here we are living in the cursed labyrinth of their lols. 

One thing about an assassination drone, though: everyone understands it as a weapon. A tool of sorts, but one designed explicitly to cause damage. Its goals and impacts are not opaque. Social media platforms were pitched as a way to connect people, to give them the power to reach out and touch anyone from anywhere. Giving this power away to anyone who wanted it with little to no accountability was described by tech companies at the time as inherently good. It took longer—some would say too long—for everyone to realize the scope of the damage it could cause. Or that this incredible communications technology could double as a custom-made playground for grifters, bullies and predators of every stripe. So yeah, people are the scary part. But people get a lot scarier when they are given great power with zero accountability. 

RIOT magazine’s editor still has fucks left to give about investigative reporting. 

Zines play a major plot point in the book. But you also made a promotional zine for San Diego Comic-Con, which included a lot of digital security advice. How do you see physical media reemerging in political life? 

Tim designed that, by the way, and I can't believe how much it looks like an actual riot grrrl zine. Zines have long been linked to comics culture, and you can see the overlap in a lot of indie comics spaces and events. But zines—or as they once called them, pamphlets—have been powerful political tools for over 500 years. They have defeated churches and kings. And they're a very compelling tool right now, as a form of dissent that exists outside of the internet and its platforms. You can't hack a printed page. And we don't think about it this way anymore, but writing on paper is a communications technology—perhaps the greatest in the history of the world—and we should regard it as such. A lot of obsolete or antiquated tech can have value today because accessibility is also vulnerability, and obsolescence is its own kind of security feature. There are some impressive Gen Z zine enthusiasts, and a great WIRED article about the scene. But I'd love to see more people pick up that torch, for both creative and political reasons. No one can stop you. 

What do you hope people will take away from Exploit? How do you hope it will make them feel? 

In the year of our Lord 2026, I would be happy just to give people a bit of distraction from the horrors. But if you feel like your life has been suffused by the feeling that you showed up after the party was over, and that it's only downhill from here, then we made this, in part, for you. It's a grim feeling we know well, a sort of miasmic dread that flattens the future and makes you feel helpless and paralyzed. And that's exactly how a lot of terrible people want you to feel. They want you to lie down and allow the terrible machine to function smoothly around you. Both Kirby and Lenox come up with their own imperfect coping mechanisms for that reality and feeling, but they do cope. They do move forward and fight, and they don't do it alone. They can't, and neither can we.

items.title: 🔵 Anthropic is Coming for Everything
items.summary: Hi product people 👋, This week, Anthropic launched Claude Sheets, Whiteboards, Data and Meetings and a new model - all in the days before its IPO. We’ll take a closer look at these and why it might represent a new strategic threat to some its own customers. Plus, Gemini 4 Hydrogen nearly matches Fable 5.2 at a fifth of the cost and the world’s top product leaders share their views on headless product strategy. Watch on YouTube | Follow on Substack Notes Subscribe now Key reads and resources for product teams New from the Department of Product Substack this week: Personal Agent Systems Explained: How 5 Leaders Run Their Work Through AI Agents How leaders at Coinbase, Notion, Linear and more have set up agents to run their day, and how to build your own. (Department of Product) The New UX of Mobile How AI, foldables and native rebuilds are changing what a phone app does, with 35+ real examples from Meta, Apple, Linear, Strava, Superhuman and more. (Department of Product) AI product management at Spotify from three angles “The AI PM” doesn’t exist - there are at least three very different jobs hiding under the same label. In this piece, three Spotify product leaders in research, foundation models, and UX compare notes on what their roles actually look like day to day. (Spotify PM) Sentry’s CPO says “we have a Slopware Factory” Sentry’s co-founder and CPO David Cramer breaks down what a real software factory looks like and why he lovingly refers to it as a Slopware Factory. (Sentry) Research in the loop - How UX keeps up when teams ship faster As AI speeds up development, it can be a challenge for research to adapt. NN Group explores how user research is evolving to keep pace with the new era of AI-assisted development. (NN Group) How to prompt Fable 5.2 - a guide from Anthropic Fable 5.2 behaves differently from earlier Claude models in several ways and in this prompting guide, Anthropic outlines how to get the most out of it. (Anthropic) Anthropic is coming for everything: Sheets, Data, Docs and more It’s been a relentless week at Anthropic as the company begins to prepare for its IPO. On Monday, it released Claude Fable 5.2 and later in the week, it took on the likes of Google Workspace and Office with a bunch of new productivity tools. Claude Sheets is its version of Google Sheets (why change the name when it works, I guess?), which lets users create a working spreadsheet inside Claude and Claude Whiteboards is almost like its take on Miro, letting teams collaborate on whiteboards together. Claude Data, formerly Dashboards, is also now generally available and lets you turn our data into stories and narrated videos you can share and a new Meet product competes with Google Meet and Granola. All of this landed days before Anthropic is set to go public in an IPO which could value the company at over $1.4 trillion, up from $965 billion in May. Anthropic is becoming a competitor to its own customers - a new feature attempts to appease them In what feels like an attempt to appease the companies it is now directly competing with, Anthropic also released a new capability this week called Interactive connectors that lets product teams ship the full version of their UI inside Claude. Companies like Adobe, Atlassian, Notion and Box have shipped initial versions of this. See examples of products using Interactive Connectors in action here: WordPress demo Box CEO Aaron Levie’s demo Carta’s demo Adobe’s live editor for Acrobat and Express Notion, Confluence, HubSpot and more in Anthropic’s round-up But what are the strategic consequences for mode suppliers building products that compete directly with its own customers? If companies like Anthropic continue to launch new products into more verticals that compete with their customers, could this accelerate those companies’ shift to alternatives by choosing open source models or outright refusing to connect to Claude via MCP? This is a tricky one to navigate for product teams, but I suspect that in the short term at least, teams will keep integrating with Claude and other AI tools in the hope that it all works out in the end. Users are increasingly demanding headless solutions and so it feels like product teams don’t really have much of an alternative than to build them. Other new features worth knowing about OpenAI has launched ChatGPT Wallet , so agents can pay on your behalf without seeing your card. It was built with Amex, Mastercard and Visa and lets users authenticate payments biometrically. For product teams, it’s another step forward in agentic payments that’s worth keeping an eye on. Google released Gemini 4 Hydrogen - and nearly matched Claude Fable 5.2 on Zapier’s AutomationBench index at about a fifth of the cost per task. Sundar Pichai says its 2.5x faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash and is now in Google Search for everyone. Meta has released Muse Ember, a lightweight model that’s priced at just 10 cents per million input tokens. Meta says it’s built for tool calls, coding subtasks, routing and document parsing, so could be worth a look if you’re looking for cheaper alternatives. Glean now works in Excel which lets you build formulas, calculations and charts using natural language based on your company’s context. Figma’s Specs, where teams write the brief and context behind a design, now also work in Figma’s iOS app , with viewing, editing and collaboration. If your product’s not headless “you’re going to miss this wave” - perspectives from top product leaders Dharmesh Sha, co-founder and CTO at HubSpot says the company is “refounding” with its co-founder and the plan is the create the “world first Customer Relationship Harness” and headless hubspot. The day before this announcement, he said that “MCP is the new HTTP” and “if you aren’t making your software product composable and callable by AI harnesses, you’re going to miss this wave”. Sam Stephenson, Co-founder, Granola says Granola now has a dedicated team for “headless Granola”. As part of this, the company has officially launched MCP 2.0 with search that uses 85% fewer tokens and tools that let agents add agendas an organise notes. Barry McCardel, CEO of Hex, argues that frontier companies are hypocritical in their approach to headless product strategy. He notes that Anthropic doesn’t even make its own products accessible via MCP, summing it up as “ MCP for thee, but not for me”. On speed and quality, Anton Osika, CEO, Lovable says that when he first said “non-engineers will build quality software”, people looked at him when he was crazy. He added that “the best ideas often sound wrong before they become obvious” - like how everyone said the idea of renting out a room in your home on Airbnb was never going to happen. Linear’s COO Cristina Cordova says while AI is making building easier, this means that “selling may become more valuable, not less. When everyone can make at least a fine / mediocre product quickly, you need to get the right people to care, trust you and choose it over something else.” 📈 Product data Hex’s average cost per agent conversation fell from a peak of $6.44 in January to just $1.64 this month, even as its monthly token usage kept climbing. Hex says newer, cheaper models along with its own internal harness helped reduce the bill. New data from OpenAI and Upwork found that out of 63 job categories, 43 that were relatively common in ChatGPT lost share of Upwork job posts, demonstrating the link between ChatGPT use and the types of jobs that are emerging. A new study from Retool has found that 89% of IT leaders say their company has at least one AI agent in production. In a study of 300 tech leaders, they found that while the vast majority of companies are building internal agents, there is no clear standard on who actually owns them. 42% said they have each team own its own agents with central oversights while 10% have no formal structure at all. Full report here. Decisions models continue to grow in adoption. The models, which classify, score or pick between different options instead of writing text, grew from zero to 26% share in Vercel’s AI Gateway requests from August to October. The full report from Vercel also found that over half of October’s AI gateway requests went to models that were less than 60 days old, showing that a typical model peaks within a month of its launch. METR, the AI safety research group, found that Anthropic’s models are improving about twice as fast as before October 2025. Staff at Anthropic self-reported being around 12x as productive with Anthropic’s latest internal models. Robinhood says 150,000+ people have opened accounts for AI agents to trade for them. Spotify’s AI DJ is now used by over 94 million Premium listeners . This week, it added new voices and personalities in English and Spanish and an option to switch it off completely. And finally We’ll end with something a bit more lighthearted this week. Back in 1994, a then 17 year old Demis Hassabis co-designed a game called Theme Park where you build and run your own amusement park. This week, as the founder of Deepmind, he went full circle and used his own model to build a brand new DeepMind branded ride , right inside that same park. In his words, he said “it’s kind of mindblowing to see!”, and it’s hard to disagree. Thanks for reading and have a great week ahead! Hi product people 👋,

This week, Anthropic launched Claude Sheets, Whiteboards, Data and Meetings and a new model - all in the days before its IPO. We’ll take a closer look at these and why it might represent a new strategic threat to some its own customers.

Plus, Gemini 4 Hydrogen nearly matches Fable 5.2 at a fifth of the cost and the world’s top product leaders share their views on headless product strategy.

Watch on YouTube | Follow on Substack Notes

Subscribe now

Key reads and resources for product teams

New from the Department of Product Substack this week:

Personal Agent Systems Explained: How 5 Leaders Run Their Work Through AI Agents
How leaders at Coinbase, Notion, Linear and more have set up agents to run their day, and how to build your own. (Department of Product)

The New UX of Mobile
How AI, foldables and native rebuilds are changing what a phone app does, with 35+ real examples from Meta, Apple, Linear, Strava, Superhuman and more. (Department of Product)

AI product management at Spotify from three angles
“The AI PM” doesn’t exist - there are at least three very different jobs hiding under the same label. In this piece, three Spotify product leaders in research, foundation models, and UX compare notes on what their roles actually look like day to day. (Spotify PM)

Sentry’s CPO says “we have a Slopware Factory”
Sentry’s co-founder and CPO David Cramer breaks down what a real software factory looks like and why he lovingly refers to it as a Slopware Factory. (Sentry)

Research in the loop - How UX keeps up when teams ship faster
As AI speeds up development, it can be a challenge for research to adapt. NN Group explores how user research is evolving to keep pace with the new era of AI-assisted development. (NN Group)

How to prompt Fable 5.2 - a guide from Anthropic
Fable 5.2 behaves differently from earlier Claude models in several ways and in this prompting guide, Anthropic outlines how to get the most out of it. (Anthropic)

Anthropic is coming for everything: Sheets, Data, Docs and more

It’s been a relentless week at Anthropic as the company begins to prepare for its IPO. On Monday, it released Claude Fable 5.2 and later in the week, it took on the likes of Google Workspace and Office with a bunch of new productivity tools.

Claude Sheets is its version of Google Sheets (why change the name when it works, I guess?), which lets users create a working spreadsheet inside Claude and Claude Whiteboards is almost like its take on Miro, letting teams collaborate on whiteboards together. Claude Data, formerly Dashboards, is also now generally available and lets you turn our data into stories and narrated videos you can share and a new Meet product competes with Google Meet and Granola.

All of this landed days before Anthropic is set to go public in an IPO which could value the company at over $1.4 trillion, up from $965 billion in May.

Anthropic is becoming a competitor to its own customers - a new feature attempts to appease them

In what feels like an attempt to appease the companies it is now directly competing with, Anthropic also released a new capability this week called Interactive connectors that lets product teams ship the full version of their UI inside Claude. Companies like Adobe, Atlassian, Notion and Box have shipped initial versions of this.

See examples of products using Interactive Connectors in action here:

  • WordPress demo

  • Box CEO Aaron Levie’s demo

  • Carta’s demo

  • Adobe’s live editor for Acrobat and Express

  • Notion, Confluence, HubSpot and more in Anthropic’s round-up

But what are the strategic consequences for mode suppliers building products that compete directly with its own customers?

If companies like Anthropic continue to launch new products into more verticals that compete with their customers, could this accelerate those companies’ shift to alternatives by choosing open source models or outright refusing to connect to Claude via MCP?

This is a tricky one to navigate for product teams, but I suspect that in the short term at least, teams will keep integrating with Claude and other AI tools in the hope that it all works out in the end. Users are increasingly demanding headless solutions and so it feels like product teams don’t really have much of an alternative than to build them.

Other new features worth knowing about

OpenAI has launched ChatGPT Wallet, so agents can pay on your behalf without seeing your card. It was built with Amex, Mastercard and Visa and lets users authenticate payments biometrically. For product teams, it’s another step forward in agentic payments that’s worth keeping an eye on.

Google released Gemini 4 Hydrogen - and nearly matched Claude Fable 5.2 on Zapier’s AutomationBench index at about a fifth of the cost per task. Sundar Pichai says its 2.5x faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash and is now in Google Search for everyone.

Meta has released Muse Ember, a lightweight model that’s priced at just 10 cents per million input tokens. Meta says it’s built for tool calls, coding subtasks, routing and document parsing, so could be worth a look if you’re looking for cheaper alternatives.

Glean now works in Excel which lets you build formulas, calculations and charts using natural language based on your company’s context.

Figma’s Specs, where teams write the brief and context behind a design, now also work in Figma’s iOS app, with viewing, editing and collaboration.

If your product’s not headless “you’re going to miss this wave” - perspectives from top product leaders

Dharmesh Sha, co-founder and CTO at HubSpot says the company is “refounding” with its co-founder and the plan is the create the “world first Customer Relationship Harness” and headless hubspot. The day before this announcement, he said that “MCP is the new HTTP” and “if you aren’t making your software product composable and callable by AI harnesses, you’re going to miss this wave”.

Sam Stephenson, Co-founder, Granola says Granola now has a dedicated team for “headless Granola”. As part of this, the company has officially launched MCP 2.0 with search that uses 85% fewer tokens and tools that let agents add agendas an organise notes.

Barry McCardel, CEO of Hex, argues that frontier companies are hypocritical in their approach to headless product strategy. He notes that Anthropic doesn’t even make its own products accessible via MCP, summing it up as “MCP for thee, but not for me”.

On speed and quality, Anton Osika, CEO, Lovable says that when he first said “non-engineers will build quality software”, people looked at him when he was crazy. He added that “the best ideas often sound wrong before they become obvious” - like how everyone said the idea of renting out a room in your home on Airbnb was never going to happen.

Linear’s COO Cristina Cordova says while AI is making building easier, this means that “selling may become more valuable, not less. When everyone can make at least a fine / mediocre product quickly, you need to get the right people to care, trust you and choose it over something else.”

📈 Product data

Hex’s average cost per agent conversation fell from a peak of $6.44 in January to just $1.64 this month, even as its monthly token usage kept climbing. Hex says newer, cheaper models along with its own internal harness helped reduce the bill.

New data from OpenAI and Upwork found that out of 63 job categories, 43 that were relatively common in ChatGPT lost share of Upwork job posts, demonstrating the link between ChatGPT use and the types of jobs that are emerging.

A new study from Retool has found that 89% of IT leaders say their company has at least one AI agent in production. In a study of 300 tech leaders, they found that while the vast majority of companies are building internal agents, there is no clear standard on who actually owns them. 42% said they have each team own its own agents with central oversights while 10% have no formal structure at all. Full report here.

Decisions models continue to grow in adoption. The models, which classify, score or pick between different options instead of writing text, grew from zero to 26% share in Vercel’s AI Gateway requests from August to October. The full report from Vercel also found that over half of October’s AI gateway requests went to models that were less than 60 days old, showing that a typical model peaks within a month of its launch.

METR, the AI safety research group, found that Anthropic’s models are improving about twice as fast as before October 2025. Staff at Anthropic self-reported being around 12x as productive with Anthropic’s latest internal models.

Robinhood says 150,000+ people have opened accounts for AI agents to trade for them.

Spotify’s AI DJ is now used by over 94 million Premium listeners. This week, it added new voices and personalities in English and Spanish and an option to switch it off completely.

And finally

We’ll end with something a bit more lighthearted this week. Back in 1994, a then 17 year old Demis Hassabis co-designed a game called Theme Park where you build and run your own amusement park. This week, as the founder of Deepmind, he went full circle and used his own model to build a brand new DeepMind branded ride, right inside that same park.

In his words, he said “it’s kind of mindblowing to see!”, and it’s hard to disagree.

Thanks for reading and have a great week ahead!

Rich

items.title: Ukraine's war robots are starting to down Russia's drones. It could eventually change the fight in the kill zone.
items.summary: Ukraine's war robot makers are increasingly looking at how the unmanned vehicles can stop drones. STR/NurPhoto via Getty Images Ukraine's war robots are starting to down Russian drones to defend themselves. They could eventually provide mobile air defense for soldiers in the kill zone. But the technology is still emerging, and widespread deployment remains a challenge. Ukraine's robots are increasingly able to down aerial drones, a capability that could eventually help soldiers move and fight in some of the war's most dangerous areas. The skies in Ukraine are full of surveillance and strike drones that make movement risky, particularly in the kill zone surrounding the front lines. Ukrainian units are increasingly trying to use robots there instead of humans, and companies are giving robots new abilities to take down drones. Oleksandr Yabchanka, head of robotic systems for Ukraine's Da Vinci Wolves Battalion, a prominent Ukrainian military unit, told Business Insider that Russian drones are one of "the key challenges" on the battlefield, and "I believe that ground-based robotic systems can play a significant role in addressing this issue. " With effective protection against those drones, he said, "the nature of combat operations along the line of contact could change substantially." He called defending the "low sky" by countering enemy drones a promising role for ground robots . Ukraine's skies are so full of drones that gaining a new way to combat them is a big advantage. Florent VERGNES / AFP via Getty Images Beyond leading front-line operators, Yabchanka also co-founded Defence Robotics UA, a non-profit that helps Ukrainian units adopt robotic technologies. "I have particularly high hopes for the use of ground-based robotic systems in defending the low-altitude airspace," he said. The kill zone Inside the kill zone, drones complicate movement, so robots are taking on new roles in logistics, casualty evacuation, and more. Some of these systems are equipped with weaponry and jamming equipment to take down hostile drones. Robots equipped for counter-drone missions could reduce the demand for short-range air defense units, which provide cover for infantry moving in and out, in the kill zone. Right now, these units face great danger and risk getting pinned down inside. These robots could also defend themselves as Russia increasingly targets them. Ukraine's ground robots are taking on more battlefield roles, including in taking down enemy drones. Diego Herrera Carcedo/Anadolu via Getty Images Mykyta Rozhkov, chief business development officer at Ukrainian robotics and technology company Frontline Robotics, told Business Insider that robots are "becoming a main target" for Russia and are defenseless without added protections. Giving robots the ability to defend themselves could make them more survivable, while turning them into mobile air defenses could help protect troops. Rozhkov said makers are now "trying to find a way how we can defend against FPVs." Yabchanka said that when it comes to changing the kill zone, "it would be incorrect to promise that this will happen specifically within the next 12 months." But he said robots have already successfully stopped some drones, and "I believe this field has a great future." Robots vs drones Most of the technology in this space is still being tested or used on a limited scale, primarily to protect the robots themselves rather than provide broader air defense. Rozhkov said that while it's key to have uncrewed ground vehicles be capable of defending themselves, he expects to eventually see UGVs functioning as a mobile, short-range air defense system to try to clear the skies. His company is working with a partner on a system that uses cameras and sensors to find hostile drones and then engages them with a separate capability. He didn't disclose how it would engage enemy drones. Ukrainian soldiers' movement is limited by Russian drones and artillery, and robots helping able to combat those drones could help in the war's most dangerous areas. ARIS MESSINIS/AFP via Getty Images Other Ukrainian robot makers are also adding anti-drone capabilities, some involving smoke, nets, and shrapnel solutions. Robots are increasingly being fitted with weaponry like machine guns, and some companies have said that these weapons can stop enemy drones. Ukrainian company UFORCE, for instance, says it has destroyed enemy drones in ambush scenarios. The company's AI-assisted Predator weapons station can be mounted on robots to track and fire at drones. The 42nd Separate Mechanized Brigade previously described a machine gun mounted on a Liut robot shooting down Russian drones. Rovertech, which advertises itself as making "robots for the kill zone," is developing a system that uses sensors, AI-assisted detection, and a net launcher to stop incoming drones, while Ratel Robotics has started serial production on a protective system that includes net launchers on its robots. Ukraine's 100th Separate Mechanized Brigade said last month that it had deployed an active protection system using net launchers and shared a video showing one of its robots firing a net at an approaching drone, which then crashed to the ground. Some Ukrainian units have also driven robots carrying electronic warfare equipment forward to jam Russia's drones, but it's an emerging capability that has yet to see widespread use. Brave1, Ukraine's state-backed innovation platform, says armed robots are starting to be used against aerial drones, but it wants more, describing anti-aircraft weaponry and protection as priorities. Rozhkov said that soon, Ukraine's robots will have "more and more sophisticated solutions" to stop drones. He said it's essential because the first side that figures out how to stop small FPVs "will gain a huge advantage on the battlefield and can create dramatic results." Read the original article on Business Insider

But he said robots have already successfully stopped some drones, and "I believe this field has a great future."

Robots vs drones

Most of the technology in this space is still being tested or used on a limited scale, primarily to protect the robots themselves rather than provide broader air defense.

Rozhkov said that while it's key to have uncrewed ground vehicles be capable of defending themselves, he expects to eventually see UGVs functioning as a mobile, short-range air defense system to try to clear the skies.

His company is working with a partner on a system that uses cameras and sensors to find hostile drones and then engages them with a separate capability. He didn't disclose how it would engage enemy drones.

Ukrainian soldiers' movement is limited by Russian drones and artillery, and robots helping able to combat those drones could help in the war's most dangerous areas.

ARIS MESSINIS/AFP via Getty Images

Other Ukrainian robot makers are also adding anti-drone capabilities, some involving smoke, nets, and shrapnel solutions. Robots are increasingly being fitted with weaponry like machine guns, and some companies have said that these weapons can stop enemy drones.

Ukrainian company UFORCE, for instance, says it has destroyed enemy drones in ambush scenarios. The company's AI-assisted Predator weapons station can be mounted on robots to track and fire at drones. The 42nd Separate Mechanized Brigade previously described a machine gun mounted on a Liut robot shooting down Russian drones.

Rovertech, which advertises itself as making "robots for the kill zone," is developing a system that uses sensors, AI-assisted detection, and a net launcher to stop incoming drones, while Ratel Robotics has started serial production on a protective system that includes net launchers on its robots.

Ukraine's 100th Separate Mechanized Brigade said last month that it had deployed an active protection system using net launchers and shared a video showing one of its robots firing a net at an approaching drone, which then crashed to the ground.

Some Ukrainian units have also driven robots carrying electronic warfare equipment forward to jam Russia's drones, but it's an emerging capability that has yet to see widespread use.

Brave1, Ukraine's state-backed innovation platform, says armed robots are starting to be used against aerial drones, but it wants more, describing anti-aircraft weaponry and protection as priorities.

Rozhkov said that soon, Ukraine's robots will have "more and more sophisticated solutions" to stop drones.

He said it's essential because the first side that figures out how to stop small FPVs "will gain a huge advantage on the battlefield and can create dramatic results."

items.title: Understanding Positional Embeddings in Modern LLMs
items.summary: This article explains how LLMs encode and process token position information by covering classic and contemporary methods like RoPE. It’s essentially a comprehensive journey where we will work through the mechanisms with visual examples, a little math, and a small PyTorch implementation. And, of course, we will then also look at how modern architectures adapt or omit explicit positional encodings. Below, you can find a preview of which positional embedding choices are used in 2026 open-weight models. We will discuss these choices later after covering the underlying mechanisms. Figure 1: A preview of the gallery’s 2026 architectures, grouped by positional encoding. Architecture figures taken from my LLM gallery . But why spending so much time writing/reading about this rather minor building block? LLMs keep evolving, and as I was preparing a new article on the latest LLM architecture trends this year, I realized that I never covered the positional information methods used in LLMs in any article so far. So, instead of letting the other article get out of hand, I thought it might make sense to publish this as a standalone building block for the upcoming LLM architecture and trends analysis. Also, over the years, many readers have asked me for a tutorial on relative positional embeddings (aka RoPE) to follow up on the learned absolute embeddings used in GPT. It’s been on my TODO list for a long time, so I finally revisited my old draft and put this walkthrough together, which will cover different positional methods in LLMs; (finally) how RoPE works; what methods are used by recent open LLMs. Note that this article assumes some familiarity with basic LLM architectures and works well as a follow-up to Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) . If the concepts and computation of the attention internals, particularly query, key, and value vectors, are a little fuzzy, I recommend checking my self-attention walkthrough as a refresher: The article is also very technical and likely too detailed for some. However, I really wanted to have this foundation out there for future articles to reference. And no worries, the next one will return to a more comfortable style. PS: I started experimenting with Substack’s new “perks” system. As a thank-you to supporters, I’ve added image exports and metadata from the architecture gallery for you to use in your own analyses. PPS: If you are already familiar with how position embeddings work, feel free to fast-forward to Section 6, Positional choices in modern architectures . Note that this article may be best read in a web browser than an email client. I recommend checking out the web view here , which also has a navigation bar on the left side. 1. Where position information enters an LLM Let’s start with the overall architecture. A tokenizer encodes the input text into token IDs. Next, the input token embedding layer of an LLM maps each of these IDs to a vector of numbers. We usually refer to these entries in that vector as “features” (similar to classic ML). The transformer blocks inside the LLM then modify these vectors using attention and feedforward layers. Lastly, the model’s output layer produces logit scores (converted into probabilities) for the next token. The following shows this path in GPT-2 (a relatively classic LLM) and MiniMax-M3 (a more recent LLM released this year; a placeholder for most other recent LLMs). As we can see, the architectures are not too different from each other, but before we get to the positional information parts, let’s focus on the orange blocks for now (the token embedding layers) and the transformer blocks above them; the other architecture differences aren’t needed for this explanation. Figure 2: Token embedding layers in GPT-2 and MiniMax-M3, highlighted in orange. (Side note: M3’s first three out of 60 feedforward layers are dense not MoEs.) A token embedding layer, shown in the figure above, maps each token ID to a vector. Position information is then added afterward. Concretely, and as we will discuss in more detail later, GPT-2 adds a position vector to each token embedding before the modified embedding enters the first transformer block. On the other hand, MiniMax-M3 adds the positional information in each transformer block using a method called RoPE inside attention. We will talk about these methods in more detail later, but first, let’s start with the big picture information explaining why explicit positional information is added or needed. 1.1 Why add positional information? Consider the following two input sentences as a simple example: “The red fox jumps over the gray fox.” “The gray fox jumps over the red fox.” Changing the word order changes which fox does the jumping, as illustrated in the following figure. Figure 3: Changing the word order changes which fox jumps. For the examples in this article, we will treat each word as one token for simplicity. (As you know, real tokenizers can split words into smaller subword tokens.) The first sentence then has eight token positions, from 0 through 7. Figure 4: Token IDs and positions in the toy sentence. # Assume the following small vocabulary. # Real vocabularies typically have 50k to 200k entries vocab = { "The": 0, "red": 1, "fox": 2, "jumps": 3, "gray": 4, "over": 5, "the": 6, } (If you are interested in how vocabularies are built, check out my tokenizer materials on GitHub .) Note that “fox”, which appears twice in the input sentence, gets the same token ID 2 in both cases. And since they both have the same token ID, irrespective of the position in the input sentence, they would get the same embedding vector from the embedding layer. Now, let’s consider a regular self-attention mechanism with no positional encoding (and no causal mask), where every input token can attend to every other token in the input. In this scenario, swapping any two words, like “red” and “gray”, would still result in the same embeddings and attention scores between each token pair. GPT-style models do use a causal (autoregressive) mask, which restricts each token to itself and earlier tokens. Interestingly, this causal mask gives the computation some implicit order information. In our example, “jumps” can attend to “red” in the first sentence and “gray” in the second. So, a causal LLM can theoretically already distinguish these sentences even without explicit positional embeddings. (We will return to this idea later when discussing the “NoPE” concept.) Nonetheless, GPT-2 and most newer LLMs include explicit positional information because it gives attention a direct signal about positions. That’s because even though the causal mask determines which tokens are accessible and provides implicit order information, it doesn’t distinguish a separation of one position from a separation of ten, for example. So, explicit positional methods are still useful (or even essential), since they supply that information. If this all sounded confusing, don’t worry, it was more meant as an overview, and we will step through these concepts a bit more slowly in the remaining article. 2. Adding a position vector to each token embedding We briefly talked about implicit positional information through causal attention masks (and we will revisit this again in more detail later). However, we now switch gears and talk about the explicit ways to add positional information. The perhaps simplest and most direct (but not “cheapest”) approach is to give each sequence position its own vector. We add that vector to the token embedding, so the resulting, modified embedding vector is then passed to the first transformer block. This exact procedure is discussed in the following subsections. 2.1 Learned absolute position embeddings in GPT-2 To illustrate the use of an explicit, learned positional vector to the input embeddings, let’s consider GPT-2 as a concrete example. GPT-2 learns a table of position vectors during training. The following figure illustrates where these vectors are used in the architecture, that is, immediately after the token embedding lookup and before the first transformer block. Figure 5: GPT-2 adds absolute position information before the transformer blocks, as highlighted in purple. The dimensions shown are for GPT-2 XL . The positional embedding layer depicted in the figure above follows the same implementation as the token embedding layer, i.e., they have exactly the same output dimensions so that the resulting input vectors can be added to each other. The code below shows that with an excerpt of a GPT-2 code implementation: class GPTModel(nn.Module): def __init__(self, cfg): super().__init__() self.tok_emb = nn.Embedding(cfg["vocab_size"], cfg["emb_dim"]) self.pos_emb = nn.Embedding(cfg["context_length"], cfg["emb_dim"]) self.drop_emb = nn.Dropout(cfg["drop_rate"]) self.trf_blocks = nn.Sequential( *[TransformerBlock(cfg) for _ in range(cfg["n_layers"])]) self.final_norm = LayerNorm(cfg["emb_dim"]) self.out_head = nn.Linear( cfg["emb_dim"], cfg["vocab_size"], bias=False ) def forward(self, in_idx): batch_size, seq_len = in_idx.shape tok_embeds = self.tok_emb(in_idx) pos_embeds = self.pos_emb(torch.arange(seq_len, device=in_idx.device)) x = tok_embeds + pos_embeds # Shape [batch_size, num_tokens, emb_size] x = self.drop_emb(x) x = self.trf_blocks(x) x = self.final_norm(x) logits = self.out_head(x) return logits And in mathematical terms, we can write it as follows. Let m be a position index and x m the token ID at that position. The input to the first block is Here, E token is the embedding layer, P m is the position info vector selected by m , and h m is the resulting summed embedding and position vector. The two vectors have the same width, so we add their entries element-wise. Figure 6 below shows this visually with a small numerical example. Figure 6: Token and position embeddings are added element-wise. (I am following the convention here that neural network diagrams are usually read from bottom to top.) In the figure above, at position 0, adding the token embedding [1, 1, 1] to the position embedding [1.1, 1.2, 1.3] gives [2.1, 2.2, 2.3] . By the way, the values in the figure are chosen to keep the illustration simple; in a real example, both embedding layers (tables) are initialized with small random values and learned during training. So, what we covered in this section is a so-called absolute positional method because the positional embedding P m depends on the token’s own position m . In the previous example sentence, the two “fox” tokens have initially the same token embeddings, but because we are adding different positional vectors P 2 and P 7 , they have different values before they enter the first transformer block. And consequently, the query, key, and value vectors inside the attention mechanisms then also receive representations that already include position information. Note that the original GPT-2 implementation has 1,024 learned position vectors. This means it only works with inputs with 1024 or fewer tokens. If we want to extend the context window, we would have to extend this embedding table. And since the embedding table (layer) is updated like any other layer during training, the context length would have to be decided before the training starts. Extending the context would be very expensive since the table can become very large. For example, in the case of GPT-2 Medium, the positional embedding layer weights only make up 0.30% of the total weights at 1,024 positions. However, if we increased the context length to a nowadays common 100k range, they would make up >22% of the total model weights, which would be very uneconomic. 2.2 Fixed sinusoidal position encodings in the original transformer The original “Attention Is All You Need” transformer from 2017, which predates GPT, uses the same addition mechanism, but computes its position vectors with fixed sine and cosine functions. Figure 7 below shows this addition before both the encoder and decoder stacks. The encoder processes the input sequence, and the decoder generates the output sequence. (The reason why it’s introduced here is that the sine and cosine functions will become relevant again later when discussing RoPE.) Figure 7: Sinusoidal position encodings added to the token embeddings as highlighted in purple. The original transformer also scales its token embeddings by √( d model ) before adding the position vectors, where d model is the embedding width. So, while GPT-2 in the previous section had the formula the formula used in the original transformer (depicted in Figure 7) is: This scaling by √( d model ) is a minor technical detail, but for those who are curious, the motivation behind this scaling factor is not explained in the transformer paper, but as I discussed with colleagues on a Twitter thread many years ago, it’s likely to put the token embeddings and sinusoidal positional encodings on comparable numerical scales at initialization, so the position vectors don’t dominate the sum when we add them. In the GPT-2 case, this scaling wasn’t necessary because the original GPT-2 code initialized the token embeddings to have an initial standard deviation of 0.02 and the position embeddings to have an initial standard deviation of 0.01 so that they were already roughly on the same scale. Now, the more interesting point is how the position embeddings P m are computed. Concretely, each position vector has the following entries: As before, m denotes the position. The index i indexes a pair of features within the vector. Here, a feature is one number in the position vector. For example, let’s assume we have a small vector with 8 values ( d model = 8) that has entries numbered 0 through 7. (In the original paper this was 512 for the small model and 1024 for the bigger model, instead of 8, but that would be hard to visualize.) We group these into four pairs so that i goes from 0 through 3. Figure 8: Sine and cosine entries for each feature pair. Here, the indices 2 i and 2 i + 1 select the two entries corresponding to pair i . As shown in the equation earlier, the angle at position m , which is then fed into the sine or cosine functions to obtain P m , 2 i or P m , 2 i + 1 , respectively, is computed as follows: Figure 9: The angle inside sine and cosine is the token position multiplied by the pair’s angular frequency. Figure 10 shows this calculation for all four pairs of our 8-feature example at position m = 2. Figure 10: The four sine and cosine pairs at position 2. For an eight-feature embedding, the four frequencies are 1, 0.1, 0.01, and 0.001 radians per position. At position 2, the first pair in row 1 is (sin 2, cos 2) ≈ (0.909, −0.416). The second pair, in row 2, changes more slowly, giving (sin 0.2, cos 0.2) ≈ (0.199, 0.980). The figure below visualizes the sine and cosine calculations for different pairs, which are then collected in a position vector. Figure 11: Sampling sine and cosine functions to form a position vector. In short, this method is a (more complicated) alternative to obtaining positional embedding vectors compared to the GPT-2 method discussed earlier. Similar to the GPT-2 embeddings, these are also absolute embeddings because each vector is computed from its own position. However, in contrast to the GPT-2 approach, the sine and cosine functions stay fixed during training. (Also, they can be extended and evaluated beyond the training positions, like beyond the context length of 1024, although that alone doesn’t guarantee that the model will perform well there, because it hasn’t seen those during training.) To summarize, Figure 12 below compares the two ways of obtaining a position vector we discussed so far. Figure 12: Fixed sinusoidal and learned absolute positional embeddings. This sinusoidal method may look like an overly complicated way to obtain positional embeddings, however, understanding it will be useful when talking about RoPE in the next section. Also, there is some rationale behind it. The authors chose sine and cosine because they make the shifting by a certain offset gives a certain deterministic difference. For example, the difference between position 2 to 5 and the difference between 102 to 105 is both 3, which then results in the same rotation. According to the Attention Is All You Need paper: “...easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset k , PE pos + k can be represented as a linear function of PE pos .” Or in less technical terms, the authors hypothesized that this property would make it easier for attention to learn relationships such as “three tokens earlier.” Figure 13 below illustrates this for one sine/cosine pair. A rotation is a linear transformation, and both three-position shifts use the same rotation. Figure 13: For a pair with angular frequency 0.1 radians per position, a shift of three positions always rotates the pair by 0.3 radians. 3. Encoding relative position with RoPE So, the sinusoidal method above is still considered an absolute positional encoding because the vector added to each token embedding represents that token’s position counted from the start of the sequence. As shown in the previous figure, for example, tokens at positions 2 and 5 receive the position vectors P 2 and P 5 . If we move those tokens to positions 102 and 105, they’re still three positions apart. But each token gets a different position vector because its absolute position m has changed. So their attention score can change even when the token embeddings stay the same. The sinusoidal structure still gives the model a way to learn relative relationships. Anyways, RoPE, which we will discuss below, builds this relative relationship directly into the attention calculation. RoPE, which Su et al. introduced in the 2021 RoFormer paper , stands for Rotary Position Embedding and is considered a relative position method. 3.1 Moving the rotation inside attention in RoPE In attention, each token’s current representation is projected into a query, a key, and a value vector. Query-key dot products determine attention scores. After masking and softmax, the resulting weights determine how the value vectors are mixed. For a refresher, see my Understanding and Coding Self-Attention, Multi-Head Attention, Causal-Attention, and Cross-Attention in LLMs article: RoPE uses the token’s position to rotate its query and key vectors before their dot product. The value vectors bypass this rotation. Figure 14 below shows an overview of where RoPE is applied in a relatively recent MiniMax-M3, where QK-Norm normalizes queries and keys before RoPE. Figure 14: MiniMax-M3 applies RoPE to queries and keys inside attention. As shown in the figure above, the LLM architecture has no explicit position vector added alongside the initial token embedding. Its explicit position signal is injected inside attention instead. Side note: MiniMax-M3 rotates only part of each query and key head, a variation known as “partial RoPE” that we will cover later in Section 6.1. But to understand the basic RoPE operation first, let’s walk through the method step by step using a small example. 3.2 From token representations to feature pairs in RoPE Attention usually divides its query, key, and value features into multiple heads, which are processed in parallel. Hence, the full mechanism is usually called Multi-head Attention (note that Grouped Query Attention also uses multiple heads). Here, each attention head computes its own attention scores and weighted sums. RoPE then acts on pairs of numbers within each query and key head. To make this concrete, Figure 12 below follows a token representation through the learned query and key projections, which are computed via the weight matrices W Q and W K . In this toy example, each projection produces 16 features, which are reshaped into two heads with eight features each. In the figure below, every small cell contains one scalar feature, meaning one numerical entry in a vector (the numbers are not shown due to space reasons). Figure 15: Projecting a hidden state, reshaping into heads, and pairing features for RoPE. For the first eight-feature head, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8] , we pair each feature in the first half with the corresponding feature in the second half. This gives (1, 5) , (2, 6) , (3, 7) , and (4, 8) . This split-half convention is used in LLM implementations, including my Qwen3 implementation . (We will compare it with the original, alternative adjacent-feature pairing method later after implementing the basic operation.) Each pair gets a rotation angle determined by the token position m and that pair’s frequency θ i . The corresponding query and key pairs use the same frequency. Figure 16 below shows how we rotate the pairs, put the updated features back in their original locations, and compute the query-key dot product. Figure 16: Pairwise rotations produce the rotated query and key vectors used to compute attention scores. The next section will walk through the figure(s) a bit more slowly. 3.3 Rotating one pair in RoPE For the following example, we’ll use the same two positions as before. The query comes from “the” at position m = 5, and the key comes from the first “fox” at position n = 2. Since, in this example, the key comes before the query, the causal mask allows the query to attend to it. To illustrate the effect that the position has, and keeping everything fixed, let’s assume we start both pairs from the same two values, (1, 5). Figure 17: The first feature pair, (1, 5), takes one entry from each half of the query head. Furthermore, for this example, let’s use θ = 20° per token position ( π /9 radians per position). At position 2, we rotate the key’s arrow counterclockwise by 2 × 20° = 40°. At position 5, we rotate the query’s arrow by 5 × 20° = 100°. Figure 18: Starting from (1, 5), RoPE rotates the key pair at position 2 by 40° and the query pair at position 5 by 100°. To illustrate what’s happening in the figure above, for example, plugging cos 40° ≈ 0.766 and sin 40° ≈ 0.643 into the rotation from Figure 16 gives the new key coordinates: Then, changing 40° to 100°, using the same equation as above, the rotated query pair becomes q′ ≈ (−5.098, 0.117). But the important point is that both arrows still have length √26. Only the rotation changes but the vectors keep the same lengths after the transformation. So, for a query pair ( a , b ) at position m , the two operations here are. For the key pair at position n , we use the same equations with nθ . (Section 4 later shows how RoPE calculates the angular frequency for each feature pair.) To close this section, for those more comfortable reading code, everything about RoPE illustrated so far can be written in code, as follows: import torch query_head = torch.tensor([1., 2., 3., 4., 5., 6., 7., 8.]) key_head = query_head.clone() # Split-half pairing gives (1, 5), (2, 6), (3, 7), and (4, 8). query_pairs = torch.stack(query_head.chunk(2), dim=-1) key_pairs = torch.stack(key_head.chunk(2), dim=-1) # Take the first feature pair from each head. q = query_pairs[0] k = key_pairs[0] m = 5 # Query position (in our example, "the") n = 2 # Key position (in our example, the first "fox") theta = torch.deg2rad(torch.tensor(20.0)) # Radians per token position def rotate_pair(pair, angle): a, b = pair c, s = torch.cos(angle), torch.sin(angle) return torch.stack((a * c - b * s, a * s + b * c)) k_rot = rotate_pair(k, n * theta) # 2 × 20° = 40° q_rot = rotate_pair(q, m * theta) # 5 × 20° = 100° print(f"Original key: ({k[0]:g}, {k[1]:g})") print(f"Original query: ({q[0]:g}, {q[1]:g})") print(f"Rotated key: ({k_rot[0]:.3f}, {k_rot[1]:.3f})") print(f"Rotated query: ({q_rot[0]:.3f}, {q_rot[1]:.3f})") The resulting values are: Original key: (1, 5) Original query: (1, 5) Rotated key: (-2.448, 4.473) Rotated query: (-5.098, 0.117) If we rotate all 4 pairs in the 8-feature query (and key) vector(s), we get the vectors below. (We’ll come back to how we go from rotating one pair to rotating all of them later.) Original key: (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8) Original query: (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8) Rotated key: (-2.448, 1.577, 2.951, 3.994, 4.473, 6.125, 7.021, 8.003) Rotated query: (-5.098, 0.928, 2.877, 3.986, 0.117, 6.256, 7.051, 8.007) 3.4 How the relative offset changes the attention score in RoPE Note that, as shown above, the query and key heads have eight features each, which we previously grouped into 4 pairs with two elements each, like (1, 5), and (2, 6), and so on. For simplicity here we’ll follow just the first pair in each head, (1, 5), formed by taking the entries at indices 0 and 4: Original key: (1, 5) Original query: (1, 5) Rotated key: (-2.448, 4.473) Rotated query: (-5.098, 0.117) As shown above, in our example, those entries have values (1, 5) in both heads before the rotation. Also, as in the code above, let’s use the notation q =( q 1 , q 2 ) and k =( k 1 , k 2 ) for these two pairs. To compute their dot product, using the standard dot product formula, we multiply corresponding coordinates and add the products: Before rotation, the pairs have a dot product of 1 × 1 + 5 × 5 = 26. Using the rounded coordinates from the previous Figure 18 gives the contribution from the first pair after rotation: We can see why by writing the dot product in terms of the lengths of the two vectors (arrows in Figure 18) and the angle ϕ between them. In both cases, the vector length is √26. The query (position 5) is rotated by 100° and the key (position 2) is rotated by 40°. The vectors (arrows) start from the same direction, so they end up being 60° apart after rotation. Their exact dot product is 26 × cos(60°) = 13. Now let’s see what happens if we move just the key from position 2 to position 3, but we keep its starting coordinates (1, 5) fixed. The key’s rotation changes now from 2 × 20° = 40° to 3 × 20° = 60°. The query still rotates by 100°, so the angle between the arrows shrinks to 40° and the dot product changes from 13 to 26 × cos(40°) ≈ 19.92. So, moving the key one position closer changed the dot product even though we started with the same feature values. Why do these dot products matter? In attention, we sum the contributions from all feature pairs to get the query-key dot products. RoPE can change those dot products and thus the weights that softmax assigns to the value vectors. In the attention equation above, Q′ and K′ are matrices that contain the rotated queries q′ and keys k′ for one head, V contains the values, and d is the head dimension. 3.5 Why shifting both positions preserves the attention score in RoPE Now that we illustrated the computation of the dot products, which is at the core of the attention mechanism, let’s return to positions m = 5 and n = 2. If we shift both positions to the right by three positions, we get m = 8 and n = 5. Each rotation gains 60° (the query goes from 100° to 160°, and the key goes from 40° to 100°), however, the angle between the vectors stays the same. The dot product for this feature pair is still 13. Figure 19: The first pair’s dot product at three different position settings. The key is that the difference between the rotation angles is If we keep the original query and key vectors fixed and shift both token positions by the same amount, RoPE adds the same rotation to both vectors. The angle between them stays the same, so their dot product stays the same. Note that Figure 20 below uses smaller angles than the actual example (20° per position) to keep the picture readable. Figure 20: A shared position shift preserves the relative angle and dot product for fixed query and key features. The examples above and Figure 20 illustrate the main idea behind RoPE. We use each token’s position to rotate the corresponding query and key in the attention module. In the query-key dot product, what matters is how much one vector rotates relative to the other. For each feature pair, this difference in rotation depends only on the offset between the two tokens. To illustrate this in the big picture context, in Figure 21, each row collects the scores for one query. If we consider row 5, the query for “the”, and column 2, the key for “fox”, the attention score between those two is computed as the dot product between the two rotated versions of the query and key vector. Figure 21: The attention scores for one head before softmax. Gray cells mark future keys excluded by the causal mask. What’s the point, again? Let’s once more consider “The red fox jumps over the gray fox.” If we add 100 tokens (e.g., think system prompt) before the sentence, the first “fox” and the second “the” move from positions 2 and 5 to 102 and 105. However, a prefix of any length shifts both positions equally, so they still stay exactly three positions apart. This means, each vector (arrow) gains the exact same additional rotation, which preserves the angle between them and their dot product (assuming we hold the unrotated query and key vectors fixed; in a real model, a new prefix of 100 tokens can change those vectors by changing what the tokens attend to). Figure 22 tracks this comparison in the attention score matrix. The right panel shows the rows and columns for the sentence after we add the prefix. In our toy example, the first pair still contributes 13 to the dot product. Figure 22: The highlighted score moves from row 5, column 2 to row 105, column 102. It keeps the same value if we hold the query and key vectors fixed before rotation. As you may recall, in the original transformer’s sinusoidal encoding, a fixed offset also corresponds to a fixed rotation within each sine/cosine pair. But that shared rotation applies only to the position vectors (added to the input vector) instead of the key and query vectors inside the attention mechanism. Figure 23 compares what this shift changes in the three methods we covered so far. Figure 23: The same position shift under sinusoidal encodings, GPT-2’s learned position embeddings, and RoPE. 3.6 Bonus: Combining the pairs into a complete head in RoPE To see how the relative offset affects the dot product, we focused on one feature pair in the query and key. Now let’s put all four pairs together and see how RoPE rotates the full eight-feature vectors in one attention head. (Please feel free to skip this section if it is too much technical detail.) Figure 24 picks up where Figure 17 left off. We rotate each of the four pairs, then put the results back in the query’s original feature order. Figure 24: RoPE rotates each pair of query features at its own angle. (The same can be applied to the key, which is not shown to keep the illustration simple). Figure 24 above shows the rotated query q′ (at the bottom). Similarly, we could get the rotated key k′ by repeating the same steps at the key’s position. Recall the two equations from Section 3.3. For query pair i with input values ( a i , b i ), let c i = cos( mθ i ) and s i = sin( mθ i ). These are the cosine and sine of the rotation angle for that pair at query position m : Figure 25 below shows the same four rotations between the four pairs as a single matrix multiplication, q′ = R m q . Figure 25: The four rotations from Figure 24 written as one matrix multiplication. The pair labels show where each rotation goes in the full matrix. 4. Computing rotation frequencies in RoPE? A full attention head uses multiple frequencies so that some feature pairs change more drastically (”quickly” in RoPE terms) with position and others change more gradually (”slowly” in RoPE terms).
