📝 Editorial: The Invisible Hand Wore a Leather Jacket

There is an appealing version of the AI boom in which thousands of entrepreneurs independently discover that the future requires NVIDIA chips. There is also a more complicated version in which NVIDIA helps finance the entrepreneurs, guarantees some of their revenue, and organizes the capital required to buy the chips. The invisible hand apparently has excellent investor relations.

NVIDIA announced Jensen Huang’s resignation this week and appointed Colette Kress interim CEO. This essay explores a perspective on the Jensen situation that has received less attention: what happens to an AI market partly designed and financed around one man’s vision when its architect leaves?

My thesis is that Huang helped subsidize competition among clouds and model developers because a fragmented customer base was exceptionally good for NVIDIA.

Consider neoclouds. A world dominated by Amazon, Microsoft and Google would leave NVIDIA negotiating with enormous customers capable of designing competing chips. Independent GPU clouds help disperse that power. Huang said in April that CoreWeave would not exist without NVIDIA’s support, and credited similar help for Nebius and Nscale. The commercial logic is attractive: if you dislike your customers’ bargaining power, help finance more customers.

This support became remarkably concrete. In August, NVIDIA described contracts guaranteeing minimum revenue on part of a neocloud’s capacity, helping lenders underwrite new projects. It also said it had invested nearly $50 billion in frontier AI labs. NVIDIA could be the supplier, shareholder and contractual backstop. The ecosystem was beginning to look like a diversified portfolio with an unusually repetitive emergency contact.

Open models fit the same logic. NVIDIA organized the Nemotron Coalition and agreed to acquire Hugging Face. Its SEC filing explicitly links demand for open models to demand for NVIDIA products. American open AI has independent roots and other patrons. But NVIDIA helped strengthen an alternative to closed platforms that suited its economics beautifully. Free software is an especially appealing public good when you sell the expensive computing machinery that runs it.

Infrastructure markets often need someone to coordinate investments that make sense together before they make sense separately. A railway needs towns; towns need a railway. Huang helped finance both sides of that problem. The demand can be real even when the market’s architecture is deliberately engineered.

The distinction matters because a strategic investor can earn several returns from the same check: equity appreciation, hardware sales and a healthier ecosystem. A conventional investor mostly gets the first. A company can therefore be worth financing to NVIDIA even when its standalone investment return looks unexciting. Replace the financier, and the same business, with the same technology and customers, can become harder to fund.

That is also how an implicit “Jensen put” could develop: investors might assume strategically important companies would receive another check because allowing them to fail would damage NVIDIA’s wider franchise. Those arrangements were never a universal rescue guarantee. But believing someone has reasons to rescue you can influence financing long before anyone writes down an obligation. Finance has built entire neighborhoods on less.

This week supplied a reminder of the distinction between ambition and committed money. NVIDIA’s preliminary August agreements targeted more than $500 billion in third-party financing. Bloomberg reported that no deals had emerged and partners were seeking stronger backstops even before Huang’s departure. That was a market still being constructed, with its principal architect now gone.

Of course, NVIDIA’s balance sheet survives its founder’s exit. Kress helped manage it for years, and the board promised continuity in customer commitments. The company still benefits from a broad ecosystem. Continued support is entirely plausible.

A founder can ask shareholders to trust that an ecosystem will repay its subsidies across many businesses over many years. A successor may face demands to justify each transaction individually. A committee can approve a financing package; inheriting the conviction behind it takes longer.

The vulnerable point is the next decision: another investment, another guarantee, another financing extension. If support becomes more selective, lenders could demand more equity, smaller clouds could slow construction or sell, and independent labs could seek shelter with hyperscalers. AI demand could keep rising throughout this process. The ownership structure would change.

That is the uncomfortable possibility. Huang diversified NVIDIA’s customers while making parts of their independence dependent on NVIDIA. What looked like a competitive landscape also contained a common source of financial confidence.

His departure could therefore produce a wonderfully perverse outcome: more concentration in precisely the platforms his ecosystem helped counterbalance. The market can keep buying more AI while becoming less like the market Jensen wanted.

🔎 AI ResearchLazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents

AI Lab: Microsoft Research

Summary: This post introduces Lazarus, a training-free backdoor that weight-reprograms fewer than 10 dormant neurons in an LLM so an otherwise normal agent executes a malicious command when a hidden trigger appears, while still passing standard evaluations. The post argues that weights should be audited like code and that reliable detection requires diffing against the original, unmodified weights.

e-means: outperforming k-means (in one-tenth the epochs)

AI Lab: FAIR at Meta, École Nationale des Ponts et Chaussées

Summary: This paper introduces e-means, an exponential moving average optimization procedure for k-means with mini-batch updates that fixes decay rate and batch size from scaling laws without a hyperparameter sweep. It beats the loss of Lloyd k-means at 25 epochs in 1.4 to 2.6 epochs, a 10x to 45x GPU wall-clock speedup versus state-of-the-art k-means implementations.

The components of agent memory

AI Lab: Anthropic

Summary: This post describes Anthropic’s approach to agent memory—knowledge Claude retains between sessions as readable context—and the use of dreaming, in which Claude reflects on logs in idle time to organize memory, correct mistakes, and build representations such as wikis. Using dreaming to build a wiki over a Stainless corpus, Opus 5 agents improved from 13% to 48% of graded criteria on 25 questions as sessions scaled from two to 128.

AlphaGenome 2: Deciphering how cells read DNA to better understand disease

AI Lab: Google DeepMind

Summary: This post introduces AlphaGenome 2, a conditional DNA sequence model that predicts how a million-letter DNA sequence and its variants affect a specified human tissue, cell type, or state. It identifies nearly twice as many variants that change gene expression in cells as the previous state-of-the-art model, and on TenK10K it found 30% of causal variants versus 16% for the original AlphaGenome. It is available today for non-commercial research via the AlphaGenome API.

🤖 AI Tech ReleasesGoogle DeepMind Gemini Decisions API

Google DeepMind introduced the Gemini Decisions API, a Gemini API endpoint powered by Gemini Decision 1 that scores up to 1,000 yes/no, multiple-choice, and rubric questions against one multimodal input in a single pass, returning probabilities in 150–250 ms for $0.10 per 1M input tokens.

Anthropic Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2

Anthropic introduced Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, models that generate outputs up to 30% faster than the 5.1 versions at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens and score 49.1% on FrontierCode 2.0 at Xhigh effort, with Fable 5.2 available today on all platforms including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure, and Mythos 5.2 available through Anthropic’s Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs.

Google Cloud TPU Sync

Google Cloud introduced TPU Sync, an open-source library for moving KV caches and model weights across TPU memory tiers that cuts KV transfer latency by over 90% and Time to First Token by an average of 90% for 235B to 480B open-weight MoE models in prefix-caching and disaggregated-serving workloads, available today with Python wheels for PyTorch and JAX and integrations with vLLM-TorchTPU, SGLang-TorchTPU, and llm-d on GKE.

OpenAI ChatGPT Wallet

OpenAI introduced ChatGPT Wallet, a wallet built with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa that lets agents pay without access to users’ actual card details and requires a security check for every purchase, beginning to roll out today in dots for ChatGPT Pro subscribers aged 18 and older in the US with eligible US-issued cards.

📡 10 AI News You Need to Know About

  1. CoreWeave Q3 Results: CoreWeave reported third-quarter 2026 results with revenue of $3.661 billion, up from $1.365 billion a year earlier and by more than $1 billion sequentially, and a net loss of $709 million, or $1.27 per share. Revenue backlog was approximately $132.5 billion as of September 30, 2026, and the company raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $13.0 billion to $13.3 billion, lifted the low end of capital expenditure guidance to a range of $37 billion to $39 billion, and raised annualized run-rate revenue guidance to $20 billion to $21 billion to exit 2026.

  2. Oura Acquires Counsel Health: Oura agreed to acquire AI-native primary care company Counsel Health for $625 million in cash, subject to purchase price adjustments, in a deal expected to close before the end of 2026. Counsel combines medical AI with in-house physicians already available in the Oura app, and after the acquisition it will continue serving existing and new enterprise partners beyond Oura’s member base.

  3. Huang Resigns as NVIDIA CEO: NVIDIA announced that Jensen Huang has resigned as president, CEO, and a board member, with CFO Colette Kress named interim CEO, days after Huang apologized for being unfaithful to his wife and the board opened an independent investigation into news reports that he had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The board said it has no reason to believe that national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.

  4. Nebius Q3 Results: Nebius reported third-quarter 2026 results with revenue of $980.8 million, up 571% from $146.1 million a year earlier, adjusted EBITDA of $465.8 million, and a net loss from continuing operations of $37.5 million, narrowed from a $119.6 million loss a year earlier. Purchases of property and equipment and intangible assets were $7.3 billion in the quarter, up from $955.5 million a year earlier.

  5. OpenAI Quarterly Revenue Hits $10B: OpenAI’s third-quarter revenue rose nearly 50% from the prior quarter to $10 billion, with an annual run rate of roughly $50 billion, CFO Sarah Friar told Yahoo Finance. Friar said the company’s enterprise business doubled quarter over quarter and now accounts for half of revenue, while consumer sales grew 20% and subscriptions topped 100 million users.

  6. OpenAI Acquires Odessia: OpenAI acquired AI travel agent Odessia, and founder Francis Davidson said he is joining the company to focus on the future of travel. Davidson, who previously founded Sonder, said the less-than-a-year-old startup planned over $60 million a year of travel over the past summer; terms were not disclosed, and Odessia’s site says the service is no longer available.

Torus Raises $500M for Foundry: Salt Lake City-based Torus announced $500 million in growth capital led by Magnetar, with participation from ICONIQ, Origin Ventures, Ridgeline Partners, and Trinity Capital, to scale Foundry, a prefabricated modular system that packages power, storage, cooling, networking, and compute for AI inference. Foundry delivers 1 to 20 megawatts of capacity per site in 12 to 16 weeks using power the grid already has, and Torus said first customers include Hydra Host, with thousands of GPUs already deployed and plans for more than 47,000 by the end of 2027.

  8. Mirendil Raises $1B Series A: Mirendil raised $1 billion in a Series A led by Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital, with participation from Battery Ventures, Doerr Capital, Gil & Co, Google, M13, Pear VC, and S32, five months after a $200 million seed round. The company said one researcher working with agents pretrained its competitive coding model, Mirendil-Base, from scratch in 3.5 months with less than $10 million in compute, and its Lor platform, now in private beta, runs hundreds of agents writing code and running experiments for days at a time.

  9. Mercor Raises $750M at $20B: Mercor announced a $750 million Series D at a $20 billion valuation, double the $10 billion valuation it reached in October 2025, in a round that included an employee tender and investors such as Benchmark, Felicis, General Catalyst, NVIDIA, Salesforce, and Zoom. The company said the funding will accelerate its investment in evals, post-training infrastructure, and environments where agents can learn complex professional workflows, as it expands beyond frontier labs to enterprises.

  10. LangChain Raises $300M Series C: LangChain raised $300 million at a $3 billion valuation in a round led by existing investor CapitalG, with participation from GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures, bringing total funding to $460 million. More than 7,000 organizations, including NVIDIA, Toyota, and Salesforce, use its LangSmith platform to run, improve, and govern agents, and the company plans to share new LangSmith capabilities at a release event on November 20.

Part I | Part II | Part III | Part IV | Part V | Part VI | Part VII | Part VIII | Part IX | Part X | Part XI | Part XII | Part XIII | Part XIV | Part XV | Part XVI | Part XVII | Part XVIII | Part XIX | Part XX | Part XXI | Part XXII The Night the “Optimization” Doubled Our Runtime At 1:42 AM on a Tuesday, the revenue-aggregation pipeline breached its SLA for the first time in eleven months. The diff was almost comically simple: .cache() after every major transformation — nine cached DataFrames, one per stage, on the theory that nothing should ever be computed twice. A big shuffle in a later stage can — and will — evict your carefully cached DataFrame block by block, LRU-first, with no warning and no ceremony. MEMORY_ONLY, the default behind .cache(), stores deserialized Java objects — each row as a graph of objects on the heap. A 4-byte integer becomes a 16-byte Integer plus object header; a modest row can inflate 2–5x versus its serialized size. You are not caching 3 GB of data. You are caching 3 GB of data wearing a 12 GB object costume, and the garbage collector has to walk that costume on every major GC. items.summary_html:
The fastest way to make a Spark job slower is to cache everything “just in case.” Here is the engine-level accounting of what `.cache()` actually costs — and the persist discipline that gets the speed back.

Part I | Part II | Part III | Part IV | Part V | Part VI | Part VII | Part VIII | Part IX | Part X | Part XI | Part XII | Part XIII | Part XIV | Part XV | Part XVI | Part XVII | Part XVIII | Part XIX | Part XX| Part XXI| Part XXII

The Night the “Optimization” Doubled Our Runtime

At 1:42 AM on a Tuesday, the revenue-aggregation pipeline breached its SLA for the first time in eleven months. The job was unglamorous but load-bearing: 3.4 TB of raw order events on S3, a nightly rollup feeding every finance dashboard in the company, running on 24 r5.2xlarge nodes with a steady-state runtime of 41 minutes at roughly $63 per run. It had been boring in the best possible way.

The week before, a well-meaning engineer had “optimized” it. The diff was almost comically simple: .cache() after every major transformation — nine cached DataFrames, one per stage, on the theory that nothing should ever be computed twice. Code review waved it through. Caching is free performance, right?

The first run after the change took 2 hours and 17 minutes. Two stages failed outright when YARN killed executors for exceeding their memory limits. The Spark UI told the real story: average GC pause per task had gone from 0.3 seconds to 11 seconds, the BlockManager had evicted 78% of cached blocks before any downstream stage read them, and the driver was spending more time serializing cache bookkeeping than scheduling work. We had spent the entire executor memory budget caching data nobody would ever read twice, and the garbage collector was charging us interest by the minute. Cost per run: $212. SLA: breached. Pager: mine.

The rollback took four minutes. The lesson took longer to sink in: .cache() is not a performance hint. It is a memory allocation with a garbage-collection bill attached, and the engine will happily let you bankrupt yourself.

So: what does a cached DataFrame actually cost, where does it live, and when is persisting data the right call versus pure overhead?

The Mechanic Underneath: The BlockManager Rents You Memory by the Byte

Every cached partition lives in the BlockManager, Spark’s per-executor storage service — the same service that holds shuffle blocks and broadcast variables. On the JVM heap, memory is split by the UnifiedMemoryManager: after a 300 MB reserved region, spark.memory.fraction (default 0.6) of the heap becomes one unified region shared by execution (shuffles, joins, sorts) and storage (cache). Inside that region, spark.memory.storageFraction (default 0.5) draws a soft line — storage is guaranteed half the unified region, and it may borrow the rest, but execution memory can evict cached blocks whenever it needs the space.

That last clause is the whole game. Your cache is not a reservation; it is a tenant with no lease. A big shuffle in a later stage can — and will — evict your carefully cached DataFrame block by block, LRU-first, with no warning and no ceremony. (Part V of this series covered this memory split in depth; here is where it bites.)

And what you store matters more than where. MEMORY_ONLY, the default behind .cache(), stores deserialized Java objects — each row as a graph of objects on the heap. A 4-byte integer becomes a 16-byte Integer plus object header; a modest row can inflate 2–5x versus its serialized size. You are not caching 3 GB of data. You are caching 3 GB of data wearing a 12 GB object costume, and the garbage collector has to walk that costume on every major GC.

MEMORY_ONLY Is a Bet You Usually Lose

The default storage level is the worst one for most production workloads, which is a remarkable design choice until you remember it was optimized for demos. Deserialized objects give you the fastest possible read — no deserialization cost on access — at the price of maximum footprint and maximum GC pressure. On heaps above ~32 GB the GC pauses on a fully cached, object-heavy RDD can exceed the time you saved by not recomputing.

The rule is blunt: use MEMORY_ONLY only when the cached dataset is small, reused many times, and the cluster has memory to waste. That combination is rarer than the tutorials suggest. In our incident, nine DataFrames cached with MEMORY_ONLY consumed a combined 41 GB of heap across the cluster to hold roughly 14 GB of actual data — and the GC was spending 11 seconds per task just traversing it.

Serialization Trades CPU for Survival: Why _SER Exists

Appending _SER to a storage level stores serialized bytes instead of objects — one compact byte array per partition instead of a thicket of objects. The trade is explicit: you pay deserialization CPU every time you read the cache, and you gain 2–5x smaller footprints plus dramatically lighter GC, because the collector sees a handful of byte arrays instead of millions of objects.

Two details most teams miss. First, the serializer matters: the default Java serializer is slow and bloated; Kryo (spark.serializer=org.apache.spark.serializer.KryoSerializer) typically cuts serialized size by another 2–10x and is the difference between _SER being a win and a wash. Second, serialized caching composes well with whole-stage codegen (Part XVI's topic): generated code operating on Tungsten binary rows deserializes less and copies less, so the CPU tax of _SER shrinks exactly where the engine is fastest.

Eviction Is Not Failure, It’s Policy: LRU and the Unpersist You Forgot

When execution memory needs space, the BlockManager evicts cached blocks least-recently-used first. This is not an error — it is the documented policy — but it turns sloppy caching into a special kind of waste: you pay the full cost of writing blocks to memory (and to disk, for _AND_DISK levels), and then the engine throws them away before the second read you cached them for.

The discipline has two halves. Cache lazily and deliberately: call .persist() with an explicit level, then force materialization with an action on your terms — a .count() right after persisting — so the cache is populated once, up front, instead of trickling in mid-stage while downstream tasks are already waiting. Unpersist aggressively: the moment the last consumer finishes, release the blocks. A cached DataFrame that outlives its last reader is not a cache; it is a memory leak with a Spark UI entry.

If You Read It Once, Caching Is Pure Overhead

Here is the decision rule, and it fits in one sentence: persist a dataset only if it is read more than once AND expensive to recompute. Both conditions. A DataFrame consumed by a single downstream stage gains nothing from caching — you pay serialization, memory, and GC, and you read it exactly as many times as you would have without the cache. A cheap-to-recompute frame (a filter over an already-cached parent) gains nothing either; recomputation is faster than the cache bookkeeping.

In the incident diff, five of the nine cached DataFrames had exactly one consumer. They were pure overhead — memory spent to avoid recomputation that was never going to happen.

Off-Heap Changes the Game but Not the Rules

spark.memory.offHeap.enabled moves storage outside the JVM heap into Tungsten's binary format, which largely sidesteps GC — the collector never sees off-heap bytes. It is the right answer when GC pauses dominate, but it does not change the accounting: off-heap memory is still finite, still shared with execution, and still evictable. It converts a GC problem into a capacity problem. The decision rule above still applies; off-heap just makes the "expensive to recompute" side of the ledger cheaper to satisfy.

Executor Memory, AnnotatedThe Fix, and What It Cost
# Naive: cache everything "just in case" — 9 DataFrames, MEMORY_ONLY default.
# raw = spark.read.parquet("s3://lake/orders/").cache()
# cleaned = raw.filter(...).cache()
# enriched = cleaned.join(...).cache()
# ... six more ...
# Result: 41 min -> 2h17m, 11s GC pauses, 78% of blocks evicted unread.
# Optimized: persist ONE frame — read twice, expensive to build — serialized,
# materialized up front, released the moment its last consumer finishes.
from pyspark import StorageLevel
base = (
    spark.read.parquet("s3://lake/orders/")
    .filter("order_date >= current_date() - interval 90 days")
    .repartition(512, "order_date")  # stable layout: cache once, reuse the partitioning
)
# MEMORY_AND_DISK_SER: serialized bytes survive memory pressure by spilling;
# Kryo keeps the byte footprint small (set spark.serializer accordingly).
base.persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK_SER)
base.count()  # materialize NOW, on your terms — not trickling in mid-stage
agg_a = base.groupBy("region").agg(...)     # consumer 1
agg_b = base.join(dims, "sku").groupBy(...) # consumer 2
agg_a.write.mode("overwrite").parquet("s3://lake/revenue_by_region/")
agg_b.write.mode("overwrite").parquet("s3://lake/revenue_by_sku/")
base.unpersist()  # last consumer done: give the memory back immediately

The numbers after the fix, same cluster, same data: wall-clock 2h17m → 38 minutes (three minutes faster than the pre-cache baseline, because the stable repartitioning also fixed a skew-adjacent shuffle). Cached footprint: 14 GB of objects → 3.1 GB of serialized bytes. Average GC pause: 11s → 0.4s. Evicted-before-read blocks: 78% → 0%. Executor losses: two per run → zero. Cost per run: $212 → $58 — and the 3 AM pager went back to sleep.

The Catch: Persist Is Not Durability, and DISK_ONLY Is a Trap

Three honest counterweights. First, persist is not durability: cached blocks die with the application. If you need data to survive a driver restart, that is checkpoint() (Part XVII's territory), which writes to reliable storage at the cost of breaking lineage. Persist is a within-application optimization, nothing more.

Second, DISK_ONLY looks like a safety net and behaves like a tar pit: every read pays full disk I/O plus deserialization, and on cloud object stores the "disk" is often network-attached anyway. It is occasionally right for enormous, rarely-read frames — but measure it, because recomputation is frequently faster.

Third, caching interacts with skew (Part VII’s playbook): persisting a skewed frame bakes the skew into every downstream consumer. Fix the partitioning first — as the repartition(512, "order_date") above does — then cache the balanced result. A cache of a bad layout is just a fast way to repeat a bad layout.

Takeaways
  • .cache() is MEMORY_ONLY: deserialized Java objects, 2–5x inflation, maximum GC pressure. It is the default, not the recommendation.
  • The decision rule is two conditions: persist only if the dataset is read more than once AND expensive to recompute. One consumer means pure overhead.
  • Serialize to survive: _SER levels trade a little CPU for 2–5x smaller footprints and GC the collector can actually traverse — pair with Kryo.
  • Your cache has no lease: execution memory evicts storage LRU-first. Cache lazily, materialize with an action on your terms, and unpersist() the moment the last consumer finishes.
  • Off-heap moves the problem: it kills GC pauses but not capacity limits or eviction. The accounting still applies.
  • Fix the layout before you cache it: persisting a skewed or badly partitioned frame just makes every downstream stage repeat the mistake faster.

Cache is a loan from the executor, and the garbage collector collects the interest.

If this saved you a 3 AM pager incident, follow me on Medium for Twice a week for the next 3 Months of Advanced Data Engineering & AI. Let’s connect on LinkedIn and X.

items.title: Is Nvidia cooked without Jensen Huang?
items.summary: Mads Claus Rasmussen / Ritzau Scanpix / AFP via Getty Images This post originally appeared in the BI Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . A post-Huang era We're about to learn just how much one person truly matters to the AI economy. Jensen Huang was larger than life at Nvidia. He was the AI boom's most recognizable evangelist, the chip maker's chief visionary and dealmaker, and the force behind Nvidia's ascent to the most valuable company on the planet. As Zak Jason writes, the cult of the tech founder has very much become America's religion . And Huang was "its most convincing saint." A week ago, Huang admitted to an affair and apologized to his family. Nvidia disclosed it was investigating whether he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. And then The New York Times reported a second affair, this one with an Nvidia executive who was one of Huang's direct reports. He resigned on Thursday. Huang's abrupt downfall is a stress test of founder worship. The market put a price on it: Nvidia's market cap tumbled $573 billion last week, more than all but 18 companies in the entire S&P 500. "It's like the Bulls without Jordan," author Stephen Witt, who wrote a biography on Huang, said on CNBC. "I don't know how they are going to replace this guy." That is the essence of key-man risk , as my colleagues Sarah E. Needleman and Tim Paradis reported. When one leader is so closely identified with the strategy, the products, and the culture, their departure can create a vacuum that no org chart (let alone one with 60 direct reports to the CEO) can immediately fill. Much of Silicon Valley came to Huang's defense in recent days. Sarah Guo, a venture capitalist, called him "one of the most extraordinary entrepreneurs of all time." Sequoia's Shaun Maguire said Huang's "contributions to American innovation and AI leadership cannot be overstated." A petition to reinstate Huang as Nvidia CEO circulated over the weekend, collecting more than 100,000 signatures, including those of Elon Musk and other prominent figures. Our own Alistair Barr also points to new reports that are casting doubt on the intelligence behind Jensen Huang's downfall. For sure, there are several examples of seemingly irreplaceable CEOs — Steve Jobs at Apple and Travis Kalanick at Uber — whose companies still thrived under new leadership. And even some of Huang's biggest proponents aren't standing by him. "No one was a bigger defender of Jensen than I was but there are rules about sex with subordinates," CNBC's Jim Cramer said on X . "Just because someone is brilliant doesn't mean he can do what he wants." The question is whether Nvidia, which lacked a defined succession plan, can prove to be more durable than its founder's legend . If it can't? Dick Costolo, the former Twitter CEO, floated an idea . "Prediction: 3-4 years from now, [Nvidia] will miss a quarter or two, and they will bring Jensen back to run the company," he said. "Like fame, everybody is outraged for 15 minutes, and there is nothing Americans love more than the comeback story." Read the original article on Business Insider

That is the essence of key-man risk, as my colleagues Sarah E. Needleman and Tim Paradis reported. When one leader is so closely identified with the strategy, the products, and the culture, their departure can create a vacuum that no org chart (let alone one with 60 direct reports to the CEO) can immediately fill.

Much of Silicon Valley came to Huang's defense in recent days. Sarah Guo, a venture capitalist, called him "one of the most extraordinary entrepreneurs of all time." Sequoia's Shaun Maguire said Huang's "contributions to American innovation and AI leadership cannot be overstated."

A petition to reinstate Huang as Nvidia CEO circulated over the weekend, collecting more than 100,000 signatures, including those of Elon Musk and other prominent figures. Our own Alistair Barr also points to new reports that are casting doubt on the intelligence behind Jensen Huang's downfall.

For sure, there are several examples of seemingly irreplaceable CEOs — Steve Jobs at Apple and Travis Kalanick at Uber — whose companies still thrived under new leadership.

And even some of Huang's biggest proponents aren't standing by him. "No one was a bigger defender of Jensen than I was but there are rules about sex with subordinates," CNBC's Jim Cramer said on X. "Just because someone is brilliant doesn't mean he can do what he wants."

The question is whether Nvidia, which lacked a defined succession plan, can prove to be more durable than its founder's legend.

If it can't? Dick Costolo, the former Twitter CEO, floated an idea. "Prediction: 3-4 years from now, [Nvidia] will miss a quarter or two, and they will bring Jensen back to run the company," he said.

"Like fame, everybody is outraged for 15 minutes, and there is nothing Americans love more than the comeback story."

items.title: Nvidia's next CEO will inherit more than Jensen Huang's job
items.summary: Huang's exit leaves his successor with the task of rebuilding the trust of Nvidia's tens of thousands of employees amid intense public scrutiny. Getty Images Huang's exit leaves Nvidia's next CEO with the challenge of rebuilding trust and refocusing workers. His successor will need to keep day-to-day operations humming amid intense public scrutiny. Companies can't let extraordinary results be a license to follow different rules, a former Netflix talent exec said. During an NBA tech summit last year, former CEO Jensen Huang described having a management style at Nvidia built on open communication. "I spend all of my time being transparent," said Huang, who has long been lauded for steering the chipmaker's extraordinary rise. Now, reports of Huang's extramarital affairs — with a direct report, another employee, and a client suspected by US intelligence officials of spying for China — have exposed a gap between his professed commitment to candor and how he may have acted behind closed doors. Huang's exit leaves Nvidia's next CEO with a difficult task: rebuilding the trust of tens of thousands of workers at a company at the center of the AI boom . "When the CEO is having a romantic relationship with someone at the company, that can erode trust and engender cynicism," said Kim Scott, a former Apple and Google executive and cofounder of executive education company Radical Candor. Nvidia didn't respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Refocusing on the work Huang ran Nvidia with a flat structure at the top, a setup he credited with helping the company move quickly. He worked out of a conference room, not a private office, and had dozens of direct reports. Nvidia didn't have a publicly disclosed succession plan. C-suite observers have said that the halo surrounding a successful tech founder, combined with an org chart light on top layers , can leave a company with a thin succession bench. After Huang's departure Wednesday, Nvidia appointed Colette Kress, chief financial officer, as interim CEO . The company launched a search for a permanent replacement, including both internal and external candidates. Kress, as well as whoever ultimately takes the reins permanently, will likely face a number of challenges. "The first thing employees want to know is: Is the company in good hands and will it continue to do well?" said Scott. "A lot of people are holding unvested options worth millions of dollars." Nvidia's new boss will have to navigate the intense public scrutiny surrounding Huang's exit, while ensuring day-to-day operations remain humming. "The combination of keeping people focused on the work while not pretending that the circus outside doesn't exist is really, really hard to do," said Katie Burke, chief operating officer of legal AI company Harvey. 'A grief process' There are no quick fixes in this situation. "Trust can be violated very quickly, but it's rebuilt slowly and consistently," said Alison Fragale, an organizational psychologist and professor of organizational behavior at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. The chipmaker's new leader will also need to help employees cope in the aftermath of the scandal and get back to work. That may be especially difficult for those who admire Huang and wanted him to stay, added Fragale. "It's like a bit of a grief process," she said. Meanwhile, other employees may be feeling betrayed or unsettled by the intense public scrutiny. "You can't pretend that everyone's family is not asking them what's going on," said Fragale. Nvidia's next leader will have at least one advantage in healing the company's culture, said Jessica Neal, a former chief talent officer at Netflix. Huang's departure shows that despite all of his achievements, he is still facing consequences for violating company standards. "One of the biggest mistakes companies can make is confusing extraordinary results with the permission to behave differently," Neal said. "Every time you make an exception for a high performer, you're sending a message to everyone else about what really matters. And over time, those exceptions become the culture." items.title: A Gen Zer shares 4 rules he followed to turn $35 into a 6-figure marketing agency from his dorm room
items.summary: Stavya Nilawar founded his creator-marketing agency, Nilawar, with about $35. Courtesy of Stavya Babson student Stavya Nilawar grew a $35 creator marketing agency into six-figure revenue. Nilawar's agency connects AI brands with YouTube creators for sponsored segments and dedicated videos. He shares four lessons that helped him grow it from his dorm room. When Stavya Nilawar isn't in class at Babson College, he's growing his creator marketing agency. His weekdays follow a disciplined routine: class from 8 to 11:15 a.m., lunch, then a five-hour work block. After dinner, he works for another hour or two. Nilawar's company connects brands with YouTube creators for sponsored segments and dedicated videos. He's worked with brands including AI companies CodeRabbit and Wispr Flow, as well as on campaigns involving Jack Link's x MrBeast. He earns a cut of the project fee, typically 20%. He said he spent about $35 to get started — for a website domain and two email inboxes. First, he built a network of creators by manually searching TikTok: "I would literally doomscroll on TikTok and just go on people's accounts and look at their emails." Once he had a roster of 10 to 15 creators, he began pitching brands. Today, his monthly expenses rarely exceed $1,500, while monthly revenue topped $100,000 for the first time in October. Business Insider reviewed monthly business-account statements to verify his revenue. "The main expenses are virtual assistants," Nilawar said. They cost him about $1,000 a month and help manage his agency's outreach, which can involve sending 200 to 300 emails a day, including follow-ups. Nilawar, who started the business during a gap semester before college, said these four rules helped him turn roughly $35 into a six-figure business. 1. Choose a niche based on opportunity — not just passion Nilawar doesn't buy into the standard advice to follow your passion when choosing a business niche. For him, the business model came first: He knew he wanted to run an agency that connects brands with creators. Then he had to decide which type of brands to serve. He chose to work with AI companies. "I was not passionate about AI at all, to be honest," he said. But he saw an opportunity: AI companies were growing quickly, and many had budgets for creator partnerships. In his view, that's the better order of operations for aspiring founders: Choose a business model you enjoy, then find a niche with clear demand and customers willing to pay. 2. Find people who are already where you want to be When Nilawar began exploring influencer marketing, an industry contact helped explain how brands work with creators and how agencies make money. He also learned that 20% was a typical agency cut on a deal. Since then, he's deliberately sought advice from people further along in the industry, including his current mentor, who runs a similar agency that generates about $10 million a year. Nilawar named his agency after his family name. Courtesy of Stavya Nilawar "I would reach out to agency owners who were in the position that I wanted to be in," he said. "I literally asked them what they're doing now in their day-to-day business and how they got to the next level." Nilawar's advice: Find someone who has built the type of business you want to build, and ask if they'd be willing to share what they've learned. 3. Build a repeatable outreach system In the early days, Nilawar did everything manually: sourcing creators, sending emails, following up with potential clients, and managing campaigns. "Emails are the main way that we get clients," he said. "If you don't have a system for that, you're not going to do very well in the beginning." For Nilawar, reaching the first $10,000 in revenue required volume. He tested different email copy and calls to action, then sent outreach to brands within his chosen niche. Today, he uses virtual assistants and software to scale that work, but outreach is only part of the system. In a crowded agency market, Nilawar said his edge is responsiveness. What sets him apart from his competitors is "our relationships and our speed," he said. His team aims to respond to clients within two to five minutes. 4. Treat mistakes as lessons, not reasons to quit Early on, Nilawar landed a big campaign involving three creators. Two went smoothly, but the third repeatedly missed deadlines, and when the creator eventually delivered the content, Nilawar said the brand was unhappy with its quality. The brand wanted to cancel that portion of the deal, leaving Nilawar caught between the brand and the creator's manager. He thought he might have to pay the brand $25,000. "I didn't have $25K," said Nilawar, who was 18 at the time. "I thought I was screwed." The parties ultimately worked out a solution, and the experience taught him that agency work involves more than landing the deal: He also has to manage expectations, maintain communication, and resolve conflicts when a partnership goes sideways. Rather than viewing that scare as proof he wasn't ready to run a business, Nilawar sees it as a lesson he got early — when the stakes were still manageable. items.title: Bland Launches Tofu-1, a Full-Duplex Speech-to-Speech Model for Calls
items.summary: Bland, the San Francisco voice-AI company, has released Tofu-1 , a full-duplex speech-to-speech model in research preview. The Tofu-1 speech-to-speech model targets calls from moving cars, hospital rooms and weak-signal lines. It listens while it speaks and reasons while it talks. For phone-agent teams, one model now handles audio in and audio out, with no transcript between. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . What is Tofu-1? Tofu-1 is a full-duplex speech-to-speech model from Bland that hears, reasons and replies in audio during phone calls. It is the first release in a planned family of Bland speech-to-speech models. How does Tofu-1 differ from a cascade voice agent? Most voice agents are cascades. They turn speech into text, pass it to a language model, then turn the reply back into speech. Tofu-1 listens to the audio directly , so tone, hesitation and background sound stay available to the model. Bland has not published the internal architecture. Audio understanding Bland lists 3 audio skills on its product page: Speaker tracking: tells speakers apart and works out who each one is addressing. Noise separation: separates voices from a crying child, a TV, highway traffic, a hospital intercom or keypad tones. Paralinguistics: hears hesitation, frustration and urgency. Full duplex and thinking while talking Callers can interrupt or correct Tofu-1 mid-sentence. While it works on a request, it keeps the conversation moving. It reports the result only when the work is done. It never claims a task is finished early. Scene generation Because Tofu-1 models the sound of a call, it can also produce one. That includes a second speaker, the room around them and line noise. What is Bland’s ‘TV Test’? The TV Test asks one question: can the model follow the caller while ignoring speech from another scene? TV audio is often louder than the caller. Bland marks its TV Test walkthrough as illustrative, not recorded model output. How does Tofu-1 compare with other full-duplex models? FDB results use different benchmark versions and are not directly comparable. How can teams access Tofu-1? Research preview access is open to a limited number of enterprises. Bland names banking, healthcare, insurance and government as target sectors. The sign-up form asks for monthly call volume, from under 1,000 to 50,000+. What is Tofu-1?

Tofu-1 is a full-duplex speech-to-speech model from Bland that hears, reasons and replies in audio during phone calls. It is the first release in a planned family of Bland speech-to-speech models.

  • Noise separation: separates voices from a crying child, a TV, highway traffic, a hospital intercom or keypad tones.
  • Paralinguistics: hears hesitation, frustration and urgency.

Callers can interrupt or correct Tofu-1 mid-sentence. While it works on a request, it keeps the conversation moving. It reports the result only when the work is done. It never claims a task is finished early.

Because Tofu-1 models the sound of a call, it can also produce one. That includes a second speaker, the room around them and line noise.

items.title: My Claude Code and Codex Workflow: The Problems I Had to Solve Myself
items.summary: A year of building across five projects, losing track of sessions, sharing my desktop with AI, and learning where the time and tokens went. AI-generated illustration. I have sent a prompt to the wrong project. I was working across five projects, with a separate VS Code window for each and many AI coding sessions inside them. The windows looked similar. Finding the right conversation was already taking more effort than I expected, and sometimes I got it wrong. Then desktop testing introduced a different problem. An agent needed to launch the application, inspect its interface, move the mouse, and type. While it did that, using my own computer could interfere with the test. I have had days when this kept me from managing other work on the same machine. After more than a year of intensive AI-assisted development, these were the problems occupying me: where the work was happening, what it needed from me, and how to keep it moving without repeatedly reconstructing its context. Prefer listening? Here’s an AI-generated audio discussion based on this article. https://medium.com/media/42581837ffc08ae6326b49c1e4f8f398/href Re-created view of my earlier workspace, with illustrative project and session data. The fixes gradually became AigoPilot , the studio I now develop and use. I am its founder. I can select a project, see its sessions, and check which ones are working or waiting in one place. That helps even when I use a single AI provider. My Claude Code workflow, together with Codex, changed as I worked through the situations below. Re-created AigoPilot interface using illustrative project and session data. Finding the session that built the feature Even in the correct window, I could spend time looking through tabs to find the conversation I needed. My Claude Code work grew to around a hundred sessions. Some were finished; others were waiting for a decision or another instruction. A bug made this particularly frustrating. I wanted the session that had built the affected feature, because it might still have the relevant design decisions in context. A fresh session had to investigate the code and reconstruct that background first. Searching titles rarely worked for me. A conversation could begin with one task and accumulate many others. Its title was a poor record of everything inside it. I could ask an agent to search the session history. Sometimes that took two or three minutes and substantial reading, then returned a session ID. I still had to work out how to reopen it, sometimes through a terminal instead of the interface I was using. So I added a voice assistant to the studio and mobile app. I can describe the project and the feature I am looking for. In my use, finding it usually takes a few seconds, and the assistant opens the session directly. If there are several candidates, I get a short description of each and choose. I use the same assistant to find and open an email. Both requests end at the item I need to work on, instead of leaving me with another identifier to look up. When the AI needs my mouse Two of my projects are desktop applications: AigoPilot and Cilevi Screen Recorder. Testing their interfaces introduced a problem I had not felt as strongly in my background development tasks. After changing an application, an agent may need to launch it, inspect the screen, click controls, and type. When that happens on my main desktop, my own input can interfere with the test. I have had days when I could barely use my computer because an agent was working through the application. Managing a second project was difficult. Running another UI test made things worse: one application would come to the foreground while another agent was trying to interact with something else. This was about the desktop available to the agents. Similar conflicts can happen whenever automation shares the same interactive environment, including a browser. I started looking at the computers I already had. A spare laptop could take a project and its sessions, leaving my main workstation free. A friend also had an unused laptop at home. Connecting to a remote machine over the internet made that useful too. Moving files was only part of the work. One project was a Unity game, and the destination laptop did not have Unity or all the prerequisites installed. That led me to add environment preparation to the transfer workflow. I have worked through Unity in this setup. I have not automated installation for every application someone might use. Other dependencies may still need an AI-assisted or manual installation. But a project that can run and test on another machine leaves me able to use my own computer while it works. I wrote more about testing desktop apps with AI on spare computers , including the environment setup problem I encountered when moving a Unity project. My AI Coding Agent Needed the Mouse. I Needed My Computer. I started measuring what a small prompt carried with it Usage limits kept interrupting me. Waiting, buying additional access, or switching subscriptions all had a cost, so I spent time investigating token consumption. Some experiments ran for three or four days, comparing an approach across projects with and without a proposed technique. A few methods made consumption worse. Reading a persuasive article was no substitute for trying it on my own work. One experiment began with a tiny request, such as generating a Python Hello World program. I wanted to understand why the input could be so much larger than the sentence I had typed. The request could carry a substantial amount of surrounding information. That made skill loading worth examining: which instructions needed to be present, and which could wait until the task required them? I worked on keeping short skill descriptions available and loading the detailed material when needed. In one of my comparisons, the input-token count fell by about 60%. That figure describes that comparison, not every prompt or a guaranteed reduction in a subscription bill. Selective loading is also documented practice today. Anthropic’s skill authoring guidance describes loading skill metadata first and reading the instructions and references as needed. My experience concerns the setup I examined and the overhead I removed; it would be inaccurate to say every coding tool always sends every installed skill in full. Prepared file-processing tools helped too. For tasks that need extracted text or tables, the studio can convert PDFs, Word documents, and spreadsheets into Markdown before handing the content to the model, instead of repeatedly asking an agent to develop a converter. The model still has to read the relevant content. A task involving a chart, formula, or visual layout may also require the original file. And token counts need interpretation. Cached input can be accounted for differently from newly processed input. I keep the size of a request separate from what it ultimately costs. Starting a new session without losing the small things As a conversation grew, I also needed a way to continue with less accumulated context. A handoff summary helped, but the next session could lose a detail that mattered immediately. On one occasion, an earlier session had worked with an API key. The new one did not know where it was stored. I had to return to the old conversation, find the location, and relay it. A short path can matter more to the next task than pages of discussion. My handoff process now pays attention to operational details: relevant files, URLs, completed work, decisions, and the next step. For credentials, the useful record is the storage location and access method; copying secrets into more summaries creates its own problems. I also removed the manual copying. From the prompt box, I can choose to continue in a new session, select the provider, model, and effort, and have the handoff prepared and passed to that session. The studio can warn me when a conversation has become heavy so I remember to consider moving on. I wrote a practical guide to starting a new AI coding session without losing the details , with a handoff template for file paths, verification status, access locations, and the next action. Starting a New AI Coding Session Without Losing the Details Switching providers introduced another gap in the setup I was using. My Codex work used AGENTS.md; my Claude Code sessions used CLAUDE.md. I added a small reference between the project instructions so I did not have to maintain separate copies. Current Claude Code documentation also describes direct AGENTS.md support in supported versions and configurations . A shared-file import also remains an option. The practical lesson is to check what a session actually loads, rather than infer it from the tool’s name. I wrote a practical guide to using CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md in the same project , including the optional import and a check for what each session loads. That gives a new session access to the recorded project guidance. It does not transfer every thought from the previous conversation. A useful handoff still has to say what is happening now. I also wrote about how I’m designing project memory for AI coding sessions to preserve decisions, technical evidence, and the conditions under which they apply. My AI Coding Sessions Had the Code. They Were Missing the Decisions. Leaving the desk without abandoning the work In the mobile workflows I tried, opening a session sometimes showed me its previous state while the latest messages loaded. I have waited five to ten seconds, or hit a Retry message and eventually returned to my computer. I built the mobile side of the studio around seeing the latest state quickly and acting on it. I can create a project on a connected machine, choose its drive and folder, and start sessions from my phone. Notifications needed to explain why I should open the app. A session requesting permission needs attention. A finished task may only need a glance. A result that ends by asking whether to perform another step is waiting on me again. The notifications now identify the project and session and take me straight there. Customer support messages and requests for a human chat operator get the same treatment. Then there was the interruption I could miss entirely. I would leave home expecting a task to finish, return an hour later, and discover it had stopped shortly after I left because of a usage limit. Even after the allowance became available again, the session could remain idle until I intervened. I added continuation after the limit resets so it can resume without waiting for me to return. The waiting period still exists; the avoidable delay afterward is what I wanted to remove. I wrote more about managing Claude Code and Codex from my phone , including the notifications and small decisions that help work continue while I’m away from my desk. Managing Claude Code and Codex from My Phone: What I Actually Needed The work after the code I kept recognizing another habit in myself and developer friends: finish a product, then start building the next idea. Finding customers and handling their questions required work we were less comfortable doing. Content production became its own long experiment. Over roughly a year, I tried skills, supplied design references, examined weak results, and refined instructions for images and video. I then turned those accumulated rules and workflows into reusable skills for the studio’s content plugin. A new conversation could start with those instructions instead of repeating all the earlier trial and error. The underlying model had not permanently learned my preferences; I had made the working knowledge explicit. Keyword research was another example. While preparing this article, I initially considered “AI coding workflow” as its main phrase. The Keyword Planner research for this article reported 390 average monthly searches for that term and 8,100 for “claude code workflow,” worldwide, in English, over October 2025 through September 2026. The latter’s September figure was 4,400, so the annual average also needed context. “Codex vs Claude Code” was larger, at 49,500, but people searching it expect a comparison. My story would not give them one. That is a practical use of the research workflow behind my Search Planner plugin. It helped choose wording that matched both the subject and measured demand. It did not promise a ranking. Sales and support added more reasons to keep the work connected. Purchases from connected Stripe or Paddle accounts, prioritized incoming email, and customer conversations now come into the same environment. An AI chat assistant can use a knowledge base prepared from available product information, with a path to a human when needed. Those needs explain why I kept extending the studio beyond coding. What I was trying to get back Many of these problems appear with a single AI subscription. Several projects and long conversations are enough to create them. Switching providers is useful in some situations, while finding the right session and keeping a desktop available matter throughout the day. I still have to decide what to build, review changes, and respond when an agent needs judgment. I want to spend less time locating the conversation that needs that judgment, or waiting to use a computer occupied by a test. The spare-machine setup is a particularly concrete improvement for me: the application can be tested on another computer while my own mouse and keyboard remain available for the next project. I’m Anoosh Ohadi, a software developer and the founder of AigoPilot. I write about the practical work of building and running software with AI. My Claude Code and Codex Workflow: The Problems I Had to Solve Myself was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: My AI Coding Agent Needed the Mouse. I Needed My Computer.
items.summary: Testing desktop apps with AI taught me why spare laptops need more than a copy of the code. Illustration: working on the main computer while AI tests applications on separate laptops. There were days when I could barely use my own computer because an AI agent was busy testing an application I was building. It would launch the app, move the mouse, click through the interface, and type. I had to leave the controls alone. If I clicked somewhere else or brought another window forward, I could interrupt the test. Meanwhile, I had other projects to work on. This was an awkward consequence of getting more development work done with AI. I could have several coding sessions making progress, but when one of them needed my desktop, I sometimes had to wait for access to my own machine. A successful build still left work to do Two of my projects are desktop applications: AigoPilot and Cilevi Screen Recorder. After an agent changed an interface, I wanted it to open the application and check what it had made. Was the control visible? Did the interaction work? Had a layout change broken something elsewhere? Reading the source and completing a build could answer some questions. They could not tell me everything I wanted to know about the running application. Much of my web development work could continue in the background. The desktop testing I was doing often needed the application in front, with the agent interacting with it much as I would. That distinction depends on how a test is run. Browser automation can also interfere with someone’s desktop, and some desktop checks can run without taking over their input. My problem was specifically the tests that needed control of the same interactive environment I was trying to use. Two agents could interrupt each other, too With one application, I could sometimes step away and let the agent finish. With several projects, that became harder. One agent could be interacting with an application while another brought its own window forward. The first agent’s next click might then land in the wrong place. Adding another coding session did not give it another desktop. Neither did opening another terminal. I was already dealing with the overhead of finding the right project and session. Now, even after finding the work I wanted to continue, I sometimes could not use the computer to do it. At one point, this constrained my work for much of a day. It was enough to make me look for a different arrangement. I started using the computers that were sitting idle I had spare machines available. Instead of having every project run on my main workstation, I wanted to move a project’s code and sessions to another computer and let development and testing continue there. The application could open on that machine. Its agent could use that desktop. I could keep using mine. I built this workflow into AigoPilot , the studio I develop and use. I am its founder. The reason for building it was practical: I needed the testing work to happen somewhere that would leave my main computer available. A friend later mentioned an unused laptop at home. I connected that machine as well, so some work could run there over the internet. That made the setup useful beyond the spare computers in my own room. A home computer and a work computer could also help each other, provided the machine, connection, and project requirements were suitable. The important part was where the application actually ran. Viewing my main computer remotely would still leave its desktop occupied. Running the project on another machine gave the test its own place to work. Moving a Unity project showed me what I had missed One of the projects I moved was a game I was building with Unity. The destination laptop did not have Unity and some of the other prerequisites available on my main computer. Transferring the project files had not made it ready to continue the work. I asked the AI to help extend the transfer workflow to handle that setup as well. In the Unity case I worked through, this included preparing the destination with the tools the project needed. I have not automated installation of every development tool. For an unfamiliar dependency, the destination may still need additional setup, either with AI assistance or manually. Any required access or software licensing also needs to be handled for that machine. That experience changed how I thought about a project transfer. Along with the code, I needed to know which environment could build and run it, and what the next session was supposed to do. What I would check before handing over a project For someone trying a similar arrangement, I would start with one project and one spare machine. Before sending several agents over, establish that the destination can complete a small, useful task. My checklist would be: Code state: identify the branch or revision, including any local changes that need to travel. Toolchain: record the editor, SDK, runtime, and versions the project requires. Launch procedure: explain how to build and open the application on that machine. Task boundary: say what the agent should test and what it is allowed to change. Evidence: specify where to return logs, screenshots, and a short account of what happened. Access should be arranged for the destination rather than assumed to exist. A handoff can record where approved credentials are managed without copying secret values into its notes. Here is an example of the kind of first task I would give a destination machine. It is a suggested brief, not a transcript from one of my runs: Open the project and report missing prerequisites before changing anything. Once the environment is ready, build the application, launch it, and open its settings panel. Check that the new control appears and responds to a click. Return the code revision, build result, a screenshot, and any errors. If you cannot complete the interactive check, say where you stopped. That last sentence matters. A report that says the build passed should not leave me assuming the agent also opened and tested the interface. Separate desktops still need coordinated work Moving a task to another computer addresses the input conflict. Other parts of the work can still collide. Two agents might edit the same files, use the same test account, or write their results to the same location. I would give parallel tasks a clear code state and separate output locations. Where appropriate, separate working copies or worktrees can help keep changes attributable to the task that made them. I would also ask the report to identify the machine and revision it tested. A screenshot is more useful when I can connect it to the build I actually asked the agent to check. The spare machine needs to suit the workload, too. Opening a basic settings panel is a different job from testing a demanding Unity scene or investigating recording behavior on particular hardware. An available laptop is a useful starting point; whether it can do the work still needs to be checked. My main computer became available again I have not attached a timing study to this article, and I cannot give a measured percentage improvement. The change I noticed was that I could continue working while an agent interacted with an application on another computer. That mattered when I had several projects in progress. I could review another session, respond to a problem, or do my own work without worrying about interrupting the test with a click. I wrote about the wider workflow in My Claude Code and Codex Workflow: The Problems I Had to Solve Myself . This was one of its most frustrating parts, because it affected the computer I needed for everything else. When I began using AI to build more software, I expected the difficult questions to be about code. I spent considerably more time than I expected figuring out who got to use the mouse. My AI Coding Agent Needed the Mouse. I Needed My Computer. was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
Testing desktop apps with AI taught me why spare laptops need more than a copy of the code.Illustration: working on the main computer while AI tests applications on separate laptops.

There were days when I could barely use my own computer because an AI agent was busy testing an application I was building.

It would launch the app, move the mouse, click through the interface, and type. I had to leave the controls alone. If I clicked somewhere else or brought another window forward, I could interrupt the test.

Meanwhile, I had other projects to work on.

This was an awkward consequence of getting more development work done with AI. I could have several coding sessions making progress, but when one of them needed my desktop, I sometimes had to wait for access to my own machine.

A successful build still left work to do

Two of my projects are desktop applications: AigoPilot and Cilevi Screen Recorder.

After an agent changed an interface, I wanted it to open the application and check what it had made. Was the control visible? Did the interaction work? Had a layout change broken something elsewhere?

Reading the source and completing a build could answer some questions. They could not tell me everything I wanted to know about the running application.

Much of my web development work could continue in the background. The desktop testing I was doing often needed the application in front, with the agent interacting with it much as I would.

That distinction depends on how a test is run. Browser automation can also interfere with someone’s desktop, and some desktop checks can run without taking over their input. My problem was specifically the tests that needed control of the same interactive environment I was trying to use.

Two agents could interrupt each other, too

With one application, I could sometimes step away and let the agent finish.

With several projects, that became harder. One agent could be interacting with an application while another brought its own window forward. The first agent’s next click might then land in the wrong place.

Adding another coding session did not give it another desktop. Neither did opening another terminal.

I was already dealing with the overhead of finding the right project and session. Now, even after finding the work I wanted to continue, I sometimes could not use the computer to do it.

At one point, this constrained my work for much of a day. It was enough to make me look for a different arrangement.

I started using the computers that were sitting idle

I had spare machines available. Instead of having every project run on my main workstation, I wanted to move a project’s code and sessions to another computer and let development and testing continue there.

The application could open on that machine. Its agent could use that desktop. I could keep using mine.

I built this workflow into AigoPilot, the studio I develop and use. I am its founder. The reason for building it was practical: I needed the testing work to happen somewhere that would leave my main computer available.

A friend later mentioned an unused laptop at home. I connected that machine as well, so some work could run there over the internet.

That made the setup useful beyond the spare computers in my own room. A home computer and a work computer could also help each other, provided the machine, connection, and project requirements were suitable.

The important part was where the application actually ran. Viewing my main computer remotely would still leave its desktop occupied. Running the project on another machine gave the test its own place to work.

Moving a Unity project showed me what I had missed

One of the projects I moved was a game I was building with Unity.

The destination laptop did not have Unity and some of the other prerequisites available on my main computer. Transferring the project files had not made it ready to continue the work.

I asked the AI to help extend the transfer workflow to handle that setup as well. In the Unity case I worked through, this included preparing the destination with the tools the project needed.

I have not automated installation of every development tool. For an unfamiliar dependency, the destination may still need additional setup, either with AI assistance or manually. Any required access or software licensing also needs to be handled for that machine.

That experience changed how I thought about a project transfer. Along with the code, I needed to know which environment could build and run it, and what the next session was supposed to do.

What I would check before handing over a project

For someone trying a similar arrangement, I would start with one project and one spare machine. Before sending several agents over, establish that the destination can complete a small, useful task.

My checklist would be:

  • Code state: identify the branch or revision, including any local changes that need to travel.
  • Toolchain: record the editor, SDK, runtime, and versions the project requires.
  • Launch procedure: explain how to build and open the application on that machine.
  • Task boundary: say what the agent should test and what it is allowed to change.
  • Evidence: specify where to return logs, screenshots, and a short account of what happened.

Access should be arranged for the destination rather than assumed to exist. A handoff can record where approved credentials are managed without copying secret values into its notes.

Here is an example of the kind of first task I would give a destination machine. It is a suggested brief, not a transcript from one of my runs:

Open the project and report missing prerequisites before changing anything. Once the environment is ready, build the application, launch it, and open its settings panel. Check that the new control appears and responds to a click. Return the code revision, build result, a screenshot, and any errors. If you cannot complete the interactive check, say where you stopped.

That last sentence matters. A report that says the build passed should not leave me assuming the agent also opened and tested the interface.

Separate desktops still need coordinated work

Moving a task to another computer addresses the input conflict. Other parts of the work can still collide.

Two agents might edit the same files, use the same test account, or write their results to the same location. I would give parallel tasks a clear code state and separate output locations. Where appropriate, separate working copies or worktrees can help keep changes attributable to the task that made them.

I would also ask the report to identify the machine and revision it tested. A screenshot is more useful when I can connect it to the build I actually asked the agent to check.

The spare machine needs to suit the workload, too. Opening a basic settings panel is a different job from testing a demanding Unity scene or investigating recording behavior on particular hardware. An available laptop is a useful starting point; whether it can do the work still needs to be checked.

My main computer became available again

I have not attached a timing study to this article, and I cannot give a measured percentage improvement. The change I noticed was that I could continue working while an agent interacted with an application on another computer.

That mattered when I had several projects in progress. I could review another session, respond to a problem, or do my own work without worrying about interrupting the test with a click.

I wrote about the wider workflow in My Claude Code and Codex Workflow: The Problems I Had to Solve Myself. This was one of its most frustrating parts, because it affected the computer I needed for everything else.

When I began using AI to build more software, I expected the difficult questions to be about code. I spent considerably more time than I expected figuring out who got to use the mouse.

My AI Coding Agent Needed the Mouse. I Needed My Computer. was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

On Sunday, sceptics were ⁠proven right when he ⁠confessed to ​using generative AI to cheat. The scandal has followed months of speculation after he scored near-perfect marks on hundreds of questions over two exams ⁠taken in April and July. It has also raised the stakes for organisers of South Korea’s annual college entrance exam this Thursday.
