items.title: 1% of Companies Drive 80% of OpenAI and Anthropic’s Revenue.
items.summary: 1% of Companies Drive 80% of OpenAI and Anthropic’s Revenue. The Rest Are Falling Behind at a Discount. Ramp’s November AI Index shows the top 1% spending $10,199 per employee per month against $16.32 for the median firm, while token prices fell 21% in a month. The gap is no longer about price or technology. It is about management. Cover image generated by the author. The AI divide between companies is no longer about technology or price. It is about management. Models have never been cheaper, and the gap between the companies that use them seriously and everyone else has never been wider. A company that spends sixteen dollars a month per employee on AI in late 2026 is not being prudent. It is falling behind, at a discount. That has been the position argued here for a long time, and on November 11 Ramp published the numbers that make it hard to dispute. Written with the help of AI tools; ideas, sources and final review by the author. The Ramp AI Index tracks AI adoption and spend across more than 85,000 American businesses, using transaction data from the corporate card and spend management company. Its November edition, written by Ramp’s lead economist Ara Kharazian, contains three figures that every leadership team should put side by side. First, among firms paying for AI, the top 1% spent a median of 10,199.20 dollars per employee per month in October, up 9% from September. Second, the median firm spent 16.32 dollars per employee per month, up 93 cents. Third, the average price per million tokens fell 21% in a single month. A 625x gap, in a market that keeps getting cheaper Divide the first number by the second. The top 1% spends roughly 625 times more on AI per employee than the median company. Over a year, that is about 122,000 dollars per employee at the top, against about 196 dollars for the median firm. Even the top 10% of spenders, at 800.84 dollars per employee per month, sit about 49 times above the median. Ramp also reports that 1% of businesses drive 80% of the revenue going to OpenAI and Anthropic, and that this top group is largely made up of venture-backed companies in tech, finance and technical services. Outside those sectors, in Kharazian’s words, AI spend is failing to proliferate, and growth in the median and top 10% groups is relatively sluggish. Now add the third number. A 21% monthly drop in the average token price means the same work costs much less than it did in September. Ramp’s dashboard shows the same effect from another angle: in the week ending November 1, total token spending rose 10.5% compared with the same week a month earlier, while total token volume rose 29%. Companies are getting more AI for each dollar, month after month. So the obvious explanation for the gap, that AI is too expensive for ordinary companies, does not hold. The price barrier is falling fast. The spending gap is not. Why sixteen dollars is a management signal, not a saving Sixteen dollars per employee per month is roughly the price of one basic chatbot seat shared across a team, or a handful of individual subscriptions bought by enthusiasts. It is what AI looks like when it is tolerated rather than deployed. Nobody owns it, no process has been redesigned around it, and no budget line expects anything from it. Ten thousand dollars per employee per month looks completely different. At that level, AI is not a tool people open from time to time. It is agents running workloads, coding tools working all day, models embedded in products and operations. It is a cost that someone approved because they expected a return, and that someone is accountable for. Neither number tells you who is getting value. A high bill can hide waste, which is exactly why companies such as Apple, Uber and Tesla have put caps and budgets in place this year. But the difference between the two groups is not that one found a cheaper model or a better vendor. Both buy from the same handful of labs, at prices that are falling for everyone. The difference is that one group decided AI was part of how the company works, and organized for it. That is a leadership decision. It cannot be delegated to procurement, and it cannot be solved by waiting for the next price cut. The next front is outside engineering The most useful part of Ramp’s November letter is new. For the first time, the index tracks AI spend by department, and the picture is lopsided. In October, engineering teams drove 72% of all classified AI spend. Coding agents made engineering the dominant customer of the AI industry, but Ramp notes that spend from those teams has fallen from the highs observed this summer, even as usage rises. The growth is coming from somewhere else. Customer success and support operations now drive 13.3% of classified spend, up from 0.8% in June. Kharazian suggests these teams may be deploying models for customer service chatbots. Ramp also sees modest growth in spending by executive leadership teams. That shift matters for the median company. Most businesses are not software companies, and their largest AI opportunity will never be a coding agent. It will be support, operations, finance, sales and the management layer itself: the places where work is repetitive, documented and measurable. Ramp’s own reading is that these use cases are good candidates for cheaper and faster models rather than the highest-performance ones. In other words, the use cases that fit the median company best are also the ones getting cheapest the fastest. The companies that will close the gap are not the ones that copy the top 1% line by line. They are the ones that find their own equivalent of the coding agent, in the department where they have the most volume. Read the data with care These figures deserve a fair reading. Ramp’s customers skew toward growth-oriented, tech-savvy firms that are larger than the average American business, so adoption is likely overstated. Free tools and usage through personal accounts may not appear in the data. Ramp itself notes that its top 1% estimate is more volatile than the median and top 10% figures, because it rests on a small group of firms. And the token metrics come only from companies using Ramp’s token spend management product. None of that changes the direction. Even if the exact multiple is off, a gap of two orders of magnitude between the leaders and the typical firm, in a market where prices fall by a fifth in a month, is not a measurement artifact. It is a choice that most companies have not yet made. What to do this quarter You do not need to spend ten thousand dollars per employee to act on this. You need to stop treating a low AI bill as a sign of discipline, and start treating it as a question. 1. Measure your own number. Add up every AI subscription, API bill and tool licence, including the ones paid on personal cards and expensed. Divide by headcount. If you cannot produce that figure in a day, you have found the first problem. 2. Pick one department outside engineering. Support, finance operations or sales are the usual candidates. Choose the one with the most repetitive volume, and give it a real AI budget with a named owner, not a pilot with no money. 3. Route by task. Reserve frontier models for work that needs them. Ramp’s data shows frontier models still took 69.5% of spend in October, but the fastest-growing use cases fit cheaper models. Every dollar saved on routing is a dollar available for a new use case. 4. Tie every budget line to an outcome. Tickets resolved, days removed from the month-end close, proposals sent per week. Spending that cannot be linked to an outcome after 30 days should be cut, and spending that can should be allowed to grow. 5. Re-run the comparison every month. Ramp publishes its index monthly. Put your own per-employee figure next to the median and the top 10% at every leadership review, and ask why you sit where you sit. Cheap AI rewards the companies that move Falling prices are often described as democratizing AI. They do the opposite when only a few companies are organized to use them. Every price cut lets the top 1% do more with the same budget, while the median company keeps its sixteen dollars and its one shared seat. The divide widens, and it widens fastest in the year AI became cheap. The technology is available to everyone at almost the same price. What is not available to everyone is a leadership team that decides what AI is for, who owns it and how its value is measured. That is where the next gap will be won or lost. Where does your company sit today: closer to sixteen dollars, or closer to eight hundred? Follow me on Medium for the next analysis of how AI is changing the way companies decide, spend and lead. Sources Ramp, Ara Kharazian, “November 2026 Ramp AI Index: New Fronts in the AI Trade,” November 11, 2026: ramp.com/data/ai-index-nov-2026 Ramp, “Ramp AI Index” data dashboard, data through October 2026, consulted November 13, 2026: ramp.com/data/ai-index Ramp, “October 2026 Ramp AI Index: Cracks in the AI thesis, part 3,” October 2026: ramp.com/data/ai-index-oct-2026 Abbas Mistrah, Towards AI, “Apple Now Caps Its Engineers’ AI at $200 a Day. Every Company Needs an AI Budget Owner,” November 10, 2026 (Apple, Uber and Tesla AI budgets, with original sources): pub.towardsai.net The Decoder, “US corporate AI spending hits a new high in October, but growth slows to 1.65 percent,” November 2026: the-decoder.com 1% of Companies Drive 80% of OpenAI and Anthropic’s Revenue. was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: pyr.js: Python and R in HTML pages, with one script tag
items.summary_html:
[This article was first published on T. Moudiki's Webpage - R, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here) Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

What if you could put Python or R code in an HTML page, double-click the file, and have it run? No server, no build step, no install, and nothing sent anywhere: everything runs in the browser.

That’s what pyr.js does. I built it this week with Claude (Anthropic’s AI assistant), which wrote the code and tests from my design decisions and verified everything in a headless browser. The heavy lifting is done by Pyodide (Python compiled to WebAssembly) and webR (same thing for R). pyr.js is the glue: a single file, about 460 lines you can actually read, that finds the Python and R code in your page and connects it to your HTML.

A first example

Save this as an .html file and open it in your browser:



count = 0

Add

py-click runs Python when the button is clicked, and py-out says where the result goes. Any DOM event works the same way (py-input, py-change, …), and for R, it’s r-click, r-input, and so on. R’s printed output and plots show up directly in the page:

Points:

Here, .value (_value in Python) holds the slider’s current value, and the histogram is redrawn as you move it.

Python and R compute, JavaScript draws

My favorite part: results can be passed as data to any JavaScript chart library. In a previous post, I used Observable Plot and Highcharts for dashboards. With pyr.js, py-then / r-then hand the result to a function of your choice. An R data frame arrives as an array of rows, ready to plot:

The same works with Python: lists of dicts, numpy arrays and pandas DataFrames are converted for you. Here’s the Observable Plot example from the repository, with a Python random walk (redrawn by a slider) and the R data frame above:

How fast is it?

The first visit downloads the engines (several MB for Python, cached by the browser afterwards), and starting Python takes about 3 seconds. Nothing magical so far.

The interesting part: when pyr.js is hosted on the same site as your pages, Python runs in a shared worker. Other tabs of the site, and even page reloads, reuse the interpreter that’s already running: in my tests (Chromium), the page was ready in under 0.1 second instead of 3. Each tab still has its own variables, and a reload still starts the page fresh. For R, webR doesn’t allow this (yet), so it starts with each page.

There’s also a live editing mode for development: put your Python code in a .py file, add data-watch to the script tag, and your changes apply to the running page as soon as you save, without reloading.

Privacy

pyr.js sends nothing anywhere. No analytics, no telemetry: your code and your data stay in the visitor’s browser. The only network requests are for the engines themselves and the packages your code imports.

Try it

The repository is on GitHub (MIT license), with four examples: the basics, Observable Plot, Highcharts and live editing. The README explains the rest (attributes, data conversion, self-hosting the engines, pinning a version with an integrity hash). Feedback, issues and stars are welcome!

items.title: Interim Analysis: My Messy Notes
items.summary_html:
[This article was first published on r on Everyday Is A School Day, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here) Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

Why can’t we just peek at our data with α = 0.05 every time? Gotta see it to believe it! Simulating the inflated error, seeing why it’s not Bonferroni, and rebuilding O’Brien-Fleming & Lan-DeMets boundaries to match gsDesign. Hope it’s not an illusion of learning

Motivations

I’ve always heard “interim analysis” thrown around in trial papers but never really understood what’s happening under the hood. Why can’t we just peek at 1.96 every time? And isn’t this just Bonferroni? Turns out it’s not! Let’s dig in and simulate our way to understanding.

Objectives:
  • What Is Interim Analysis?
  • What’s O’Brien-Fleming Method?
  • How To Perform It?
  • How To Do It From Scratch?
    • O’Brien-Fleming Method
    • Lan De Mat & Obrien Fleming Method
    • Comparison
  • Opportunities For Improvement
  • Lessons Learnt
What Is Interim Analysis?

An interim analysis is a planned look at the data half way through a study, before all participants have been enrolled or followed up. They do it for practical and ethical reasons: if a treatment is clearly working, or clearly harmful, it isn’t right to keep randomizing people to the worse option, and if it’s clearly going nowhere, they can save time and resources by stopping early. The catch is that every extra look is another chance to find a “significant” result purely by luck. Peeking twice at the usual 5% threshold pushes the false-positive rate up. Interim analysis methods, such as O’Brien-Fleming boundaries, fix this by setting a stricter bar at the early looks so that the overall error rate stays at 5%.

Now you know me, I’m the see it to believe kind of person. Let’s try to simulate this with multiple trials and see if that’s true

library(tidyverse)
n <- 500
prob <- 0.5
peek <- c(n/2,n)
zscore_vec <- c()
trial <- 100000
count_false <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = trial)

for (trial_i in 1:trial) {
  # for reproducibility
  set.seed(trial_i)
  
  # get sim data
  control <- rbinom(n,1,prob)
  rx <- rbinom(n,1,prob)
  
  # look at when n is 250, and when n is 500
  for (i in 1:length(peek)) {
    m  <- peek[i]
    pA <- mean(rx[1:m])
    pB <- mean(control[1:m])
    p_pool <- (pA + pB) / 2
    se <- sqrt(p_pool * (1 - p_pool) * (2 / m))
    
    # calculate z score
    zscore_vec[i] <- abs(pA - pB) / se
  }
  # record zscore if > 1.96 (~pval 0.05)
  if (any(zscore_vec > 1.96)) { count_false[trial_i] <- 1 }
}

# what percent of family-wise error?
(val <- count_false |> mean())

## [1] 0.08952

Lots of code, I hope some of the comments on the codes are self-explanatory. So we basically simulated a no difference result of 2 groups. We used zscore of 1.96 which is our 5% alpha to see if any of these z scores were above the threshold (it’s not supposed to, remember, there is no difference in this truth!). We expect it to be ~5% but we got 8.952% instead! Wow! That’s 3.952% higher than our threshold, not good!

Note to self: The confusion of false postive/discovery/family-wise examples. If you test 90 placebo and 10 real rx and get 15 “significants”, 5 of them wrong: the false positive rate is 5/90 (how often placebos get credit) aka (1 – specificity), the false discovery rate is 5/15 (how many of your hits are wrong) aka (1 – ppv [aka precision]), and the family-wise error rate is the chance of getting even one false hit across the whole set, which is what interim analysis controls across looks.

wow, doesn’t that remind us of something here? Multiplicity, yea? Maybe, kind of. Now, what if we’re being conservative like bonferonni and split that 5% twice? and see how much false positive did we get?

count_false <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = trial)

for (trial_i in 1:trial) {
  # for reproducibility
  set.seed(trial_i)
  
  # get sim data
  control <- rbinom(n,1,prob)
  rx <- rbinom(n,1,prob)
  
  # look at when n is 250, and when n is 500
  for (i in 1:length(peek)) {
    m  <- peek[i]
    pA <- mean(rx[1:m])
    pB <- mean(control[1:m])
    p_pool <- (pA + pB) / 2
    se <- sqrt(p_pool * (1 - p_pool) * (2 / m))
    
    # calculate z score
    zscore_vec[i] <- abs(pA - pB) / se
  }
  # record zscore if > 2.24, two tails with two looks (divide 5% to 2)
  if (any(zscore_vec > 2.24)) { count_false[trial_i] <- 1 }
}

# what percent of family wise error rate?
(val <- count_false |> mean())

## [1] 0.04093

What !?!?! 4.093% !?! It’s a bit lower than expected and we may be wasting 0.907% of our threshold! This is also not good! If there truly is a signal, we may be missing it because we are being too conservative. So, what if we use the O’Brien-Fleming method to set our threshold? Let’s see how that works out.

What’s O’Brien-Fleming Method?

O’Brien-Fleming is a way of setting stopping boundaries for interim analyses, and it’s the most widely used method in clinical trials. The idea is to be very strict early and lenient late. At the first look, when you have little data, you need overwhelming evidence to stop, a z-score of about 2.80 (pval = 0.005110261) with two looks. By the final analysis, the bar drops back to about 1.98 (pval = 0.04770353), barely above the usual 1.96. Because so little alpha is spent early, the trial almost never stops on a fluke, and the final analysis keeps nearly all of its power. Let’s take a look of its family wise error rate like before

count_false <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = trial)

for (trial_i in 1:trial) {
  # for reproducibility
  set.seed(trial_i)
  
  # get sim data
  control <- rbinom(n,1,prob)
  rx <- rbinom(n,1,prob)
  
  # look at when n is 250, and when n is 500
  for (i in 1:length(peek)) {
    m  <- peek[i]
    pA <- mean(rx[1:m])
    pB <- mean(control[1:m])
    p_pool <- (pA + pB) / 2
    se <- sqrt(p_pool * (1 - p_pool) * (2 / m))
    
    # calculate z score
    zscore_vec[i] <- abs(pA - pB) / se
  }
  # record zscore if > O'Brien-Fleming, two looks, notice the zscores are no longer 1.96
  bounds <- c(2.80, 1.98) 
  if (any(zscore_vec > bounds)) {count_false[trial_i] <- 1}
}

# what percent of family wise error?
(val <- count_false |> mean())

## [1] 0.0489

Alright! That’s much better! Closer to the 5%. As I was learning this, I just realized that this is very different from multiplicity because the second look technically is correlated to the first look because it looks at the same data again! The two looks share half their data, so their z-scores have a correlation of √0.5 ≈ 0.71. Bonferroni treats them as if they were barely related, so it over-adjusts. Wow, that totally makes sense now! Ok, now how do we get sample calculation + obrien fleming method with gsDesign? Take note below, the history of obrien-fleming and Lan De Mat

How To Perform It?

Let’s say we want to design a RCT of cefdinir vs cephalexin. Looking at this study, without adjustment, cefdinir had a 23.4% treatment failure compared to cephalexin 12.5%. With 80% power, what sample size, what’s the upper boundary of z score we need if we want 3 looks on our interim analyses?

library(gsDesign)
p1 <- 0.234
p2 <- 0.125

# fixed design: total sample size, both groups together
(n_fix <- nBinomial(p1 = p1, p2 = p2, alpha = 0.025, beta = 0.2))

## [1] 386.8202

Total sample size needed is 386.820172, will have to divide this by 2. Let’s have gsDesign tell us the upper boundary zscore and when to look.

# group sequential: 3 equally spaced looks, O'Brien-Fleming spending
d <- gsDesign(k = 3, test.type = 2, alpha = 0.025, beta = 0.2,
              n.fix = n_fix, sfu = sfLDOF)

sample <- d$n.I / 2           
bound <- d$upper$bound           
pval <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(d$upper$bound))  
(table <- tibble(number_per_group=sample,zscore_needed=bound,p_value=pval))

## # A tibble: 3 × 3
##   number_per_group zscore_needed  p_value
##                           
## 1             65.3          3.71 0.000207
## 2            131.           2.51 0.0120  
## 3            196.           1.99 0.0463

Per group, we will need the above numbers to take a peek. Hooray! Now we kind of understand the surface of the goal and why we need to do this so we don’t inflate our family-wise error rate. Now, let’s try to do this from scratch and see if we can get the same numbers as gsDesign did. Take note that this time we will be using the first simulate DGP with no diff, not the cefdinir study.

How To Do It From Scratch?

So who came up with what? O’Brien and Fleming came first (1979). Their idea: be super strict early when data is thin, and relax at the end. Every boundary is just one number c divided by √t, and you search for the c that keeps the family-wise error at 5%. Simple, but you had to fix when you’d look ahead of time. Then Lan and DeMets came along (1983) and said, “great idea, but what if we can’t stick to the schedule?” So they made the spending function: decide how much of the 5% you’ve used up at any point, and each look only spends its share. Same strict-early shape, but now you can peek whenever you need to. That’s what gsDesign’s sfLDOF does, and why everyone just calls it “O’Brien-Fleming” anyway!

Too many words? Yea, I know how you feel. Let’s break things down and code it to understand it.

Let’s start with the simplest O’Brien-Fleming method. We will simulate 3 looks at n=500, with 100,000 trials first and calculate the zscores for each look.

n <- 500
prob <- 0.5
trial <- 100000
k <- 3
zscore_mat <- matrix(nrow = trial, ncol = k)
gp <- round(n/k)
peek <- c(gp, gp*2, n)

for (trial_i in 1:trial) {
  # for reproducibility
  set.seed(trial_i)
  
  # get sim data
  control <- rbinom(n,1,prob)
  rx <- rbinom(n,1,prob)
  
  # peek at respective k
  for (i in 1:k) {
    m  <- peek[i]
    pA <- mean(rx[1:m])
    pB <- mean(control[1:m])
    p_pool <- (pA + pB) / 2
    se <- sqrt(p_pool * (1 - p_pool) * (2 / m))
    
    # calculate z score, record it
    zscore_mat[trial_i, i] <- abs(pA - pB) / se
  }
}
O’Brien-Fleming Method
  1. Start with final z score, let’s choose 1.96 as a guess and search upwards.
  2. Then back calculate second and first look by dividing by square root of information fraction (t). For example, if we have 3 looks, the first look will be 1/3 of the information, second look will be 2/3 of the information and final look will be 3/3 of the information.
  3. Then calculate the total family wise error rates for each trial and call it alpha_final.
  4. Then look at the simulated data and filter out alpha_final between 0.045 and 0.05, then see what z scores for first and second look.
# obrien fleming
df <- data.frame(zscore_mat) |>
  as_tibble()

final_z_seq <- seq(1.96, 2.5, 0.001)
t2_z_s_seq <- final_z_seq / sqrt(2/3)
t1_z_s_seq <- final_z_seq / sqrt(1/3)

for (i in 1:length(final_z_seq)) {

# record 1 if zscore passes the respective threshold for each look
alpha_final <- df |>
  mutate(crossed = case_when(
    X3 > final_z_seq[i] ~ 1,
    X2 > t2_z_s_seq[i] ~ 1,
    X1 > t1_z_s_seq[i] ~ 1,
    TRUE ~ 0
  )) |>
  pull(crossed) |>
  mean()

if (alpha_final < 0.05 & alpha_final >= 0.045) { print(paste0("total alpha: ", alpha_final ," .found it, it's on ",i, " ", t1_z_s_seq[i], " ", t2_z_s_seq[i], " ",final_z_seq[i])) }
}

## [1] "total alpha: 0.0494499999999998 .found it, it's on 65 3.50567083451941 2.47888361969658 2.024"
## [1] "total alpha: 0.0463299999999999 .found it, it's on 66 3.50740288532698 2.48010836456797 2.025"
## [1] "total alpha: 0.0454099999999999 .found it, it's on 67 3.50913493613455 2.48133310943936 2.026"

Nice! That worked! Alright, now let’s look at the Lan De Mat & Obrien Fleming method. The idea is to calculate the alpha spent at each look and then find the z scores for each look.

Lan De Mat & Obrien Fleming Method

So Lan De Mat introduced spend function, which makes the O’Brien-Fleming method more flexible. The idea is to calculate the alpha spent at each look and then find the z scores for each look. The formula for the spend function is 2 - 2 * pnorm(qnorm(1 - alpha/2) / sqrt(t)). here is the paper that derives it, might be a good blog post next time to learn. For now we’ll take it as is and roll with it. The idea is that it’s the chance a random walk crosses a fixed line by time t (the reflection principle)

  1. Calculate spending for look 1 with the formula. (note the alpha here is 0.025 for one tail). This spending will be in percentage (like p val).
  2. Sort descending of the first look zscore from our simulation data, then remove the spending percentage of the first look, but record the first zscore value (that would be our first z score on first look). Save into a new dataframe. PS: this is like saying, I’m OK with the false positive of these much on first look.
  3. Calculate the spending for look 2 with the formula, the subtract the first look spending.
  4. Sort descending of the second look zscore of the new dataframe, then record the second zscore value, and remove the spending percentage of the second look on the new dataframe.
  5. Calculate the spending for look 3 (which is 0.025), then subtract of the third look spending to second+one (cumulative) look spending, then do the same as above, record zscore and filter out the rest based on spending 3 percentage.

Wow, ok too many words above. Use code to help understand.

# calc spend1 
t <- 1/3                                   
alpha <- 0.025                                 
spend1 <- 2 - 2 * pnorm(qnorm(1 - alpha/2) / sqrt(t))

# filter for those X1 with less than zscore1
df1 <- data.frame(zscore_mat) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  arrange(desc(X1)) |>
  slice(round(spend1*trial*2+1):trial)

zscore1 <- data.frame(zscore_mat) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  arrange(desc(X1)) |>
  slice_head(n = round(spend1*trial*2)) |>
  slice_tail(n = 1) |>
  pull(X1)

# calc spend2
t <- 2/3
spend2_cum <- 2 - 2 * pnorm(qnorm(1 - alpha/2) / sqrt(t))   
spend2 <- spend2_cum - spend1                                

# find how many to look at 
head_num <- round(spend2 * 2 * trial)                                             

# head of however many false positive allowed
zscore2 <- df1 |>
  arrange(desc(X2)) |> 
  slice_head(n = head_num) |>
  slice_tail(n = 1) |>
  pull(X2)

df2 <- df1 |>
  arrange(desc(X2)) |>
  slice((head_num+1):nrow(df1))

# calc spend3
spend3 <- alpha - spend2_cum      
head_num <- round(spend3 * 2 * trial)                

zscore3 <- df2 |>
  arrange(desc(X3)) |>
  slice(head_num) |>
  pull(X3)

zscore1 ; zscore2 ; zscore3

## [1] 3.612396

## [1] 2.480686

## [1] 2.023874

Alright, not too shabby. Looks OK. Let’s use new data to calculate our total family wise error rate.

### check family wise error
count_false <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = trial)

for (trial_i in 1:trial) {
  # for reproducibility
  set.seed(trial_i + trial)
  
  # get sim data
  control <- rbinom(n,1,prob)
  rx <- rbinom(n,1,prob)
  
  # peek at respective k
  for (i in 1:length(peek)) {
    m  <- peek[i]
    pA <- mean(rx[1:m])
    pB <- mean(control[1:m])
    p_pool <- (pA + pB) / 2
    se <- sqrt(p_pool * (1 - p_pool) * (2 / m))
    
    # calculate z score
    zscore_vec[i] <- abs(pA - pB) / se
  }
  # new bounds we found 
  bounds <- c(zscore1, zscore2, zscore3) 
  if (any(zscore_vec > bounds)) {count_false[trial_i] <- 1}
}

# what percent of family wise error?
(val <- count_false |> mean())

## [1] 0.05027

Sweet! Alright, let’s see how the professionals do it?

## gsDesign
d0 <- gsDesign(k = 3, test.type = 2, alpha = 0.025, sfu = sfLDOF)
d0$upper$bound      

## [1] 3.710303 2.511427 1.993048
Comparison

Let’s put them all on a table

look O’Brien-Fleming sim O’Brien-Fleming gsDesign Lan-DeMets sim Lan-DeMets gsDesign 1 3.51 3.47 3.61 3.71 2 2.48 2.45 2.48 2.51 3 2.02 2.00 2.02 1.99

Not bad at all! Our sims land within about 0.1 of the professionals on both methods. The small gaps are from our binary outcome ?maybe. The z-scores come in little jumps, so we can’t hit the boundaries exactly. Also, take note that we got here by brute-force simulation, not the real math. gsDesign uses the multivariate normal distribution with the correlation matrix between looks (remember sqrt(t1/t2)?) to calculate these boundaries exactly. That’s a project for next time!

Opportunities For Improvement
  • Calculate the boundaries exactly with mvtnorm::pmvnorm (no simulation noise)
  • Simulate power under a real effect, not just the null
  • Add a futility boundary (test.type = 4) to stop when it’s clearly going nowhere
  • Look at how stopping early overestimates the effect size
  • Use a continuous outcome to get rid of the binary lumpiness
  • Learn derivation of reflection principle behind the Lan-DeMets formula
Lessons learnt
  • learnt the simple interim analysses
  • learnt basic gsDesign
  • learnt that alpha borrowing in interim analyses is not the same as multiplicity, because the second look is correlated to the first look. Bonferroni treats them as if they were barely related, so it over-adjusts.
  • learnt interim analyses true zscore estimation requires multivariate normal distribution
